en: [Page 1] Ānandāśrama Saṃskṛta Granthāvaliḥ | Book Number 13
The *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya, together with its commentary (*ṭīkā*).
This volume has been edited by the scholars of the Ānandāśrama.
And that was composed by Hari Nārāyaṇa Āpaṭe.
Printed by means of iron type at the Ānandāśrama Press in the city named Puṇya.
Published.
This is the second edition.
Śālivāhana Śaka year 1833.
A.D. 1911 (All rights reserved by royal decree). Price: two and one-quarter rupees (2¼). (242)
The names of those whose manuscript copies of the Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika were collected, along with details of the manuscripts:
The designations are shown as follows:
(ka. thus designated—the *Taittirīyavārtika* with its commentary, [the work] of the residents of Baḍalīgrāma.
Of the illustrious Mārtaṇḍadīkṣitas, born in the lineage of Ve. Śā. Saṃ. Rā. Rā. Cidambaradīkṣita; the date of writing is Śaka 1809.
(kha) Thus designated: the *Taittirīyavārtika* with its commentary, belonging to the venerable Rājarājā Kṛṣṇarāva Bhīmāśaṅkara, surnamed Paṭavardhana, residents of Vaṭodara.
The work marked with the symbol (ga) is the *Taittirīyavārtika* by Nānāśāstrin, known as Draviḍa, Vaidya Śāstri Saṃskṛta Rājakīya, a resident of Karavīrapura.
The work marked with the symbol (ba) is the *Taittirīyavārtika* with commentary by Śrīyu... [the rest of the name is truncated], a resident of Viñcūrapura.

Of those [manuscripts], Rā. Rā. Rāvasāheba and Aṇṇāsāheba—[the latter] dated Śaka 1690 (designated as Ṅa)—and the *Taittirīyavārtika* with commentary belonging to the residents of Puṇyapattana, Śrīyu-...
Of those whose secondary name was Khājagīvāla and whose [primary] name was Tātyāsāheba— [this work],
known as the *Taittirīyavārtikaṭīkā*, [was composed by] the venerable [author] residing in Viṃcūrapura.
Of these [works], [the owners were] Rā. Rā. Rāvasāheba and Aṇṇāsāheba.
The date of writing is Śaka 1633. This concludes the descriptive list of the manuscript copies.
[Page 3] Now, the introduction to the *Vārtika* on the *Bhāṣya* of the *Taittirīyopaniṣad*.
Indeed, it has long been known that two *Vārtikas* composed by the teacher Sureśvara exist here in the land of Bhārata.

[The work] was in circulation. However, until this time, not even a single one of these *Vārtikas* had been published by anyone—whether due to the unavailability of manuscripts containing the entire text along with commentaries on these works which constitute the very essence of Vedānta, or due to a slackening of effort in collecting such manuscripts, or perhaps due to a lack of familiarity with the tasting of the nectar of Vedānta. By such [circumstances...]

Reflecting that works which serve as a cause for the joy of the learned should not remain in the darkness of obscurity, the proprietor of the printing press named Ānandāśrama— the sole cause for the publication of rare and unknown texts—
has brought forth this *Vivaraṇa* on the commentary of the venerable Śaṅkara, which is the very essence of the *Taittirīyaka* and is overflowing with non-dual bliss (*advaitānanda*).
He brought to light the *Vārtika* in the form of a commentary composed by Sureśvarācārya.

Now, who was this Sureśvarācārya? How did he—who had shown such devotion to the Vedānta scriptures—despite being a proponent of ritual action (*karmavādin*), take up the initiation into the fourth stage of life (*turīyāśrama*) and accept discipleship under the venerable Śaṅkarācāryas?

The inquiry titled *Tattva-saṃgraha-pañjikā* is now introduced. Now, once upon a time, the venerable Śaṅkarācāryas set out toward the southern region at the command of the illustrious Vaipāyana (Vyāsa), for the purpose of uprooting the sprouts of pride in those who propound contradictions.
Thereafter, it was Kumārilabhaṭṭa—renowned as Bhaṭṭapāda, who had mastered the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*)—who was first to be conquered.

Reflecting thus in their minds, they went to Prayāga, the king of holy fords. Having rested there on the banks of the Triveṇī, the teachers heard a public rumor that Bhadrabāhu, wishing to remove the great fault incurred through his addiction to the churning of the preceptor, had entered a fire of chaff. Upon hearing that report, the teachers proceeded with haste.

[They] beheld the Kumāra seated amidst a heap of snow. Then Bhaṭṭapāda, seeing his supreme gurus having entered the path of his vision, became delighted in heart and honored them along with his circle of disciples.
Having accepted the hospitality, the venerable ones said this to Kumārila: "O great one, you who have bestowed the path of pure non-duality..."
"I am Ṛśyaśṛṅga; I have come here for the sake of a certain occasion. Upon hearing this, the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda said:

"O sir, I have taken initiation for the purpose of purifying myself from the fault of disrespecting my guru by burning my body in a fire of chaff. If, by abandoning the vows prescribed and intended in the Vedas, I were to become an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy), I would then be censured by the virtuous."

If the Blessed One is the sole cause for illuminating the path of non-duality (advaita), then he must be known to me as one who has returned [to worldly life] under the name Maṇḍanamiśra, renowned on earth by the title Viśvarūpa. He was a great householder, a leader of the assembly of those devoted to sacrifice, a proponent of ritual action (karmavādī), a follower of the Kāṇva recension, residing in the northern regions in the city named Māhiṣmatī.
"He dwells in the city; if he is conquered, the entire world will be conquered. Having spoken thus, that Bhaṭṭapāda gave up his life while gazing upon the form of the illustrious Śaṅkara.
Then, once Bhaṭṭapāda had departed from the mortal world, the venerable Gurus, desiring to conquer Maṇḍana Miśra—
They went to the city of Māhiṣmatī; having arrived there, they saw that the house of Maṇḍanamiśra had its doors closed.

They entered by way of the sky alone. Then, Maṇḍana Miśra, having set out for the performance of the *śrāddha* ceremony, saw that lord of ascetics and, wondering in his mind, "Who could this be who has reached my house even though the door is closed?", asked that best of ascetics with wonder, "Who are you? That king of mendicants [replied] regarding the alms of debate—

"I have come into your presence out of a mistaken notion," he said to him. Then Maṇḍana Miśra also consented to do so. Thereupon, that Lord of Ascetics (Yatīndra), perceiving Maṇḍana Miśra’s eagerness for debate, said to him:
"O sir, if I should be defeated, then I shall renounce my ascetic life and become a householder."
"May I become [one of them]. Then Maṇḍana Miśra, having heard that, spoke with great joy at the mention of the word "becoming":

"O sir, if I should be the one to suffer defeat, then I shall adopt the path of renunciation. As the two of them, having thus made their respective pledges, debated, many days passed. And finally, Śaṅkarācārya—

By these [arguments], Maṇḍana Miśra was defeated. Then, to Maṇḍana Miśra who had thus experienced defeat, Śaṅkarācārya—the caravan leader of those seeking liberation—conferred the initiation of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-dīkṣā*) in accordance with his prior vow. And so it is stated in Mādhava’s *Śaṅkaravijaya*:
While the preceptor Śaṅkara was swiftly performing all the rites for this learned man according to the rules of the *saṃnyāsa-gṛhya*,
he whispered the sentence "That thou art" into his ear.
"Whispering [this] into the ear, one destroys all the sufferings of worldly existence.

From that time forward, Maṇḍana Miśra, having received the name Sureśvara, accepted discipleship under the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya. Then, as the days passed, Sureśvarācārya [approached] his own guru...
Having prostrated, he spoke thus: "O Blessed One, whatever task remains for me to perform, please instruct me therein.
Then, having heard those words, Śaṅkarācārya replied to him: "You must compose a treatise on my Bhāṣya entitled the Vārtika. Having heard the words of his guru, that Sureśvarācārya—

Having said, "Even though I do not possess the power to study your *Śārīrakabhāṣya* along with its reasoning, nevertheless, through your very grace, I shall strive to compose a commentary to the best of my ability," he received the permission of the venerable teacher, saying, "So be it," and having accepted it upon his head, he departed.
Then, after Sureśvara had departed, all the disciples, including Citsukha and others, gathered together and said this to the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, Ācārya Sureśvara has indeed applied his soul to ritual actions from birth.
If such a person as he were to compose a commentary on your Bhāṣya, then undoubtedly everything [would be established]."

"The commentary will be devoted to ritual action (*karma*). Having spoken such various words of censure, this Sureśvara insisted that the composition of a commentary on the [Brahma]sūtras by the venerable [Śaṅkara] must not be undertaken; thus, everyone persistently questioned the venerable commentator. Then, having heard the words of all, the non-dualist...
The venerable masters hold that the highest pleasure consists in this: that all [the disciples] become compliant toward a single task.
Therefore, [page 5] (3)
Having said, "A doubt has arisen even in me," he summoned his own disciple named Sureśvara in secret and spoke thus:

"O Bhikṣu, do not compose a *vārttika* on my *bhāṣya*. These disciples of mine are ill-informed and will not tolerate it. Hearing these words, [Sureśvara], who held the teacher's word as authoritative, [acted accordingly].

Sureśvara spoke with humility to his teachers: "O Blessed Ones, although I previously, while still a householder, composed treatises on logic and other subjects, from this point forward I desire to do nothing at all except serve the lotus feet of your honors. Thus did Sureśvara speak with humility.

Having heard this, the venerable teachers—the best among those in the fourth stage of life, whose darkness of ignorance had been destroyed by the lamp of knowledge—said this to him: "O mendicant, if it is so, then I command you to perform a certain task.
I possess the Taittirīya branch [of the Veda]; at its conclusion is the commentary known as the *Māṣya*."
"I also possess a commentary (nibandha). Therefore, for my sake, let a Vārttika on it be composed by you.
Furthermore, you are a student of the Kāṇva recension; I also possess my own Bhāṣya belonging to the end of that recension.
A Vārttika on that as well must be prepared by you. And so it is stated in Mādhava’s Śaṅkaravijaya:
O disciplined one, what you have said is true; that commentary on the Yajurvedic branch which is established within its conclusion should be composed by you as a *vārttika* for my sake.
His conduct was well-known for having the sole fruit of benefiting others. || 1 ||
Indeed, your Kāṇva recension is likewise mine, and within it lies the Mādhyama section;
its Vārttika as well is intended to be prescribed, for the activity of the virtuous is for the benefit of others. (2)
Thus commanded by his gurus, the lord of mendicants named Sureśvara composed the two *Vārtikas*.

By this same eminent scholar, the ocean of logic, the teacher Sureśvarācārya, in accordance with the command of his gurus, composed the work titled *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*, which takes the form of a refutation of the dualistic school. There are also certain other [works] on the system...

That he composed these foundational texts (*pādakā granthāḥ*) is known precisely from his dialogues with the venerable commentators (*bhagavadbhirmāṣyakāraiḥ*). The *Vārtika* on the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* belonging to the Kāṇva recension will soon be published.
This *Taittirīya Vārtika*, which destroys the root of ignorance and illuminates the knowledge of Brahman, [is intended for] the learned...
May this be an object of affection for the people— such is the prayer of Kāśīnātha, son of Vāmana, whose surname is Lele.
The Taittirīyopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya,
together with the commentary (ṭīkā) composed by Ānandagiri.
Truth, knowledge, infinite, one, stainless, having destroyed darkness, supreme, non-dual, residing in the center of the heart-lotus, the witness of all cognitions,
the object of the realization established by the Vedāntas— [I meditate upon that] as the Inner Self.
Having prostrated with devotion before him, the head of the Vedas, I shall set forth the excellent commentary (*sadvārtika*) for the sake of yogins. || 1 ||
Salutation is offered in three ways to Kṛṣṇa, whose body is existence, consciousness, and bliss, the Supreme Self; and likewise to the Guru, who is identical with Him. || 1 ||
Placing faith and devotion at the forefront, I shall expound, according to my ability and in accordance with the tradition, this commentary on the Taittirīyaka.

Desiring to compose a *Vārttika*— consisting of a critical inquiry into what has been stated, what has been left unstated, and what has been poorly stated— regarding the *Taittirīyaka-śākhā-upaniṣad* and its commentary, the Teacher, for the sake of completing the intended *Vārttika* without obstacles, for its widespread propagation, and for the observance of the conduct of the learned, first recollects the true nature of the subject matter of the scripture and [commences] that...

Having performed the auspicious invocation (maṅgalācaraṇa) in the form of salutation at the outset, and having indicated by implication the necessary set of introductory topics (anubandhajātāni), he makes a formal declaration regarding a portion of his subject matter with the words beginning with "Truth" (satyam). Having bowed down three times with great intensity through devotion and faith toward that very Supreme Self under discussion, [he proceeds from] the Taittirīya, which is the head of the Veda...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "I shall state the *Vārtika*, which is composed of ever-uncontradicted logic and consists of the consideration of ill-spoken [arguments] and the like, regarding the *Yajñopaniṣad*. Although, in reality, there is no such thing as "ill-spoken" because the *Upaniṣad* is clear in meaning, the establishment of this consideration arises from the delusion that there is something ill-spoken; however, what has not been explicitly stated therein is to be supplied by the principle of the "synthesis of qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhāra*).
It can be contemplated; indeed, the contemplation already described is easy to perform.

He introduces the true nature, the state of being pure existence (*sanmātratva*), and the status of being the substrate for all conceptual constructions of the Supreme Self—the referent of the word *tat* under discussion as the object of salutation—by stating "Truth" (*satyam*), because it is the opposite of the unreal. Of that very same [Self], he describes the state of being pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*) because it is the opposite of insentience (*jāḍya*).

He demonstrates its self-luminosity with the word “knowledge” (*jñāna*). He describes its omnipresence and eternity through its being undivided by time and space with the word “infinite” (*ananta*). And in reality... [text fragment]. (Note: The Sanskrit fragments provided appear to be corrupted or non-standard; they have been transcribed as found in the source.)
ka. Primarily; 5 ga gha. The state of being expressed; 6 ga gha. Its establishment.
[Page 7]!
The Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika composed by Sureśvarācārya— [In the Śīkṣādhyāya]
To avoid the fault of partiality (*pariccheda*), he illustrates its freedom from distinction between the similar and the dissimilar (*sajātīya-vijātīya-bheda*) with the word "one" (*ekam*).
He declares its supreme excellence by virtue of being devoid of contact with cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-saṃsparśaśūnyatva*) with the word "destroyed" (*dhvasta*).

He states its freedom from all superimposed particularities (*samāropita-sakala-viśeṣa*) with the word "non-dual" (*advaitam*). [He thus describes] the meaning indicated by the word "That" (*tatpada-lakṣya-artha*).

Having thus introduced the subject, he points out the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (you) with the words "in the heart" (*hṛdi*). "In the heart" refers to the lotus of the heart; the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative, or it is a compound with elision of the case-ending (*aluk*). The meaning is: "that whose abode is precisely in the center of that [lotus]," i.e., the Self residing in the intellect.
Having stated the referent of the term *tvaṃ* as qualified by the collective intellect (*samaṣṭi-buddhi*), he [now speaks] of that very same [Self]...

He states the intended object (*lakṣya-artha*) with the words "niḥśeṣa" (without remainder). Desiring to express the scriptural subject matter—the unity of the word-meanings established through the mutual grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words whose referents are the two aforementioned categories—he says "vedānta" and so forth. [The subject matter] is for the yogins, those renunciants steadfast in knowledge; for them, the...

The construction is as follows: having prostrated before the Supreme Self, who is the object of that realization established in the Vedāntas through statements such as "That thou art"—a realization consisting of the nature [of the thought] "I am Brahman"—I shall speak the Vārttika. And here, since oneness is indicated as the subject matter, the relationship between the object and the subject is implied.

The relationship [between the subject matter and the purpose] is implied. By the words "darkness destroyed" (*dhvastāndhakāram*) and so forth, the fruit—consisting of the cessation of all misfortune and the attainment of supreme bliss—is shown. It should be understood that the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*), desiring that fruit, is thereby established. || 1 ||
He whose fame pervades all directions with rays resembling the light of the entire stainless moon,
who— overcome by compassion— acted for the benefit of those in distress,
and before whose thunderbolt-like speech those of shattered intellect fell in every direction; [to him I bow].
Having bowed with devotion to him, the most worthy of worship, I shall now strive in the method of his commentary. || 2 ||

Accepting that, just like devotion to the deity, devotion to the Guru is also an internal means for knowledge—according to the scriptural teaching, "Whose devotion to the Deity is supreme, as it is to the Deity, so it is to the Guru"—the author, while performing a prostration toward the Guru preceded by the recitation of His distinguished qualities, declares the remaining subject matter to be expounded: "Of whom... (yasya).

By these words [and so forth]: having bowed down with excellence—through devotion and faith—to that Blessed Commentator, who is distinguished by special qualities, most worthy of worship, and our supreme object of veneration; I shall now apply myself—that is, I shall exert effort—in the *nīti*, which is the guidance and analysis, of the *Taittirīyaka-bhāṣya* composed by that very Guru. [Regarding] the ill-spoken...

The connection [of the sentence] is: "I am composing a *vārttika* consisting of a determination of what has been said. First, the consideration of what has been stated and what has not been stated is indeed easily accomplished here; however, the consideration of what has been poorly stated (*durukta*) also appears to be applicable there, given the unsurpassed [authority] of the Teacher.
1. Ga, Gha, Ṅa, Ca: *eketi*. 2. Ma: *ṣayamāha*. 3. Gaṃ, Gha, Ṅa, Ca: *to bo*. 4. Ga, Gha, Ṅa, Ca: *bhivadati*. [page 8]
The first section (*anu-vāka*).
He extols his quality of possessing fame with the words "of whom" (*yasya*). Indeed, this entire universe in its totality belongs to him.

The world is perceived as pervaded by the rays of glory belonging to the Blessed One, the author of the commentary; he distinguishes those very rays of glory by their quality of bringing joy to the entire world with the word "sakala. Of the moon—the "sakala" meaning complete and "amala" meaning free from the touch of impurities such as clouds and mist—those which are the beams (kiraṇāḥ) and rays (raśmayaḥ)...

"By those similar to him"—that is, by those equal to him. It refers to that very author of the Bhāṣya who, having perceived the suffering of the miserable transmigrators, was overcome by compassion; and being thus helpless, seeing no means other than the knowledge of the reality of the Self (ātmatattvajñāna) for their deliverance, he acted as the author of the Bhāṣya and other spiritual treatises (adhyātmagrantha) regarding the means for achieving their welfare, namely the cessation of suffering.

He states that [the truth] is well-known by way of its exposition: "And he who... He mentions another quality [of the Lord], namely that the logicians such as the Vaiśeṣikas and Vaināśikas—who have set out to obstruct the path of right vision—cease their activity solely through the power of the Commentator's words: "Or rather, his speech... His speech is indeed *yadvāṇī*.

The meaning is that those logicians whose intellects were shattered and broken by the *kuliśa*—that is, the *vajra* (thunderbolt)—fell in all directions, having perished. Having bowed with devotion to such a commentator, the construction of the sentence is: "I shall strive according to his method of commentary. || 2 ||
By the grace of my teacher, this commentary on the essence of the Taittirīyaka is being composed by me for those who desire a clear understanding of its meaning. (3)

Thus, under the pretext of paying homage to the successive line of gurus, he stated in two verses that he is composing a *vārttika* on the *Taittirīyopaniṣad* and its commentary; and in this way, demonstrating that his own work is preceded by a traditional lineage (*saṃpradāya*),
he makes it manifest with the words "of the *Taittirīyaka*," etc.— referring to the *Upaniṣad* of the *Taittirīyaka* branch.

And by the grace of the author of the Bhāṣya alone, this commentary called the Vārttika is being composed, which—free from doubt and error—is consistent with uncontradicted logic. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the meaning of the Upaniṣads can be understood through the Bhāṣya, and the meaning of the Bhāṣya can be understood by the very words of that [Upaniṣad] itself, what is the use of this commentary? To address this doubt, [the author] provides a specific...
He states that this commentary is useful for those who desire the meaning clearly: "vispaṣṭā" (clear).

By the word "hi" (for/indeed), it is indicated that because this commentary is composed according to logical reasoning (*nyāya*), it possesses the capacity to reveal the meaning of the Upaniṣad and its Bhāṣya. || 3 ||

The obligatory rites prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, which are the causes for the destruction of evil, as well as the optional rites performed here that yield both seen and unseen fruits, [all went to him].

Objection: Since the Upaniṣads have already had their purpose fulfilled by the ritual section (vidhi-kāṇḍa) alone, and since that purpose is possible through the power of ritual action itself, there is no remaining subject matter; therefore, the undertaking of a separate commentary on the Upaniṣads and its sub-commentary is useless. 1. ga, gha [readings]; 2. ga, gha [end].
[page 9] 4
Having raised this doubt, Sureśvarācārya, relying on the commentary on the *Nityānityādi* section, restates the meaning of the *Karmakāṇḍa*: "duri—" etc.

Those [rites] for which the destruction of accumulated evil (*durita*) is the motive (*hetu*) that impels one to perform them, being something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*), are the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.

Those [works] pertaining to the duties of friendship are established in the first section of the text, the *Brāhmaṇa-kāṇḍa*, which prescribes them; for they do not have liberation as their purpose, since it is understood from the Vedic scripture, "By dharma one dispels evil," that their purpose is the destruction of accumulated sin. And thus [it begins]: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma."

The meaning is that because the *Sūtrakāra* has excluded the investigation of established entities by using the term "dharma," the *Upaniṣads* do not have their purpose already fulfilled by the section on injunctions (*vidhikāṇḍa*). Not only are the duties necessarily to be performed while living already covered in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*), but even those rites based on specific desires, such as the *Citrā* sacrifice, are likewise included.
Rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma, which yield visible results and eightfold results, are established in that very [context];

yet even these do not have liberation as their purpose, because there is no scriptural injunction stating, "Desiring liberation, one should perform this rite," as there is for "desiring heaven" or "desiring cattle. Therefore, the intention is that ritual action has only saṃsāra as its fruit.
He says: "And those which are optional. || 4 ||
Now, this knowledge is introduced, which brings about the awakening to reality as it truly is;
for it alone is capable of uprooting those causes that lead to the appropriation of karma.

Having explained the meaning of the *karmakāṇḍa*, [the author] now demonstrates the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections (*pūrvottarakāṇḍayoḥ saṃgati*) by means of the commentary beginning with "Now" (*idānīm*), while stating the meaning of the *Upaniṣads* which was not investigated therein: "Knowledge" (*vidyā*).

Following the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇaśuddhi*) through meritorious deeds performed either in this life or in previous births, and subsequently, through their maturation, [there arise] discrimination (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and so forth.
Since there are two [sections], and because liberation is desired for the sake of accomplishing that liberation, the knowledge designated by the term *upaniṣad* is now commenced.

And since that [knowledge] is the cause for the manifestation of the reality of the oneness of Brahman and the Self as they truly are, the meaning is that the relationship between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*) is characterized as that of cause and effect. Now, [one might object]: "But how can ritual actions be a cause for the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)?"
One might object: "Since it is well known that even for a seeker (mumukṣu), it is specifically ritual action (*karman*) that is prescribed, why is knowledge (*vidyā*) introduced here?
To this he replies: "Karma... Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), desire and the like are the causes for the performance of ritual action;
knowledge alone is capable of uprooting them, because it is the cause for dispelling ignorance (*avidyā*), which is their root. Therefore, it is knowledge alone [that is required].
The meaning is that she is fit to begin [the instruction] for one who desires liberation. || 5 ||

The Śruti has proclaimed that bondage and liberation have as their sole causes, respectively, desire and the absence of desire, saying: "He is according to his desire," and "He who is without desire. (6)

Intending to express that desire and the rest are the causes for the activity of karma which is the cause of bondage, it is stated by implication that liberation occurs through the cessation of desire and the rest. Regarding that, he states the authoritative proof for bondage through desire and the like, and for liberation through their cessation, with the words: "It is just as... (6).
1 ca. Nivāraṇa.
[Page 10] [First Anuvāka] Accompanied by the commentary of Ānandagiri.

In reality, which is free from duality and is at all times the very nature of the Self, there is misconception due to lack of realization; from that [misconception] comes desire, and from that, ritual actions.

Since desire and the like are effects, they require a cause; thus, [the author] first demonstrates their cause and then reveals how they serve as the cause of bondage by acting as its instigator—beginning with the words "apaviddha" (cast away). The non-recognition of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the sole cause of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*); from that arises desire and so forth, and from those, through the gateway of engagement in auspicious, inauspicious, and mixed actions...
The meaning is the attainment of pleasure and pain. || 7 ||
Since that activity which arises from ignorance would cease upon the knowledge of that [reality], therefore knowledge is sufficient for the pacification of all activities. 8.

The objection that it is incorrect to say that activity proceeds from desire and so forth caused by false knowledge—which itself arises from ignorance regarding one's own Self—because activity is observed even in the case of the wise, is addressed by the statement: "That which [proceeds] from ignorance.
He states the conclusion: since activity caused by knowledge is impossible apart from the persistence of what has been sublated after the arising of knowledge.
Therefore, [it is so]. || 8 ||
One who seeks liberation should not engage in optional or prohibited rites; however,
one should perform obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid transgression.

When it is stated that "liberation results from knowledge," the author raises the doubt of the Mīmāṃsaka—expressed in the Bhāṣya beginning with the words "for one desiring [the fruits of] optional or prohibited acts"—by means of the principle of the oneness and immutability of Truth, using the phrase "one who desires liberation" (mokṣārthī). || 9 ||
Thus, having rejected the claim made by the Mīmāṃsakas and others that ritual action is the means to liberation,
the final determination on this matter is established through reasoning based on the knowledge of the Self.

However, accepting that karma whose fruit has already begun (prārabdhaphala) reaches exhaustion only through the experience of its results, liberation occurs for one who conducts himself as described, even apart from knowledge, because there is no cause for the production of another body.

He states the result [of the preceding argument]: "Thus [the view] of the Mīmāṃsakas [is refuted] by others. He refutes it, saying "In that case," [implying] that upon careful consideration of the reasoning, this position is not tenable. || 10 ||

This cannot be so, for it would be illogical that [all] actions yielding contradictory results could not coexist; for according to the teachings of the scriptures, many such actions are possible for a person. (11)
He clarifies that very point by relying on the commentary beginning with "not so, because of the multiplicity of actions" and so forth: "This is not [the case].

Although one who desires liberation does not intentionally undertake optional (*kāmya*) or forbidden (*niṣiddha*) actions while in the present body, nevertheless—[as indicated by the various readings]:

*Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika)*— [In the Śīkṣādhyāya:
Because it is possible for many accumulated karmas to exist, the absence of a cause for a future body is unestablished.

This is the meaning: all actions, manifested by the common departure [from the body], combine together to produce a single body. To refute the claim that there is no accumulated karma (*saṃcita-karma*) because all karma is exhausted through experience in that state, it is stated "of those yielding contradictory results. This refers to the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites whose fruits are heaven and hell.

The meaning is that since it is impossible for [the fruits of] such acts as the killing of a Brahmin to be experienced within a single body, and since there is no evidence [for their simultaneous fruition], and furthermore because there is no proof that death manifests all karmas simultaneously, it is established that a weak karma remains suppressed by one that is stronger. By means of the strong karma manifested at the time of death, which acts as the primary initiator, [the new body is begun].
Regarding the point that what remains is the state of being weak and obstructed karma which does not initiate action, he states the proof for this: "Because it is seen in the scriptures" (sūtra 11).
There exist here millions of actions whose fruits have not yet begun; let the persistence of such actions be understood through the expression "it exists. (12)
He elucidates the scripture itself by way of restating the opponent's position: "anārabdha... (not commenced). The word "here" (*iha*) is spoken from the perspective of the agent.

The passage beginning with "those here whose conduct has been pleasant" (*tadya iha ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) shows that for those descending from heaven, there is the assumption of a body in the world of humans and so forth due to their good and evil deeds. Therefore, [the new body] does not originate from heaven.
The meaning is that all karma is exhausted by virtue of its nature as such. || 12 ||
Furthermore, the fruits of killing a Brahmin and performing a horse sacrifice do not manifest within a single body,
because they are causes of contradictory results for a deluded person and one of pure sattva-nature respectively.

[Objection: But since the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) have happiness and suffering as their respective fruits, and since the experience of these two can occur within a single body, how can it be said that actions yield contradictory results? To this, he says: "And not... [The meaning is: because it is accepted that the horse-sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin are the causes of the fruits of happiness and suffering in *contradictory bodies*, they consist merely of happiness and suffering [in different births].
The meaning is that the qualification "of those which yield contradictory results" is not inconsistent, because [the former] lacks the status of being a result. || 13 ||
It is heard in the treatises on Dharma that even the effect of a single action here may follow one for seven births; how much more so, then, for many actions?

He refutes the notion that the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) pertains to only a single birth with the words "seven births. The mention of "seven" is made by way of an illustrative statement (*upalakṣaṇa*), because there are scriptural accounts of taking on more than seven births; for instance, from such Smṛti texts as: "The killer of a Brahmin enters the wombs of dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, cows, goats, sheep, deer, birds, Cāṇḍālas, and Pulkasas."

The meaning is as follows: if even a single action initiates multiple births, then it must be stated that various kinds of actions initiate various kinds of bodies. || 14 ||
If it is held that [knowledge] is for the destruction of those obligatory duties whose effects have not yet begun, this is not so;
because it destroys the very evil which is the cause of activity directed toward one's own self. (15)
"Whatever good or evil has been performed here that has not yet begun to bear fruit always brings about the cessation of *karma*;

therefore, even in the absence of knowledge, liberation occurs for the seeker of release upon the fall of the present body"—thus he raises this doubt with the words "anārabdha" (unbegun). In the commentary beginning with "of those having desired and undesired fruits," the mention of "desired" (*iṣṭa*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the commentary beginning "Not so," on the grounds that the Mīmāṃsakas themselves accept that the fruit of the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) is simply the cessation of undesirable consequences caused by their non-performance; therefore, it is not the case that the non-commencement of previously begun good and evil karma ceases through the performance of obligatory rites, nor is there any scriptural mention of sin (*pratyavāya*) arising from their non-performance. || 15 ||
The term "transgression" (pratyavāya) is used to denote the effect of an evil deed;
its destruction occurs through the obligatory rites (nitya), but not through those that bestow desired fruits.

Furthermore, explaining the commentary beginning with "yadi nāma," he states: "pāpasya" (of evil), [meaning] that even when evil karma whose fruit has not yet begun is ceased through the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*), there is no cessation of meritorious karma (*puṇya*) from those [rites], because there is no contradiction between them. || 16 ||
And desire is the cause of action; its destruction is not possible without the realization of the inner Self (pratyagbodha), for it is said that this [destruction] cannot occur otherwise. || 17 ||

Regarding the statement that "one seeking liberation should avoid optional rites (*kāmya-karma*)," he now refutes it with the commentary beginning with "nor by the cause of action" (*na ca karmahetunā*), stating "and desire" (*kāmaśca*). Since desire, which is the cause of action, is an effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*), its cessation is impossible without the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*); therefore, for one whose conduct has been described as above, [knowledge arises]—
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that liberation occurs without [knowledge]; the meaning is that liberation comes from knowledge alone, not from ritual action. || 17 ||
Since the self is the fruit of that [action], every action is prescribed for its sake;
because the self is already attained, there can be no action for the sake of attaining it. (18)

Furthermore, if liberation is not achievable through ritual action (*karman*), it cannot first be something produced, because it is eternal; nor can it be something refined (*saṃskārya*), because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and free from defects (*nirdoṣa*); nor can it be something modified (*vikārya*), because it is immutable (*kūṭastha*); and even its being "attained" is untenable, since it is eternally attained as one's very self (*ātmatvena*). Therefore, he says that ritual action is useless with respect to liberation: [The verse: Since liberation is not something to be produced, nor something to be purified, nor something to be modified, nor something to be attained—because it is eternal, stainless, immutable, and ever-present as the Self—therefore, ritual action is useless for liberation. [The commentary: Moreover, if liberation is not achievable through ritual action, it cannot first be something produced, because it is eternal. Nor can it be something refined, because it is devoid of qualities and free from defects. Nor can it be something modified, because it is immutable. Even its being "attained" is not possible, because it is eternally attained as the nature of the Self. Thus, he states that ritual action is purposeless regarding liberation.
Regarding the phrase "yaddhi": the fruit distinct from the self consists of heaven, cattle, sons, and so forth. || 18 ||

Furthermore, for obligatory rites there is no performance; how then could there be a transgression?
For existence cannot arise from non-existence, since there is no means of valid cognition [to prove it]. (19)

Regarding the statement that obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) are for the purpose of avoiding the transgression (*pratyavāya*) caused by non-performance, he provides the answer through the commentary beginning with "And of the obligatory [rites]": "And of the obligatory... The transgression is future suffering; its cause is not its non-existence (in the form of merit), because it is caused by the performance of what is prohibited.
The meaning is "of suffering. He establishes the impossibility of the arising of existence from non-existence by means of the absence of proof, stating: "Not indeed... (verse 19).
The hundred [strokes] would serve as the indicator for that act of transgression which results in the agent returning to his previously accumulated karmas.

"One who fails to perform prescribed action, performs censurable action, and becomes attached to the objects of the senses, that man incurs downfall"—by this [verse] containing the present participle (*śatṛ*), it is established that even non-performance is a cause for sin;
anticipating this doubt, he says "pūrva... (in the previous verse). The meaning of "tasmāt" (therefore) is: because the production of existence from non-existence is impossible. || 20 ||
Since the non-performance of obligatory rites is characterized by the immediate occurrence of a transgression, the suffix *śatṛ* must be used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
He clarifies the very point already stated by relying on the commentary beginning with "pūrvopacita" (accumulated previously), stating: "nityānām" (of the obligatory rites).
If there were a proper performance of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, then the destruction of accumulated demerit (*durita*) would indeed occur;
however, one who has not performed what was enjoined will become a transgressor (*pratyavāyin*), as is understood from the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭas*).
The meaning is that because the suffix *śatṛ* is established even in other ways, the fact that non-performance is a cause of sin (*pratyavāya*) is not proven by the force of that [suffix]. || 21 ||
If an entity were to arise from non-existence, there would be a contradiction with all means of valid cognition;
therefore, the claim that the self exists effortlessly is utterly trivial.

Now, since the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in both cases by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*, why is it that only the sense of "cause" (*hetutva*) is not accepted there? To this, he explains the commentary beginning with "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth, starting with the word "all":

"All... [etc.]—that is, it is established through perception and other means of knowledge that for every effect which is of the nature of an entity (*bhāvarūpa*), the cause is also of the nature of an entity.

The meaning is that if one were to designate non-existence (*abhāva*) as a cause by means of the suffix *ṛta* (the suffix for the agent), it would contradict all valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In our position, however, there is no contradiction, because the cognition of non-performance serves as the indicator of transgression (*pratyavāya*), and not [transgression] from a known non-performance.
Therefore, he characterizes it as having three marks. 1. Ga. Gha. Mādhyotta 1: 2. From that, he defines it; 3. And in the Atri [tradition], it is said: "He who... 4. Ṅa. Thus.
5. And of those [states], etc. 6. Ga, Ma, Kṣe, Gha: "Because of being that, and because of being that, it is considered to exist."

[Regarding] the arising of demerit (*pratyavāya*): because it would follow that there could be no demerit from [an action] alone, even the non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is a cause for the cognition of absence only when it is itself known. As for the status of the absence of an inhibitor as a cause, however, that is untenable due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).

Intending to show that [the view] is authoritative, he concludes that liberation does not come from practicing as described— because obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) are not performed for the sake of avoiding the demerit (*pratyavāya*) caused by non-performance, but rather have the attainment of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth as their fruit due to the authority of the Śruti— stating "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 22 ||
Since you have stated that "excessive joy shaken off" is the cause of action, that which [you claim] regarding the sense organs is unjust; this is now explained. (23)

In the passage concerning one who desires heaven (*svargakāmavākya*), since liberation—which is unsurpassed bliss—is expressed by the word "heaven," and since ritual action is enjoined as the cause thereof, liberation must be achievable through action; thus, having accepted this second prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated in the Commentary, he refutes it with the verse beginning *nirdhūta*. (23)
Because liberation consists of the nature of immutability, action is not its means;
for if it were the fruit of action, it would be non-eternal, like heaven and other such rewards.
He establishes the impossibility of liberation being the effect of action with the commentary beginning with "nahi" (not so), starting from the words "mukteḥ" (of liberation).

Having stated that because liberation is the very nature of the Self and is eternally immutable, it cannot be accomplished by action, he points out the flaw in the opposing view with the words "svargādivat" (like heaven and so forth). || 24 ||
If it is argued that action devoid of knowledge yields impermanent results, whereas action possessed of knowledge yields eternal results—this is my view. (25)

The proponent of the theory of combination (samuccayavādin) states—via the commentary beginning with "vidyāsahitānām" and so forth—that even though liberation is accomplished through ritual action, it is not impermanent: "anitya... (verse 25).
For one who begins [an action] in this manner, there is a connection with permanence;
nor is knowledge capable of warding off impermanence that has already been attained. (26)

If liberation were to be commenced by action even when accompanied by knowledge, then—by the principle that "what is produced by me is impermanent"—the impermanence of liberation would be unavoidable; therefore, [the author] refutes this with the words "not so" (*naivam*), beginning with "because there is no contradiction. [The opponent might argue: "Let the impermanence be warded off by the power of knowledge acting as an auxiliary."

Suspecting this, he says: "No. First of all, knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not remove the non-eternality of liberation, because it is not its cause. But meditation (*upāsanā*), being unable to even remove the non-eternality of its own fruit, how could it remove the non-eternality of the fruit of ritual action (*karman*)? This is the meaning. || 26 ||

Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[In the Śīkṣādhyāya]: If the fruit of action were also necessarily non-existent like a subsequent negation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), then liberation, being positive in nature (*bhāvātmaka*), would not at all be possible for me. (27)

Regarding the claim that liberation (mokṣa) would be impermanent if it were an effect of action—based on the observation of the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is produced is impermanent"—the author raises an objection concerning the breakdown of that concomitance with the words "pradhvaṃsa" (destruction). [The opponent argues: "Whatever effect is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is impermanent.
Since, according to you, liberation consists of unsurpassed bliss and is therefore of the nature of a positive entity, it must necessarily be something produced, and thus impermanent.
He refutes [the opponent's] notion with the words "bhāva" (existence), etc. || 27 ||
An effect is distinct from its destruction; it is impermanent because it arises through action, like a jar and so forth. Since the subject of the proposition is thus qualified, there is no fault.
This very point—that "whatever is produced while existing is impermanent"—is established by the term "effect" (*kārya*).

Since the reason (*hetu*) of "being an effect" is qualified by its existence within the proposition (*pratijñā*) of "impermanence," it follows that there is no fault of a breakdown in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the proposition and the reason; this is what is stated in the phrase "in the proposition. || 28 ||
From destruction, fragments and so forth would arise, and like a jar or other objects, that [destruction] would be impermanent.
Since it is merely a mental construction, it cannot be produced by actions. || 29 ||
Even though destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is an effect, it was stated [by you] assuming its eternity; however, that very point is unestablished.
Thus he says: "From destruction" (*pradhvaṃsāt*). The meaning is this: from the action of destruction, effects such as shards and so forth arise, and these, like a jar and the like, are non-eternal;
therefore, there is neither the destruction intended by you nor the state of being its effect. What, then, is [the nature of destruction] in your view?

Regarding that, he says "conceptualization" (kalpanā) concerning destructive non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva). Since, in our view, destruction is a mere conceptual construction like a rabbit's horn, it lacks both permanence and impermanence; therefore, this does not constitute a logical deviation (vyabhicāra). This is the meaning. || 29 ||
Through their manifestation and disappearance,
all properties such as jars and the like always exist within the substrate, the clay; they do not reside in non-existence.

Fearing that if destruction were as non-existent as a hare's horn, then because jars and other objects would always exist within their constituent materials such as clay, their non-perception at the time of the production of shards and so forth would not be established, he says: "In manifestation... and so on.
The meaning is that even though an effect such as a jar exists, it is sometimes not perceived because it is obstructed by a contrary effect. || 30 ||

There is no connection of non-existence (abhāva) with either action or quality.
Because it is devoid of self-nature, it is not at all capable of being connected with anything anywhere.

Regarding the opponent's view that the quality of non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is permanence, while that of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is impermanence characterized by the activity of destruction, and that of the other [mutual non-existence] is characterized by the activity of origination—that too is not tenable; thus he says:
"It does not exist. He clarifies this very point: "Because it is devoid of self-nature" (nirātmakatvāt). || 31 ||

Therefore, for the sake of establishing conventional usage, this non-existence such as destruction and so forth should be merely a conceptual construction; it is false, like [the expression] "son of a stone" (*śilāputra*).

He concludes that in the case of non-existence such as destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), since it is devoid of self-nature (*nirātman*), the relationship between property and its substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is difficult to maintain, and thus it is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātratva*). This is the meaning of the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*): for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of the four kinds of non-existence, non-existence is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) and does not exist in reality. || 32 ||
Therefore, upon the cessation of ignorance, there would be abiding in the Self;
and the abandonment of ignorance cannot occur anywhere except through the knowledge of Brahman.

Since liberation, characterized by abiding in the Self alone, cannot be described as resulting from means such as the avoidance of optional or prohibited actions, he concludes that such isolation (*kaivalya*) occurs through knowledge alone upon the cessation of ignorance and its effects:
"Therefore," [verse 33].
Therefore, one should know that the supreme Upaniṣad has been commenced for the sake of knowledge;
it serves to remove ignorance and leads knowledge to its destination within the Self. (34)

Since the cessation of *avidyā*—the cause of transmigratory existence—occurs precisely through the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, the commencement of the *Upaniṣad* is possible for the purpose of attaining that knowledge of the Self; thus he concludes the introduction with the words, "Therefore, [it is] knowledge.
He further qualifies that very knowledge with the words, "That indeed... (34).
Because it completely destroys the fetters of rebirth, such as conception and birth, for those who practice knowledge, it is therefore called an *upaniṣad*.

Intending to show that the well-known application of the word *upaniṣad* to *brahmavidyā* (the knowledge of Brahman) is also proof for the fact that this very knowledge is the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), he explains the commentary beginning with "Upaniṣad" and "knowledge" by saying: "Knowledge.
[It is called] *brahmavidyā* because it loosens the cycle of transmigratory existence along with its causes, or because it is the cause of its ultimate destruction.
The meaning is that she is denoted by the word "Niṣad. || 35 ||

Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[In the Śīkṣādhyāya]:
Having approached or having sat down, that which is the ultimate good from which [it proceeds]...
Therefore, the Upaniṣad is to be known as that which pertains to its meaning, though it is also the name of the text itself. || 36 ||
The absolute good is Brahman; that which has knowledge as its cause, being seated within the self, leads one to realize it within the self by means of this knowledge.
Thus he says, "It approaches," indicating that the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is what is denoted by the word *upaniṣad*.
[An objection is raised: "If the science of Brahman is thus expressed by the word *upaniṣad*, how then is that word applied to the book?"
Regarding that, he says: "But the text... (sūtra 36).
Likewise, the deity presiding over the vital breath and the day is Mitra; here, Brahman is entreated that "may he bring us happiness (śam). (37)

Having thus established that the Upaniṣads and their commentary are to be explained, he begins the word-by-word exposition with the words "of the function of prāṇa" (prāṇavṛtteḥ). Regarding the mantra "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (śaṃ no mitra), by the word *mitra* is meant the deity who is the self presiding over the day and the function of *prāṇa*; and may he be the bringer of happiness to us (*naḥ*), meaning to ourselves—thus [says] the Sūtra.
Brahman, which is of such a nature, is sought by the seeker of liberation; it is apprehended in the sentence through the locative case. || 37 ||
May Varuṇa, who presides over the night and the downward movement of breath, be auspicious to us everywhere; and may the Sun, Aryaman, who resides in the eye, be auspicious to us. (38)

• Regarding the mantra "śaṃ varuṇaḥ," here too, by the word *varuṇa*, the deity who is the presiding self (*abhimānidevatātman*) over the function of the downward breath (*apānavṛtti*) and over the night is denoted. As before, the [mantra] consisting of the *sūtra* [is recited] with the thought: "May he be the bringer of happiness to us."

Intending to express the prayer to Brahman, he says: "Of the night... and so forth. Likewise, in what follows, he states that Brahman alone is the object of the prayer: "...everywhere. Regarding the phrase "May Aryaman be auspicious to us," he explains that Aryaman is the presiding deity of the eye, while Āditya is the presiding deity of the day; thus he says: "And residing in the eye... (38).
May the Lord Indra be in our strength; may Bṛhaspati be in our speech and intellect; and may Viṣṇu of the wide stride—indeed, he whose step is vast—be for our welfare. (39)

Regarding the mantra "May Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us," he says "Bala" [in the commentary], meaning that Indra is the deity presiding over strength, while Bṛhaspati is the deity presiding over speech and the deity presiding over the intellect. Regarding the mantra "May Viṣṇu be auspicious to us," Viṣṇu is the deity presiding over the feet; he says this so that he may be the bringer of happiness to us.
And [the word] "Viṣṇu. He clarifies his quality of wide-striding (urukrama) with the words "vast" (vistīrṇa). || 39 ||

May all the deities of the inner self (adhyātma) and those beginning with Mitra be auspicious to us.
For among those who are happy, there would certainly be a lack of pacification [of suffering]. || 40 ||
He states the summarized meaning of the sentences already explained: "adhyātma... (beginning with "the self").

Anticipating the objection—"Why are the aforementioned deities prayed to by those desiring to know Brahman?"—he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "for in them... as follows: "sukhakṛtsu" (in those who bestow happiness). || 40 ||
In this way, hearing, retention, and application are accomplished;
therefore, one should pray for the absence of obstacles to knowledge. (41)

When those deities who bestow happiness are present, the approach to the feet of the Guru by those seeking liberation (mumukṣus) for the purpose of hearing the Vedānta is accomplished without obstacle; and from that, there follows the ascertainment of the purport of the Vedāntas, which is "hearing" (śravaṇa), the non-forgetting of what has been heard, which is "retention" (dhāraṇa), its application, and its communication to disciples. || 41 ||
For the sake of pacifying obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman, one who desires to know Brahman should perform the acts of salutation and speech directed toward Him who has the form of Vāyu. 42.
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Salutation to Brahman" as follows: "The knowledge of Brahman. (42)
Since all fruits of action are indeed dependent upon Brahman, may there always be power for that Vāyu-Brahman. (43)

One might ask: "Why are the acts of salutation and worship performed toward Brahman in the form of Vāyu, and not toward some other deity for the sake of pacifying obstacles? The meaning is that because [the Veda] is dependent upon the Sūtra and the Brahman, the acts of salutation and worship belong to Him alone and not to anyone else. || 43 ||

Therefore, I shall speak of you alone, for you are perceived directly.

He states the purport of the passage "You alone are Brahman directly perceived" as follows: "Directly perceived. O Vāyu, although you are indirect (parokṣa) in the form of the *sūtra*, you are directly perceived (aparokṣa) in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for the eyes and other senses [perceive] form.

While eating and so forth are mediated [in their cognition] by being inferable from perception and the like, and are thus cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), however, is cognizable by the witness-consciousness without mediation.

Furthermore, because it is in close proximity to the enjoyer, it is intended here as "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*). Since it is well known that the nourishment of the body and other organs results from what is performed by the vital breath, its nature as Brahman is exceedingly manifest; therefore, you yourself are the directly perceived Brahman.

The meaning is that the praise of the deity Vāyu is intended here. He states the purport of the passage "I shall speak of you alone as the perceptible Brahman" with the words "tvāmeva" (you alone). Just as someone desiring an audience with a king, upon encountering a certain doorkeeper, says "You yourself are the king," so too [does one address] the doorkeeper of the Brahman within the heart.

Dependent upon the vital breath (prāṇa), one who desires to know and desires liberation says: "I shall speak of you alone as the directly perceived Brahman," because you are directly apprehended by the witness-consciousness; therefore, "I shall speak of you alone as Brahman. The meaning is that this act of speaking of Brahman is indeed a praise of the deity of the vital breath. || 45 ||

"In accordance with the scriptures and according to what must be done, having firmly resolved it in my mind—that which is truth (ṛta) because it depends upon reality (tattva)—I shall speak. This is the connection [of the verse]. (46)

He states the intended meaning of the phrase "I shall speak the truth" as "according to the scriptures. That which is to be done—the duty characterized by the Agnihotra and other rites—is not to be transgressed; that very action, when determined according to the scriptures to be fit for performance, being well-ascertained and resolved upon, is called "truth" (*ṛta*). And because it is dependent upon that [determination], it is of the nature of that [truth].
The meaning is that, because of this, the statement "I shall speak of you alone" is indeed a praise of the deity. || 46 ||
That very same [truth] abiding in practice is designated as "the truth";
yet, since that too is dependent upon you, I shall indeed speak of it now. (47)
He states another praise: "prayogastham" (situated in performance). That which is being performed as *ṛta* is called *satya*;
since that too has you as its essence, I shall speak of you alone—this is the meaning of the non-redundancy of these two sentences intended for praise. || 47 ||
May the True One, praised by the seeker of knowledge, protect me and my teacher;
may He always protect us both with the power of receiving and imparting knowledge. 48.

Having praised him along with Brahmā, [the author] offers a prayer: "May he protect and guard me, the teacher. When the desire arises as to *in what manner* he should protect, he says: "By means of the acquisition of knowledge," etc. Through the medium of the Vedas and so forth, by the teacher...

The meaning is that the two bodies of both disciple and teacher must be protected in such a way that my capacity as a listener to grasp the true nature of what is taught is not impaired, and likewise so that the teacher’s capacity for speaking remains unobstructed. || 48 ||
The threefold pacification of obstacles to the attainment of knowledge is now declared;
for it is through that [pacification] that both teacher and disciple are able to know Brahman. (49)

For the teacher who intends to impart knowledge, and for the disciple who has set out to acquire it, obstacles are possible: the internal (ādhyātmika) caused by fever and the like; the external (ādhibhautika) caused by tigers, thieves, and so forth, as well as by the eyes, ears, and other senses; and the celestial (ādhidaivika) occasioned by rain, thunder, and similar phenomena.

To ward off the fear of redundancy—namely, that the threefold pacification (*śānti*) is taught for the purpose of avoiding the three kinds of calamities and obstacles (*upasarga-vighna*), since it is only when those obstacles have been pacified that the instruction and reception of knowledge become possible—the author says: "vidyā" (knowledge). || 49 ||
Since the Vedāntas primarily aim at the knowledge of the meaning for the wise, the instruction (Śikṣā) is set forth so that no effortlessness in their recitation may occur. (50)

First, he states the reason for commencing the chapter on training (*śikṣādhyāya*) with the words "knowledge of the meaning" (*arthajñāna*). He raises the objection that since the Vedāntas have as their primary subject matter Brahman and the Self, whereas the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) has ritual action as its primary subject matter, those who act with deliberate intelligence might lack interest in the correct intonation (*svara*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and accents (*udātta*); consequently, the intended meaning might not be established. Anticipating this, he provides the following refutation:
The meaning is that this engagement occurs for the sake of this very purpose. || 50 ||

That by which one is trained and by which the pronunciation of phonemes is directly known is called *śikṣā*; alternatively, it may be understood as "training" (*śikṣā*) in the sense of an object of action. We shall now explain that very subject.
He shows the two-fold etymological derivation of the word *śikṣā* by way of possibility: "it is learned" (*śikṣyate*).

Since the science of phonetics (*lakṣaṇaśāstra*) is established elsewhere, he accepts that here only the derivation as an object (*karman*) is to be understood, and states the meaning of the sentence: "it may be... (51).

The letters beginning with 'a' are the phonemes (varṇa), while the accents such as udātta are the vowels (svara). Short, long, and protracted durations are the measures (mātrā), and effort (prayatna) is known as strength (bala).
