Then, from the thorough understanding of the meaning of the Vedas, she bestows food and drink.

He states the meaning of the verse beginning with "kurvāṇā" (performing) as follows: "kurvāṇām" means both the bringing of garments and the like, and their spreading out. The vocative "deva" (O God) is used in the sense of non-difference from Brahman. The phrase "immediately after the full knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas" is the ellipsis to be supplied. In the absence of that [knowledge], prosperity is likely to lead to misfortune. || 79 ||
"Endowed with hair and joined with sacrificial animals, and [present] at every single time"—this utterance of "svāhā" is stated for the purpose of indicating the end of the mantra. (80)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with *lomaśām* as follows: "Lomaśām. He indicates the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) thus: "Obeisance to Śrī, who is 'hairy' (*lomaśā*) by virtue of being naturally possessed of goats, sheep, and so forth; who always brings—that is, causes to expand—clothes, cows, and food and drink for me. [The word] *prati-*... [end of fragment].
Regarding the word "kam": he states the intention behind the application of the *svāhākāra* [exclamation] with the words "at the end of the mantra" (mantrānte). || 80 ||
In the same way, even further on, the word "svāhā" should occur because it arises from that;
[one achieves] both the otherworldly and the worldly through divine and human wealth.
Since it is capable of performing action, that pair is therefore requested.

In the subsequent mantras as well, the utterance of *svāhā* serves solely to indicate the end of the mantra, because it is possible to indicate the end of a mantra by means of *svāhā* in each respective case; thus he says, "in the same way. Now, for what purpose [is this]?
One who desires liberation seeks both knowledge and wealth; regarding this, he says: "By fate," etc. Divine wealth is knowledge;
human wealth consists of gold and the like. || 81 ||
"May all those who desire to study and hear [the scriptures] come here for my sake. || 82 ||
For the sake of supreme excellence, let the celibate students strive diligently;
let them assemble by the tens of millions and come toward me with all haste. (83)
He states the meaning of "May they come" and so forth: "May they come. || 82 ||

Some recite the two sentences: "May the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) attain excellence, svāhā! May the students of sacred knowledge attain tranquility, svāhā! Regarding their meaning, he says: "For the sake of pre-eminence" (prakṛṣṭyartham). || 83 ||
1. In the versions *ga* and *gha*, [the reading is] *mannānteṣu*. 2. In the versions *ka* and *kha*, [the reading is] *kṛṣṭārthe*. 3. In the version *ka*, [the reading is] *kṛṣṭā*.
1. [End of section].
[Page 28] Third Anuvāka. Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
"May I be among people, and may I have fame"—this is the purpose of the preceding [mantra].
May I be superior to my master and greater than him in terms of qualities.
In the expression *vasīyaso vasyasaḥ*, the elision of the vowel *i* may occur by virtue of Vedic usage. || 84 ||

For what purpose is the arrival of many fellow-students (brahmacārins) requested? To this he says: "May I be among the people. If many fellow-students were to receive knowledge from me, then my fame in the assembly of the learned—
The meaning is that he becomes [so]. He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "śreyān" (more excellent): "vasyaso 'ham" (may I be better than the wealthy one).
In the sense of "vasīyasaḥ" (from the more wealthy one), the elision of the vowel *ī* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). The meaning is: "May I be superior to the more wealthy person. || 84 ||
The suffix *īyasun* may follow either *vasu* or *vasumat*, because it expresses a desired excellence over something of the same class that possesses superior qualities. (85)

Regarding the suffix *īyasun* applied after words such as *vasitṛ* (dweller) or *puruṣavan* (possessing men), he says "the suffix *īyasun*" because it is intended that this suffix follows the word and not the verbal root. He states the reason for this: "because it is desired. This means that excellence is intended in relation to its own class (*sajātīya*) by virtue of possessing superior qualities.

Alternatively, from the two verbal roots *vas* (to dwell) and *vas* (to clothe), the suffix *u* is applied; thus, in the sense of habitual action, *vasuḥ* means "one who is habitually dwelling" or "one who is habitually clothing others. From that which is most excellent as a dweller (*vasīyān*), may I become superior (*syām*). Or, one who possesses wealth (*vasumān*) is indicated by the word *vasu*.
Therefore, the meaning is: "May I become even more excellent than Vasumattara. || 85 ||
O Blessed One, I enter into you, who are the treasury of Brahman;
and do you enter into me with your all-pervading self; be gracious unto me.
May there be oneness between us; destroy the cause of our difference.
Then, within you who possess infinite diversity, I shall wipe away my evil deeds.

He states the purpose of the aforementioned prayer with the words "of Brahman": the meaning is that, since the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) is preeminent, his desired oneness with Brahman—the referent of the syllable *oṃ*—will be accomplished.
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "in that" (*tasmin*) with the word "infinite" (*ananta*): because I am of the nature of Your self, therefore [I am] caused by You...
The meaning is that by that very [act], there shall be the destruction of my evil karma. || 86 || 87 ||
1 ṅa. having bestowed | 2 ga. gha. "yaḥ | dwell in well-built houses for the sake of virtue; and he who...
| 3 kha "in houses for the sake of wealth"; ṅa. "for the sake of virtue, dwell in your own houses.
[page 29]
Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad—[In the Śīkṣādhyāya]:
Just as waters flow swiftly toward the ocean, the abode of Makaras, by way of a downward slope...
In that very same way, let all these celibate students come toward me from every direction. || 88 ||
That day in which [all things] grow old is called the "day-wasting" year;
just as months pass within the self of the year, which is the day-waster. (89)
Regarding what was said, "May the celibate students come to me," he explains the two examples stated in the Śruti with the words beginning "drutam" (quickly), etc. || 88 || 89 ||
In this context, "neighbor" refers to one whose household is nearby;
you are like such a neighbor, for you remove all suffering. (90)
Regarding the phrase "You are the neighbor" (*prativeśo'si*), he explains the meaning of the word "neighbor" (*prativeśa*) with the word "near" (*āsanna*).
He states the meaning of the sentence—"You are the cause for the cessation of all suffering"—by saying "neighbor" (*prativeśa*), just like one who lives in an adjacent house. ||90||
Or, because you enter into every living being, you are celebrated as the "Pervader" (Prativeśa);
therefore, shine forth toward me and swiftly bring about my destruction.

He states another meaning—namely, that you are the "neighbor" (*prativeśa*) because you enter into all living beings like space—with the words "to every living being. He explains the meaning of "measure me" (*māṃ pramihi*) and so forth with the words "toward me" (*māṃ prati*). Since you are omnipresent, therefore "measure me"—that is, reveal your own nature—and "approach me"; this is the meaning. Regarding the subjects at hand:
Since mantras originate from Brahmins, they possess that same nature; therefore, matters such as their *ārṣeya* (lineage of seers) need not be considered. || 91 ||
Thus ends the third section. || 3 ||
Now, the meditation upon the self consisting of the Vyāhṛtis is being described for the sake of attaining the fruit of self-sovereignty; therefore, its greatness is proclaimed. (92)

It has been stated that Brahman is the object of meditation either as being denoted by the syllable *oṃ* or as its symbol. The mantras intended for recitation (*japa*) and those intended for oblation (*homa*) have been explained. Now, the purpose of the subsequent section is stated: it is to describe the meditation upon the lower Brahman, which consists of the *vyāhṛtis*, and which yields specific results. Thus, [the text says] "meditation" (*upāsana*).

Because the meditation on Brahman as having the *vyāhṛtis* as its self is intended here, he says "its greatness" (*mahimā*) to indicate that the praise of such a Brahman is intended by the immediately following sentence. || 92 ||
The three well-known vyāhṛtis—bhūr, bhuvaḥ, and svar—are to be known by men; however, the seer declared that their fourth is "mahaḥ. (93)

Having thus stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he explains the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) with the word "mūri. Regarding the phrase "the vyāhṛtis," the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative;
he states the meaning of the three sentences beginning with "of them" (*tāsām*) as follows: "of them" (*tāsām*). || 93 ||
1 ka. kha. ga. gha. ‘bāyāntu | 2 ga. gha. ‘śagirocya | 3 gha ca paryārthamā | 4 ka bā.na. gha. ‘turthī tu [page 30]
[Fourth Anuvāka] Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:

Because he belongs to the Mahācamasa lineage, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would have the sense of "lineage. Thus, the term *Māhācamasya* directly denotes one who knows the Great [Veda], the Supreme. (94)
He states the meaning of the secondary derivative (taddhita): "In the great cup," etc. (94).
This mention of the names of the seers (ṛṣis) may serve as an ancillary part of the meditation;
for here, meditation is said to be conjoined with the recollection of the lineage of the seers.
He states the purpose of mentioning the names of the sages with the words: "upāsanā" (meditation). || 95 ||
This fourth utterance, which is "Brahman," should be meditated upon as such;
it is to be known as "Great" (mahat), because by means of it one attains the Self.

He states the meaning of the phrase "that is Brahman" with the words "the fourth," etc. He explains that it is called "Brahman" because of its greatness and "Self" (ātman) because of its all-pervasiveness, by saying "because of its greatness. || 96 ||
Because he is all-pervasive, having become the sun, the moon, Brahmā, and food. || 97 ||
The world, the gods, and so forth are pervaded by that Self; thus, there may be "greatness.
And here, the mention of the deities is an elliptical indication for the remaining [categories] as well. (98)
It establishes its all-pervasiveness with the words "āditya" etc. || 97 ||

Because the *vyāhṛtis* are grasped by faith, the Brahman described through their abandonment does not ascend to the intellect. Therefore, having stated that the Brahman known as Hiraṇyagarbha, whose body consists of the *vyāhṛtis*, resides within the heart, one should perceive the principal Brahman in the *mahas*-vyāhṛti due to the commonality of greatness and pervasiveness; and the other *vyāhṛtis* belong to it.

They are conceived as constituent parts beginning with the feet. It has been stated that the injunction for the origination [of this meditation] is: "One should meditate upon Brahman as having the *vyāhṛtis* as its limbs—the first *vyāhṛti* being the feet, the second the arms, and the third the head. Now, regarding the phrase "the other deities are the limbs," he states the intended meaning of the mention of "deities" [as follows]: "The deity... (9).
The worlds, the gods, as well as the Vedas, and the vital breaths as all the limbs—these indeed are to be known as the "great" (maha) aspects of the self that consists of the vyāhṛtis. 99.
He states the established meaning regarding the indication of what remains: "The worlds," [verse 99].
Since all the Ādityas are magnified by means of the Supreme Self,
and because the word "maha" has been thus spoken, the Self should therefore be known as "Mahaḥ."

In the preceding section, the nature of the Self was stated on account of the pervasiveness of the fourth *vyāhṛti*. Now, he states that its nature as the Self is due to its being the cause of the increase of the worlds and so forth: "They are magnified" (*mahīyante*). || 100 ||
1. ka. ṅa. lokā de | 2. ṅa. 'noktaṃ ma' | 3. ga. kalpante | 4. kṣaṇasiddhyartha | 5. gha. dyā yathā pa° | [page 31]
Sureśvarācārya, *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, Chapter on Learning (Śīkṣādhyāya):
"For it is by the Self that all the limbs, including the hands and feet, are magnified in every respect."
Just as the worlds and so forth [are supported], in that same way, they are nourished by the Self, which is like the sun. || 1 ||

He establishes the stated point by means of an illustration with the words "by the self" (*ātmanā*). Just as Devadatta’s feet and other limbs are called "members" (*aṅga*) and his torso is the "body" (*aṅgin*) because it is the cause of the growth of those members, so too the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) is the middle portion of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha, who consists of the worlds and so forth, [and she is the cause] of the worlds and so forth.
The meaning is that it is called "Self" (ātman) because it is the cause of growth by way of its nature as the earth and so forth. || 1 ||
This world, the Ṛgveda, and the vital breath—these are the fourfold [manifestations].
The Vyāhṛti "Bhūḥ" is to be known, and likewise the others in their proper order. (2)
Since the rule for origination has already been stated, [the author] now proceeds with the rules for the specific subsidiaries.
He says:
"This"—namely, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), the wind (*vāyu*), the *sāman*, and the *apāna*—these four are considered the second *vyāhṛti*, "Bhuvaḥ. || 3 ||
"Yauḥ," "Ādityaḥ," "Yajuḥ," and "Vyānaḥ" constitute the fourth;
"Maheśva" was proclaimed of old—these four are of four kinds.
He explains "likewise others" and so forth with the words: "the intermediate space," etc. (3).

In the phrase "and Vyāna," it is understood that the third *vyāhṛti* is intended; likewise, "and Mahas" refers to the fourth *vyāhṛti*. Thus, he says "the fourth also," meaning that just as with the previous *vyāhṛtis*, the fourfold nature is declared here in the passage beginning "as the sun, moon, Brahman, and food. In the manner demonstrated, the four *vyāhṛtis* are fourfold.
He concludes by saying: "There would be four. (4)
The repetition of what has already been stated is intended for the purpose of providing an object of meditation:
"But that man who meditates upon these aforementioned Vyāhṛtis as the Vedas..."
He knows the entirety of Brahman, characterized by the attributes that are about to be described.

By the passage beginning with "This world," it has already been stated that each of the *vyāhṛtis* is fourfold; why then is it stated again? To this he says: "Of those mentioned. The fourfold nature is not stated for the purpose of praising the *vyāhṛtis*, but rather because meditation upon each of them as being fourfold is intended to be mandatory. Thus...
vṛ | 1 ka. sva. *to be understood*; 2 ga. pa. ṅa. *and likewise pu*; 3 ga gha gha. *or else ityā*; 4 ka. [page 32]
The Fifth Anuvāka, accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.

The fact that the Puruṣa consisting of sixteen parts is the object of worship will be established here; the meaning is that the additional statement serves to indicate a specific distinction in the sense. With the intention of explaining the injunction regarding the qualification for the practice, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "He who knows them" as "as previously described. This refers to the prescription of attributes for the meditation on Brahman taught in the section on the Vyāhṛtis. Immediately thereafter—
Intending that it will occur in the Vākya, he specifies it as "to be stated" (vakṣyamāṇa). || 5 ||
If it is asked why the phrase "he knows Brahman" is repeated,
there is no fault, because the intention is to explain the meaning of the subsequent section that is about to be recited.

Regarding the objection that the statement "That is Brahman" is a redundant repetition because Brahman has already been described as the self of the fourth *vyāhṛti*, he says: "Brahman. To show that a single meditation is not intended across the two sections (*anuvāka*), he states:
"To be mentioned," thereby asserting that there is no redundancy due to the restatement of what was previously said. || 6 ||

"He who knows that very one who is within," and so forth—as will be stated in the subsequent section—refers to the reality to be meditated upon; the phrase "he knows it" is repeated here for emphasis.
He elaborates on what was already stated by relying on the Madhyama [method] beginning with "Truth" (satyam): "He who... (sa yaḥ). || 7 ||
Therefore, there is syntactic unity between these two sections (anuvākas).
The worlds and the gods and others bestow upon this worshipper an offering and enjoyment according to their power; this is the fruit for the one who worships.
Therefore, he states the meaning of the commentary beginning with "by the subsequent section to be recited," etc., as follows: "the state of being a single syntactical unit.
This means: because of this unity of meditation. || 8 ||
He states the meaning of the passage "all the gods bring him tribute" with the words "the worlds. This means for the worshiper who has attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). || 9 ||
Thus ends the fourth section (anuvāka). || 4 ||
I have explained the three *vyāhṛtis* as the limbs of that Brahman; now, for the sake of establishing its locations and other attributes, the supreme composition concerning it is being declared. (10)

He states the purport of the subsequent explanatory passage (*uttarānuvākyasya*) with the words "three" (*tisraḥ*). By the phrase "and those," the internal [levels] are shown. By the word "etc. in the expression "the place, etc., of Brahman," which consists of the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), [the qualities (*guṇa*) are indicated].
The path is grasped. || 10 ||

lokādyāsmi | ga. gha. ca. tācetyādyātmi | 5. gha. ṇo vyā [page 33]
Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika: In this chapter, he who was indicated indirectly is now shown directly.
Behold the Self within the space of the inner heart by means of the self.

He explains the meaning of the words, stating that the Brahman which was indicated in the preceding section in an indirect manner is now shown directly within the space of the heart, with the words "That... he. He states the intended meaning of the phrase "In him this person" as follows: "Within... (11).
For that piece of flesh shaped like a lotus is called the heart;
in its center is the space which is always the locus of the intellect.
In that [state], he is to be known as the person consisting of mind (manomaya) here in this world.
He states the meaning of the word "heart" (hṛdaya) with the words "in the lotus," etc. He explains the sentence-meaning of "within," etc., with the words "the ether," etc. || 12 ||
Like Rāhu residing in the moon, it is directly perceived within the mind itself.

Because one thinks with the mind (*manas*), it is for that reason called "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*); or rather, because of the identification with it, it is traditionally taught as being "made of that" (*tanmaya*) based on this indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The verse beginning with "śaśistha" establishes in various ways that his nature is composed of mind (manomayatva), as declared by the Śruti. || 13 ||
"It conceives of the collection of objects"—this is the ellipsis; the meaning is that it is understood by means of that mark, namely, by the mind as its indicative sign (liṅga). || 14 ||
The immortal one is of the nature of non-death; gold is called light (*jyotis*).
This person (*puruṣa*) is to be meditated upon as consisting of that; it is now described as the gateway for attaining that. (15)
Having restated the meaning of the two terms, he states that Brahman is to be meditated upon as consisting of these two qualities with the word "immortal" (*amṛta*).

He explains the purport of the sentence beginning with "without" (*antareṇa*) with the words "in attaining that. The meaning of the word "then" (*atha*) is the immediate succession following the completion of those actions intended for the maintenance of the body. || 15 ||
A single channel, Suṣumnā, extends upward from the heart; having reached the two palates, O wise one, it passes through their middle, containing the Udāna breath.
A piece of flesh hangs from the neck, facing downward;
this is known as the path of Indra, and by means of it, one should proceed through exhalation (recaka).
Therefore, apply this statement regarding the disciple’s journey along the path designated as the "door" and his arrival at that door: "By himself, [he attains] the one Brahman.
[Page 34] (Variants: 1. ca; 2. svenaikaśya bra; 3. ga, gha, ṅa. śābdi)
Fifth Anuvāka, with the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
[The teacher says] "upwards," etc., referring to the *suṣumnā* channel which begins from the heart and is to be meditated upon.
That path for the attainment of the Supreme Brahman is to be understood according to the Yoga scriptures. || 16 ||

And by means of that [practice], the wise lay follower (*upāsaka*), having pierced the piece of flesh situated at the throat—which resembles a breast, is downward-facing, and hangs down—without going into the middle of the two palates, should cause it to move by the power of the exhalation breath-control (*recaka-prāṇāyāma*), filled with the natural wind of death; such is the construction of the sentence. || 17 ||
Having gone by that [path], he who is tranquil shall proceed;
having pierced the two skull-halves of the head, he enters the fire with the utterance "Bhūḥ. || 18 ||
Then, by the second *vyāhṛti*, one becomes firmly established in Vāyu;
by "Suvaḥ," one becomes firmly established in Āditya, the lord of the world.
Having thus remained within the constituent parts, one becomes established in the whole;
and having remained in the Self as the Great, one attains self-sovereignty.

In response to the expectation of "where would it go?", he explains with the words beginning with "where" (*yatra*), using the term *tayā*. The meaning of the word *atha* is immediate succession following the orientation toward the attainment of the fruit. Having pierced the skull and reached the crown of the head, immediately thereafter—
He states that one attains Brahman which exists in the relationship of part and whole through the passage beginning with "Bhūḥ" (18), (19), and (20).
There is no other king here whose king he is; rather, he who is himself his own king is a self-ruler (svarāṭ), and his state is celebrated here as "self-sovereignty" (svārājya).
Regarding the phrase "he attains self-sovereignty" (*svārājyam*), he explains the meaning of the term *svārājya* with the words "none other.
Here, the two terms "worldly transaction" (*vyavahāra*) and "sentence" (*vākya*) are referred to by the words "this" (*iha*) and "here" (*atra*). || 21 ||
One who attends upon [the deity] attains sovereignty over the mind, speech, sight, and also hearing and consciousness; of this there is no doubt.
From such worship as described, this divine fruit shall arise. 22.

He explains the passage beginning with "he attains the lordship of the mind" by stating, "the mind is speech. By explaining that "this arises from that," he concludes the result with the word "from that. || 22 ||
1. [The letter] *ga* and *gha* are situated in the forehead (*paḍa*). 3. Or else, the *saṃga-yaṃtra* is in the hair (*keśa*).
[Page 35] 30 Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika – [In the Śīkṣādhyāya]
Now, for the purpose of fashioning the form of this very Self through the *vyāhṛtis*, the subsequent portion of the text is introduced with the desire to prescribe its meditative worship. (23)
He states the purport of such passages as "Brahman has space for its body" with the words "of the nature of the Vyāhṛtis.
To the question, "Where is the conceptualization of the form of Hiraṇyagarbha employed? he replies: "for meditation" (upāsanā). || 23 ||
This body-less Brahman is indeed like the sky;
it possesses the nature of both the formed and the formless, and arises as the self of the three worlds and so forth. (24)

Having stated the purport (*tātparya*), he explains the meaning of the words: "Viyat" (the ether). This [Brahman] is called "Brahma" because it has space as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); and its similarity to the ether (*viyat*) consists in qualities such as subtlety and all-pervasiveness. He states the meaning of the phrase "satyātman" (whose self is truth) as follows: "mūrtāmūrta... etc. The five elements—both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)—are "truth" (*satya*); that is its self.
That whose intrinsic nature is such is Brahman; the meaning is that its essence is truth. || 24 ||
Delightful to the senses and truly pleasing to the mind, this supreme Brahman is exceedingly enriched by tranquility and is immortal. (25)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "prāṇārāmam" (delighting in the vital breaths) as follows: "indriya... etc. The meaning is that Brahman is *prāṇārāma*—that in which there is delight (*āramaṇam*), or play (*ākrīḍā*), within the vital breaths, that is, the senses—or wherein their delight resides; and that Brahman is likewise *manaānandam*, meaning it is the very source of bliss for the mind. Now, the meaning of the two words *śāntisamṛddham amṛtam*: The meaning of the word *śāntisamṛddham* is that Brahman is fully perfected by peace, being free from all agitation caused by the fluctuations of the mind and the senses. The meaning of the word *amṛtam* is that Brahman is immortal, being eternal and devoid of birth, death, and other such transformations. Thus, the meaning of the entire passage is: "O Gārgi, you should know that Brahman, which is the support of space, is characterized by these qualities. This is the intended sense.
He said: "By means of peace. || 25 ||
"Prācīnayogya, you should worship this [Self] characterized as it has been explained"— thus the teacher Māhācamasya spoke to his pupil. (26)
He shows the teacher’s instruction to the disciple that the other Brahman, characterized as previously described, is to be meditated upon as one's own Self— beginning with the words "prācīna" (26).
Thus ends the fifth section.
Now, for the sake of attaining even more exalted fruits, another meditation upon this [Self] in its fivefold form is described as "the Earth. (27)
He states that the subsequent section begins because the meditation on the very Brahman under discussion, namely Hiraṇyagarbha, must be described in its fivefold form: "pāṅka... (27).
1. *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*: ‘*rbhasya ru*’; 2. *ka*, *kha*: ‘*tmano bha*’; 3. *ca*: ‘*sya vi*’; 4. *ṅa*: ‘*ti | bhu*’;
5. *gha*: ‘*mī*’; 6. *ka*, *kha*, *ga*: ‘*ndaka*; 7. *ka*: ‘*naṃ kartavya*’ [page 36].
Sixth Anuvāka— [With the commentary composed by Āmandagiri].
Since the world was begun by the five [elements], therefore its destruction would likewise occur through them.
"In this way, the sacrifice becomes properly prepared; 'the sacrifice is cooked,' so says the Śruti. || 28 ||

Anticipating the question, "How is Hiraṇyagarbha fivefold? [the author] says, "By the five," explaining that because he is composed of the five elements, Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the self of the world, is fivefold. This being so, for the one whose self is the world...
He states that the status of Hiraṇyagarbha as a sacrifice is also established: "The sacrifice," [verse 28].
Through a sacrifice properly prepared, one attains the Self of the three worlds;
therefore, this supreme Śruti was commenced for the sake of accomplishing the state of the fivefold (pāṅkta).

Since the sacrifice is to be accomplished by means of five factors—the wife, the sacrificer, the son, and the two kinds of wealth (divine and human)—it must be stated that the world is of the nature of the sacrifice. To the question of why the world is thus conceived as the sacrifice, he says: "By the sacrifice. The meaning is that through the meditation on Prajāpati in the form of the sacrifice consisting of the fivefold set, one becomes Prajāpati himself. [This concludes] the meditation on the world as consisting of the fivefold set.

He concludes by stating that because the *nasya* possesses distinguished results, the fivefold nature (*pāṅktatva*) of the world must be explained; thus, the subsequent portion of the text proceeds: "Regarding the fivefold nature... (29).

The group of five consisting of the world-protectors extends to the ends of the quarters; the group of five consisting of deities extends to the ends of the constellations; and the group of five consisting of elemental beings extends to the end of the self, according to the jurisdiction of the Virāṭ-self.

Relying on three statements, he demonstrates the division of the sequence with the words "to the ends of the quarters. To the question "Who is this Self?", he says "the Virāj," explaining that because of the context of the elements (bhūta), the word "Self" refers to the Virāj. || 30 ||
This may be understood as an illustration for both the falling from the world of the deities and the falling from the world of men;
we shall speak of the "objective" (adhibhūta) hereafter, and then follow with the "subjective" (adhyātma).

Regarding the phrase "thus with respect to the elements" (*ityadhibhūtam*), he states the intended meaning of the inclusion of the term "elements" (*bhūta*) as "it is an illustration" (*upalakṣaṇam*).
Regarding the phrase "with respect to the self" (*adhyātmam*), he states the underlying purport as "we shall explain" (*vakṣyāmaḥ*). || 31 ||
That which is cooked by Vāyu ends with Samāna; likewise, the sense organ ends with the skin.
The elements beginning with skin are said to be cooked by the five [elements]; all of this is called the universe. || 32 ||
Relying on three statements, he analyzes the three internal pentads, beginning with: "The wind is fivefold. (32)

Sureśvarācārya’s *Taittirīyopaniṣaddhānyavārtika*—[In the Śīkṣādhyāya,] having perceived that the entire universe is indeed fivefold (*pāṅkta*), the Seer declared: "Indeed, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, this world is fivefold; there is nothing else. (33)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Having prescribed this" (*etad adhividhāya*) as follows: "It is indeed fivefold" (*pāṅktam eva*). Whether it be a seer (*ṛṣi*), the Veda, or someone endowed with the aforementioned vision; the two particles [are used] for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of any other entity. || 33 ||
By means of the internal fire, through the commonality of number, he completely consumed the external fire by means of his own bodily form. (34)
Based on the principle that "one should regard the superior as the inferior," it is intended that one should understand the three internal *pāṅktas* by means of the other three *pāṅktas*.

With this in mind, demonstrating the method of meditation upon the six *pāṅktas*, [the author] states "by means of the internal" (*ādhyātmikena*) to explain the meaning of the phrase "one preserves the *pāṅkta* by means of the *pāṅkta*" itself; [this refers to] the commonality of number.
The state of having five as its number. || 34 ||

Now, the meditation upon the *praṇava*, which is supplementary to all meditations and is sufficient for the attainment of both Brahmas, is being described. (35)

He states the purport of the section beginning with "Oṃ is Brahman" as follows: "All... By the word *upāsanā* (meditation), all scriptural ritual action (*karma*) is indicated; the remainder of the sense is that meditation consists of the realization of the higher and lower Brahman. He provides the reason for this by stating, "It is sufficient," because the Praṇava, when thus meditated upon, is the means for attaining That (Brahman). [The text continues: "The Veda..."

All beneficial rites are set in motion by uttering the syllable *praṇava*; because faith has been captured by that [syllable], the Brahman taught apart from it would not enter the intellect. Therefore, the meaning is that the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of both kinds of Brahman upon this [syllable] is enjoined. || 35 ||
Since it is taught as the designator of both the supreme Brahman and that which is other than it, therefore it alone is designated here. (36)

Furthermore, because the syllable *oṃ* is prescribed as the object for the meditation upon the higher and lower Brahman in passages such as "the higher and the lower," it is stated that by following that precedent, the meditation upon [the syllable] as Brahman is intended here; thus he says: "of the higher... (verse 36).
One should always mentally maintain that the form of the sound "Oṃ" is Brahman for the sake of its praise; for this purpose, the subsequent section is now introduced.

The intended meaning is that the syllable *oṃ* is mentioned here as an object of meditation (*dhyeya*), and not as being subordinate to everything else; having stated this, [the author] said "Oṃ! Just as by means of a peg [the whole house is supported], so everything is joined with "Om";
for without the designation, the thing designated does not exist. || 38 ||

Regarding the question of how the *oṃkāra* is said to be "all" in the statement "Oṃ, this all,"—anticipating the objection that it is so because everything is its effect—the author demonstrates the scriptural authority (*śruti*) and reasoning (*yukti*) for its being all, in sequence, with the words "tadyathā" (just as...). 38.

He states the meaning of "With 'Om', Brahmā gives the impulse" as "he impels. He states the meaning of "The Brāhmaṇa [saying] 'Om'... and so forth as "about to proclaim. || 40 ||
He who seeks the Vedas shall obtain the Vedas. || 41 ||
Whether it be another self or that [very self], he certainly attains it preceded by the syllable *a*;
of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one should worship with "Oṃ."
With what intention does one perform the study of the Veda preceded by the syllable *oṃ*? To this he says: "I shall meditate upon. By the word *brahman*, the Veda is intended. || 41 ||
Having stated another meaning for the word *brahman*, he applies the sentence to that as well: "The Supreme Self. The practitioner is referred to by the pronoun "that" (*parātmā*). || 42 ||

*Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya: [In the *Śīkṣādhyāya*,] since the fruit of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) is attained solely through the aforementioned meditation, it would follow that ritual actions (*karman*) are fruitless; therefore, the subsequent section is intended to establish their efficacy. (43)

He says "yathokte" [as stated above], meaning that since one attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) through meditation alone—as is heard in the scripture—one might suspect the futility of ritual actions; therefore, the subsequent section beginning with "ṛtaṃ ca" is commenced in order to declare their purposefulness. || 43 ||

Svādhyāya is to be understood as study, as well as the supreme act of teaching; likewise, for the sake of one's highest good, the sacred fires should be established according to the scriptures, the Agnihotra sacrifice should be offered, and one should perform the honoring of guests. || 44 ||

Since the meaning of the words *ṛta* and *satya* has already been explained in the first section (*anuvāka*), he now states the meaning of the words *svādhyāya* and *pravacana*: "Self-study" (*svādhyāya*). He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "and the fires" (*agnayaśca*) as follows: "They are to be established" (*ādhātavyāḥ*). || 44 ||
And in that way, human social interaction would undoubtedly come into being. || 45 ||
Regarding the phrase "and human," etc., he explains the meaning of the word "human" with the words "likewise. Worldly social interaction refers to marriage and so forth. || 45 ||

Having procreated worthy offspring and engaged in sexual union according to the seasons, one should establish a household for one's son; let it be understood that this is the true propagation of progeny. (46)

He states the meaning of the two words *prajā* and *prajananam* with the phrase "and that which is to be produced. He shows the intended meaning of the word *prajāti* with the term "establishment" (*niveśanam*). || 46 ||
Even when occupied with the aforementioned duties, he should exert effort specifically toward his own study and teaching; for each of these two, he should remain established as a householder.
He states the purpose of repeatedly studying, reciting, and grasping [the teachings] with the words: "In the cases mentioned... (47).

Since there is no comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas without the private study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya), and likewise not through teaching (pravacana), these two are therefore for the sake of dharma by householders. 48.

He states the reason why self-study (*svādhyāya*) and exposition (*pravacana*) must be performed even when one is occupied with other duties: "because of the meaning of the Veda," etc. Therefore, the implication is that each of these two is to be mentioned separately. "Truth alone must be spoken," thus spoke the sage Satyavacas; "It is indeed so," said the Rāthīta sage. (49)
The son of Puruṣiṣṭha, a man of great asceticism,

The purpose of private recitation (svādhyāya) should also be understood; for the subsequent passage beginning with "I am the purifier of the tree" results in the purification of the intellect. (51)

He states the purport of the Vedic revelation beginning with the mantra "I am the tree" (*ahaṃ vṛkṣasya*) as follows: "And it is for the purpose of private recitation" (*svādhyāyārthaśca*). For in this context, the recitation of the mantra is understood to be for its own sake; since no other application is perceived through direct injunction (*śruti*) or other means—unlike the case of "With *iṣe* [I cut] the branch" (*iṣetvā śākhāmāchinatti*)—nor is there any basis for it being a subordinate element (*aṅga*), as in the case of "Thou art the axle-pin" (*ne cākṣitamasi*).

The meaning is that it is possible to state that this [mantra] has the status of a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*) because the injunction for the ritual action that is the means to knowledge was introduced at the outset.
He states the fruit of the recitation of the mantra: "purity" (verse 51).
Since the arising of right knowledge occurs for one whose mind is purified,
this supreme tradition of mantra has been commenced for this very reason.
He states the purpose of purification: "Purified," [verse 52].
I am the eternal progenitor of this entire universe, which is characterized by destruction; I am the impeller of this tree of worldly existence.
He explains the meaning of the verse "I am the stirrer of the tree" (RV 4.58.1) with the word "I rise up. Here, the word "I" refers to the one who has become Brahman through the mantra. || 53 ||
My fame and renown should be known as elevated like the ridge of a mountain;
that cause is the upward-pointing Brahman, which is pure because it brings about the destruction of worldly existence.
He states the meaning of the verse "Fame like the ridge of a mountain" with the words "Fame," etc. [The meaning of] "with the strainer held above" is as follows:

"Vāja" should be understood as food; it is present in abundance in the sun.
"Sva" is my own supreme Brahman, which I always perceive within this intellect. (56)

He clarifies the state of being pure with the words "the supreme purifier. The construction is: "I am one whose own nature is this Brahman characterized as described above; therefore, I am the one with the sacred grass [pavitra] held upwards. || 55 ||

They say that "draviṇa" means wealth; here, however, it refers to the awakening of the Self.
It shall be resplendent and brilliantly shining, bestowing the fruit of liberation and immortality.
He states the meaning of the word *draviṇa* with the words "draviṇam iti. Therein, he introduces and explains the subsequent term as the reason for it, saying "savarcasam" (57).
It is imperishable because its nature is undecaying; this recitation of the Vedas, however, is the supreme visionary insight of the seer Triśaku, who has become one with Brahman.
Regarding the phrase "sumedhā amṛtokṣitaḥ," since the two words have well-known meanings, they are not intended to be further explained;

He then states the meaning of the passage beginning with "triśaṅkoḥ": "he knew," referring to the seer Triśaṅku who had attained the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*).

The meaning is that this statement is precisely the manifestation of that supreme vision of one's own Self, which is for the sake of realizing Brahman and is characterized by its own inherent experience. || 58 ||
The recitation of this [mantra] is purifying and superior for the birth of the knowledge of Brahman;
therefore, one desiring liberation, being self-restrained and composed, should recite it.
Since the application of karma has already been explained, this meaning is thus determined. || 59 ||

It was stated in this section that "the tradition of mantras (mantrāmnāya) would be Pārtha"; with the intention of explaining further, he restates this, saying "he is purifying" (pāvana). For one who desires liberation and is thus devoted to the rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis,
the Ṛṣi-knowledge and intuitive knowledge that bestow liberation manifest.

He states that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman belongs not only to recitation (*japa*), but to all actions as well: "For one desiring liberation" (*mumukṣoḥ*). For one who is free from attachment to the fruits of Vedic and Smṛti rituals performed for the sake of the Lord, who engages in them with the sole intent of offering them to the Lord, whose intellect is purified, and who looks toward liberation alone—[for such a person], [the result] is according to reality.
The meaning is that it brings forth the knowledge whose fruit is liberation, independently of individual instruction. || 60 ||
Thus ends the ninth section.
The commencement [of the rule] is for the purpose of restriction prior to the arising of self-knowledge; for the Śruti indeed instructs thus: "Having recited the Veda... (Vedam anūcya). 61.

Having recited the Veda, he states the purport of the first section (*anuvāka*) with the words "The commencement" (*ārambhe*). One rule is that before the arising of knowledge—which has the Self as its object and is the means to liberation—one must necessarily and invariably perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. Another rule is that these must be performed even earlier [than that].

The restriction: the meaning is that the commencement [of the study] of the Veda, according to the scriptural text "Having studied the Veda," is for the sake of accomplishing both kinds of that restriction. He states the authority for this restriction—that actions must necessarily be performed prior to knowledge—by saying "and the scripture. This refers to the scriptural text beginning with "They desire to know," etc.; by the word "and" (ca), the [text regarding] *kaṣāya*...
The meaning is that the Smṛti passage beginning with "yapaṅktiḥ karmāṇi" expresses the matter exactly as stated. || 61 ||
These rites to be described hereafter must be performed by one seeking liberation for the sake of the arising of knowledge, until the realization of the Self. (62)
Since liberation is established by itself, following the dawning of self-knowledge and culminating in the ultimate human goal, the ritual section [of the Veda] is purposeless.

Nevertheless, the restriction that ritual actions must be performed even before [the arising of knowledge] is not tenable; for, even after knowledge has arisen, they must be performed as long as one lives, according to the scriptural injunctions (*yāvajjīva*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Knowledge," etc.
(verses 62–63).

Therefore, for the sake of complete purification, those seeking liberation must perform their duties according to the rule even before the realization of Brahman; such indeed is the Śruti.

One might raise the objection that there is a tautology: since actions alone were prescribed as duties in passages such as "Truth" (*ṛtam*) and so forth, and those same actions are also stated as duties in the present scriptural context beginning with "Having studied the Veda" (*vedam anūcya*), he says "on account of futility" (*ānarthakyāt*) to address this.
For, since sovereignty over one's own realm (*svārājya*) is heard to result from meditation (*upāsanā*) alone, one might suspect the actions are purposeless; therefore, [the author] states that...

The meaning is that there is no tautology, because the mantra beginning with "ṛtaṃ ca" is for the purpose of purification (rihāra), whereas the mantra beginning with "vedam anūcya" is for the purpose of establishing two specific observances (niyama). || 65 ||

Whatever statement has been perceived as being free from violence and deceit, the wise who know all dharmas declare that to be truth. (67)
In this regard, he states the meaning of the word "truth" (satya): "as it has been perceived. It is free from violence (hiṃsā) and guile (kalka). Guile (kalka) is a defect of intention. || 67 ||
The wise declare that the performance of the Agnihotra and other rites is dharma;

Sureśvarācārya’s Commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhāṣya [In the Śīkṣādhyāya]:
Indeed, one should give with faith alone, even to those who are vessels of lack of faith. (77)
Prosperity (*śrī*) is one's power; through that, one should give, and one should always give out of a sense of shame (*hrī*).
One should also give out of fear (*bhī*), that is, from dread, and likewise out of conscious friendliness (*saṃvin-maitrī*).

He states the meaning of "it should be given with faith" as "by faith alone. By the use of the word "alone," it is expressed that giving preceded by faith is praiseworthy, whereas one should not give without faith, because the latter is devoid of fruit. || 77 ||

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "one should give out of *śrī*" (prosperity) as follows: "Prosperity" (*śrī*). Out of shame (*hrī*), one feels bashful upon seeing gifts given to those with less wealth than oneself; this is what is meant. Out of fear (*bhī*), such as the fear of kings and so forth, there arises the well-known worldly transaction regarding marriage and the like; this is called "social intercourse through consciousness" (*saṃvin-maitrī*). || 78 ||
If, while one is engaged in the rites prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis,
a doubt or uncertainty should arise regarding one's conduct due to a confusion of the mind;
When that rite has been performed, those Brahmins who possess subtle insight—

Now, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "atha yadi" (if, however) as "evaṃ cet" (if it be so). To the question, "How can there be doubt for one who acts here and there in accordance with the Śruti and Smṛti?", he replies with "mati" (intellect). He explains the meaning of the term "saṃmarśinaḥ" (of the reflective one) as "sūkṣma" (subtle), etc. || 79 ||
Independent, diligent, upright, and free from desire—
just as they conduct themselves there, so should you likewise conduct yourself.

Being appropriate, independence, not being prompted by others, being engaged, being devoted, being non-harsh, being upright, being non-cruel, desiring dharma, and having the unseen goal as one's purpose. || 80 ||
Likewise, one should establish the stated [reason] regarding those whose faults are suspected;
here, "injunction" (ādeśa) is to be understood as a rule (vidhi), and "instruction" (upadeśa) is for the son.

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "Now, regarding those who have been falsely accused" (*athābhyākhyāteṣu*) with the word "tathā" (so). The meaning is: "Just as such persons behave even when they are falsely accused, so too should you behave. He states the meaning of the phrase "this is the instruction" (*eṣa ādeśaḥ*) with the words "the instruction is here" (*ādeśo'tra*). The meaning expressed by the injunctions beginning with "Speak the truth" (*satyaṃ vada*) is the rule (*vidhi*), the instruction (*ādeśa*), which is to be performed.
This is the meaning. He states the meaning of the phrase "this is the instruction" as follows: "The instruction," [verse 81].
This is called the secret of all the Vedas, the Upaniṣad of the Veda;
it is to be known as the instruction of the Lord, the Supreme Self. (82)
He explains that "this is the secret doctrine of the Vedas" by saying "it is a secret. He analyzes that "this is the instruction" by saying "it is an instruction. || 82 ||

Therefore, for this reason, the virtuous who have applied themselves with effort as described should worship [the teacher] and act accordingly; thus one should practice this.
He explains the meaning of the two words "to be worshipped" (*upāsyam*) and "should be worshipped" (*upāsitavyam*) with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).

Since it has been stated thus through the instruction and teaching of the *Ādeśa* and so forth, and because this is declared in the Veda, therefore, by the virtuous who have applied themselves with effort—

That which has been previously mentioned, such as the Truth (satya) and so forth, is to be worshipped; it is to be meditated upon in the intellect as something to be performed. Therefore, the meaning intended by the word "to be worshipped" (upāsya) is that one should act exactly as it has been explained. || 83 ||
Thus ends the tenth Anuvāka. || 10 ||
When hatred arises between a teacher and a disciple due to an improper course of action born of negligence, this [chapter] on peace is taught for the sake of pacifying that enmity. (84)

At the beginning of the *Saṃhitopaniṣad*, a general peace invocation (*śānti*) was recited; now, at its conclusion, since the meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavidyā*) have been taught, he recites the specific peace invocation for them, beginning with "From negligence...
This is intended to bring about mutual harmony between the disciple, who seeks lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*), and the teacher who instructs him.

The meaning is that this peace-chant beginning with "śaṃ no mitraḥ" is recited here for the purpose of pacifying the mutual hatred between those two, which might be suspected to arise from faults committed through negligence, injustice, or transgression. || 84 ||
Since knowledge would bear fruit when the teacher’s internal organ is tranquil,
and because he is non-different from the Lord, therefrom follows this further tranquility.

However, that [meditation] must be abandoned so that it does not lead to the misconception that the self is Brahman; for [the author] will later declare that the self's state of being Brahman is established by its very nature. (186)
Thus the Vārttikas on the Śikṣā are completed.
Regarding the question of what fault there might be even if hatred persists between the teacher and the disciple, he says: "It would be so.

Only when the teacher's mind is gracious does the knowledge taught by him—which has been attained through his favor—become fruitful for the disciple who is free from attachment, aversion, and the like; therefore, the persistence of hatred between the two is improper. This is the meaning.
He states the reason why the disciple must be diligent for the sake of clarifying the teacher’s understanding with the words "of him" (*tasya*).
He explains the purport of the recitation of the *śānti* verses beginning with "May he protect us both together" (*saha nāvavatu*) with the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).
For it is said here, in this intermediate *śānti*, that "he"—namely, that Supreme Brahman—has protected (*avīt*), meaning has guarded, both me, the teacher, and [the student].

It is seen. Therefore, because knowledge concerning the subject matter of saguṇa-vidyā has proceeded so far, this peace (śānti) being further specified will pertain to the subject matter of nirguṇa-vidyā. Even there, it must be understood as possible.

The meaning is that since this collection of afflictions (*upasarga*) has been described, the repetition of "peace" (*śānti*) is purposeful for the sake of its removal. Where, then, is the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇavidyā*) declared?
To this he says: "Of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*). This refers to the Self which is the indicated sense of the term *tvam* (the "thou").

The meaning is that the state of Brahman, which is the indicated sense (*lakṣya*) of that word [“That”] and is eternally established, exists for the purpose of removing the concealment caused by ignorance; for the scripture will later declare, "Therefore, one who knows Brahman... and so forth. Consequently, the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman will occur in both subsequent chapters (*vallī*). || 186 ||
Thus ends the commentary on the *Śikṣāvārtika* of the first Vallī.
The Brahmavallī:
Since desire and the like arise from ignorance, their cessation occurs through knowledge;
therefore, that supreme identity with the One, which devours ignorance, will now be explained. 1.

Having spoken of the knowledge with attributes (saguṇavidyā), he begins to speak of the knowledge without attributes (nirguṇavidyā); under the guise of an obeisance, he summarizes the meaning of the two creepers (vallīs). || 1 ||
Salutations always to that which is not future, not based on tradition, the innermost self, unique, and changeless; that which is neither to be acquired nor abandoned. II.2.

"Not future" means that the reality of the Self—the eternally unchanging (kūṭastha), which is not delimited by the three periods of time, and which is neither to be rejected nor accepted, consisting solely of consciousness—is to be established through these two chapters. The meaning is: "May there be a threefold prostration toward that [Self] with devotion and faith. || 2 ||
Whatever forms of worship are not in conflict with ritual actions from the outset—such as those concerning the *saṃhitā* and so forth—those indeed lead to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). (3)

Having stated the purport of the two *vallīs* under the guise of the salutation (*namaskāra*), one might raise the objection that since the desired liberation is accomplished solely through the previously mentioned forms of worship, there is no need to begin the *Upaniṣad* for the sake of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*). Anticipating this,
[the author] restates the aforementioned meditations and declares that they result only in prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and not in liberation (*mukti*).
"As many as... || 3 ||
And by relying on this much alone, there can be no eradication of delusion—the sole seed of all misfortunes—since it arises from desire and karma. (4)

Anticipating the objection that although the previously mentioned meditations (*upāsanā*) do not have liberation as their fruit when practiced alone, they may have liberation as their fruit when combined with ritual action (*karman*), the author says: "And not... The word "only" (*etāvat*) [refers to] ritual action and meditation...

If a combination [of causes] were accepted,
then by its power, ignorance— which is an independent cause regarding every object— would not exist at all.

The meaning is that since desire and action are the causes that produce that cycle of transmigration, it is logical that the cessation of that [cycle], along with its effects, occurs through knowledge alone, as knowledge is the direct opposite of those causes. || 4 ||
Therefore, for the sake of utterly destroying the root of saṃsāra, self-knowledge, which consists in the awakening to the reality of things as they truly are, will now be correctly expounded. (5)
Since ignorance is removed by knowledge alone, the Upaniṣad must therefore begin for the purpose of providing that knowledge which effects such removal; thus he says: "Therefore," etc. (5).
Through the performance of daily rites and other duties, the person’s inner organ becomes purified;
and, becoming detached from worldly gains, he regards them as no more desirable than the acquisition of a son or other such things in a dream.
Although the Upaniṣad begins with the purpose of knowledge, one might wonder who would be qualified for that knowledge;

therefore, in order to state that the renunciant (saṃnyāsī) who has abandoned all ritual actions possesses such qualification, the author declares that purity of the internal organ and dispassion are the specific qualifications of the seeker—thus [begins verse] 6: "The eternal... etc.
For, having understood through direct perception, scripture, and inference that whatever fruit arises from action is subject to decay, one becomes dispassionate, just as one is toward hell.

Anticipating the objection as to how detachment from pure consciousness is established, [the author] says "perceptible," etc., stating that it is through seeing the impermanence of the fruits of action— either by direct perception in some cases, by inference based on the principle that "whatever is produced is impermanent" in others, or by scripture such as "just as here... in yet others— that the exhaustion of the fruits of action is observed.
The meaning is that, consequently, one becomes dispassionate toward it as if toward hell and other such states. || 7 ||

That which has cast off all defects and effects the rejection of all desires is unattainable [by others], for it is well known that such a state arises solely from the removal of darkness (ignorance).

He states another reason why only the seeker who has renounced (saṃnyāsin) and is endowed with the fourfold means (sādhanacatuṣṭaya) possesses the qualification for the knowledge that is the means to liberation: "apāsta... etc. The meaning is that since liberation is eternally established as being mediated by knowledge, the renunciant who seeks knowledge possesses the qualification for it. And that...
Intending to show that ignorance, designated as "darkness" (tamas), is established through experience itself because it is incapable of being an object of valid cognition, he says:
"By its very well-known nature. (8)
That [means] is not capable of destroying the ignorance that prevents the attainment of That;
therefore, one who has performed the previously mentioned means is the qualified candidate for the knowledge of the Inner Self (pratyag-jñāna).

He states "tadanāpti" (the non-attainment of that) because knowledge is opposed to it, whereas ritual action is not opposed to it; therefore, it is not so.

Since knowledge is the remover of ignorance, whereas action is not, for this very reason he concludes that the renunciant (saṃnyāsī)—who has abandoned action and possesses the previously mentioned qualifications—is the one qualified for knowledge: "The inner self... (9).
Renunciation alone is indeed the supreme means for all to attain liberation;
for it is by renouncing that the knower must realize that supreme state which is inwardly present within the one who has renounced.
"Abandon both dharma and adharma, as well as truth and falsehood;
furthermore, the Taittirīya Śruti declares that Brahman is the 'deposit' (nyāsa). (11)
He shows the conformity with Śruti and Smṛti regarding the eligibility of the renunciant (saṃnyāsin) for knowledge: "Renunciation," etc. (Verses 10–11).
Having understood that all actions, which are subject to decay, must be accomplished until they are entirely exhausted,
one therefore applies oneself to the knowledge of the inner self (pratyag-jñāna) as the means for their renunciation.
He states the meaning realized from both Śruti and Smṛti in the verse beginning with "kṣayiṣu" (in perishable things). || 12 ||
If origination and so forth were to occur through themselves, what would be the purpose of karma?
And if they did not occur through themselves, tell me, what would be the use of karma in this case? (13)

Furthermore, since liberation cannot consist in any one of the four—origination, attainment, modification, or purification—if it were inherently existent, effort would be useless; nor could it be attained if it were inherently non-existent, for then effort would likewise be futile.
Therefore, he states that the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutā*) intended here is the abandonment of karma: "Origination, etc. (Verse 13).
But at the time of its arising and so forth, it depends merely upon a cause;
its dependence on karma is just like that of clay in the production of a jar. (14)
If action were useless in liberation, where would its purposefulness lie? To this he replies: "But in [the stages of] origination and so forth... (14).
That which is eternal does not undergo becoming, nor does that which is eternally existent; for neither of them possesses the state of being produced, just like a sky-flower or space. (15)
He elaborates on what was stated in the verse beginning with "If origination and so forth were from themselves," starting with the word "eternally" (nityam). || 15 ||

The state of being something to be done is not enjoined because the object to be accomplished is already known; nor is it enjoined for the sacrifice itself because it is of the nature of suffering; rather, it is the means that is made known. (16)

Now, an objection: just as the *karmakāṇḍa* possesses authority because it culminates in the injunction of ritual action (*karmaniyoga*), so too the *jñānakāṇḍa* must possess authority because it culminates in the injunction of knowledge (*jñānaniyoga*), since [liberation] is to be accomplished by means of knowledge that is itself produced by such an injunction.

Anticipating the objection that eligibility (*adhikāra*) might be established there [in heaven] by means of action (*karman*), he refutes the example with the words "kartavyatā" (the state of being a duty).
Since the fruit such as heaven is established by one's own experience as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), there is no Vedic injunction (*vaidhī*) regarding its being a duty;
furthermore, because even the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—such as sacrifice—is of the nature of suffering, it cannot be a duty, and thus there is no [eligibility] there either.

It is possible to speak of "that which is to be done" (*kartavyatā*). Therefore, the *karmakāṇḍa* teaches only the fact that sacrifice and so forth are means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*)—a fact previously unknown. Likewise, by the *jñānakāṇḍa*, the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmatva*), which was likewise unknown, is to be taught.
Consequently, since there is no room for *niyoga*—which is synonymous with "that which is to be done"—liberation arises from knowledge alone.
The meaning is that for one who has abandoned ritual action, there is the accomplishment of qualification therein. || 16 ||

"Desire to know that"—this impels one toward the knowledge of Brahman; and the scriptural statement "from whence [all this arises]" is the declaration of the definition of that which is to be known. (17)

Anticipating the objection— namely, that if one does not accept the necessity of an injunction (*niyoga*), what then prompts one toward either action or knowledge?— the author states "desire to know" (*vijijñāsasva*) with the intention that passion (*rāga*) is the prompter. Regarding that knowledge qualified by Brahman, for which the prompting role of passion is intended, what is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of its qualifier, Brahman?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "to be known" (jijñāsya). The meaning is that its *tāṣṭasthala-lakṣaṇa* (definitional characteristic based on its effects) is being the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, while its *svarūpa-lakṣaṇa* (essential characteristic) consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), as stated in the Śruti. || 17 ||

By entering directly into the sheath through the successive abandonment of each preceding one, and by the negation of the agent and other factors, there is indeed the means for the realization of Brahman. (18)
He shows the means for the knowledge of the Brahman as described above with the words "the sheaths" (*kośa*).
By the abandonment of each preceding sheath—beginning with that consisting of food (*annamaya*)—on account of its being an object of perception, its being limited, and so forth;

and by the removal of duality consisting of action, agent, and fruit, there arises the certain realization of the Self as the innermost subject (*pratyak*) within the sheaths composed of cause and effect.
The meaning is that since knowledge of the categories (padārthajñāna) is a means to the knowledge of Brahman, the mind should not be distressed by the contemplation of those means. || 18 ||

Whatever fruit has been imagined by a person whose craving has arisen from ignorance, the restatement of that [fruit] is for the sake of accomplishing infinite fruits and for the purpose of inciting activity. (19)

Having shown the *vallī*, the *yati*, and so forth, and beginning the word-by-word commentary, he states the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the initial mention of the purpose in the verse "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*), starting with the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
[He explains: Although the fruit is one's own self and is eternally attained, due to its concealment by ignorance, the desire arises, "May this be mine."
The purpose of the knowledge of Brahman— which is conceptualized by one who possesses [the means] and desires liberation as something delimited and as an object to be attained—

is restated in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. And this restatement is intended to direct the seeker of liberation toward the knowledge that is the means to that [attainment].

The meaning is that, by means of its function (*vṛtti*), it will lead to the manifestation of the fruit—which is already complete and constitutes one's very nature. || 19 ||
For the actions of an agent, as previously described, do not yield fruits for the self but are intended solely for the sake of the task; therefore, he does not act otherwise.

Anticipating the objection that, even though liberation is restated as a fruit [of knowledge] for the sake of inducing those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) to engage in its means, people might still engage in ritual actions alone because they are well-known as means to human goals (puruṣārtha), he says: "Of the agent," etc.

The "task" (*kārya*) is that which is to be accomplished, the fruit (*phala*); those actions performed for the sake of its attainment are the very means for attaining that fruit—which is not the self of the agent, such as heaven, cattle, or sons—as taught in the ancient *Karmakāṇḍa*. Since the fruit of action is fourfold, [the means] do not lead to liberation, which is of the nature of the Self. Therefore—
Since this is so because it is his defining characteristic, therefore that seeker of liberation does not engage in ritual actions out of attachment.
Rather, on the contrary, he becomes engaged in knowledge through the desire for liberation by means of the renunciation of action; such is the meaning. || 20 ||
Having realized that the fruit is perishable and dependent upon means, one becomes free from thirst;
yet, because desire is not yet extinguished, one seeks what is higher than the highest.

It has been stated that one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), having abandoned actions through the desire for liberation, becomes engaged in knowledge; this is now explained in detail with the words "In perishable things" (*kṣayiṣu*). The fruit achievable by means—whether pertaining to this world or the next—is of a perishable nature.

Having realized that [the self] is perishable, and because detachment has been accomplished through that practice, ignorance— the cause of attachment, aversion, and so forth— is no longer shrouded by karmas alone. Consequently, desiring to attain liberation— which is superior to other fruits of karma and distinct from the phenomenal expansion of cause and effect, and which is characterized as being different from both cause and effect— one seeks, by means of that desire, the means to liberation.
The meaning is that the seeker of liberation becomes averse to the means of knowledge, such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. || 21 ||

The Śruti, which enters into the inner self, declares the statement "He who knows Brahman attains [Brahman]"—a sentence containing both the goal and the means—in order to establish a reality that is the opposite of that [dualistic world]. (22)

He concludes that the formulation of the result at the beginning of the treatise is appropriate with the word "sādhya" (to be accomplished): "The goal is liberation (*kaivalya*), the unsurpassed fruit; the means is knowledge (*jñāna*). Since both of these appear here, this statement—'The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme'—is distinguished by them, and it serves as a *sūtra* because it is not contradicted by the goal and the means."

The construction of the sentence is as follows: for the sake of accomplishing the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Self, the present Śruti—generating a desire for that [isolation] by means of stating the fruit of liberation—enters into it as if delighted and speaks the aforementioned words. || 22 ||

"O child, your crest-lock is growing; drink guḍūcī with faith.
One should urge a child toward the attainment of what is possible and impossible, just as a mother does. (23)
He clarifies with an illustration that the statement of the result in the aphorism is for the sake of inducing activity— namely, "Like a mother":
just as a mother encourages a child to drink medicine by means of mentioning a result desired by the child, so too [does the author].

The meaning is that [the scripture] impels the seeker of liberation who desires to hear, for the sake of accomplishing liberation—which cannot be brought about by any means other than knowledge. || 23 ||
The notion of defects that arises here from the connection between the probandum and the probans shall perish, consumed by the flame of the cognition of their single nature. (24)

Anticipating the objection that liberation would result in being non-eternal because it is admitted to be accomplished by knowledge—even though it is not accomplished by any other means—the author says: "sādhyeti" (regarding what is to be accomplished). Here, the word "iha" refers to liberation.

Since the conventional usage of "means and end" and so forth is created by ignorance, when there arises the knowledge that Brahman—which is neither an end nor a means—is of a single uniform nature, the aforementioned doubt is resolved.
The meaning is that there is a cessation of the notion of "I. || 24 ||
"May there be no suffering for me, and may I always remain in a state of bliss"—this natural desire can only arise when its object actually exists. (25)
However, some do not even accept liberation, and their desire for it is cast far away; regarding this, he says: "Let it not be so. (25)

Even one who does not know the nature of liberation exerts himself for the sake of isolation (kaivalya); how much more so one whose intellect is kindled by what has been said and who is terrified by worldly existence! || 26 ||
Anticipating the objection that the object of the aforementioned desire is not known as liberation, he says: "Though unknown.

The meaning is this: although that object is not known as liberation, it nevertheless serves as the cause for engaging in the knowledge of the Self—which has liberation as its fruit—for one who is detached from saṃsāra due to the aforementioned desire. || 26 ||
Since a motive is necessary everywhere to produce activity, the Śruti says, "The knower of Brahman attains [the Supreme]," in order to entice the person. (27)
He concludes by stating the intended meaning of the very first demonstration of the purpose: "In [the verse beginning with] 'pravṛtti'... (27).

For knowledge and sacred revelation (śruti) likewise declare that [knowledge] is preceded by that.

He clarifies this very point—that activity toward the means arises from hearing about the fruit—by stating: "The declaration of the fruit. To the question, "Why does one engage in hearing and so forth, abandoning other means? he says: "Preceded by that. For knowledge is obtained only through hearing and the rest; since the scripture itself says, "It is to be heard," and so on.
The meaning is that she has stated that the knowledge of the Self is preceded by hearing and the other [stages of practice]. || 28 ||
Whatever activity there may be here, whether worldly or Vedic, it does not occur without a purpose; therefore, that [purpose] alone is the cause of activity.

Although worldly activity is dependent upon a purpose according to the maxim "one does not engage in action without aiming at a purpose," nevertheless, one might suspect that Vedic activity could occur even without a purpose solely by the force of the Veda; anticipating this, he says: "worldly... (verse 29).
"He who knows Brahman knows Brahman"—he thus attains that Supreme.
That Brahman, characterized by truth and other qualities, will now be clearly explained through a Vedic verse. (30)
Having stated the purpose at the beginning of the treatise and explained its purport, he connects the sentence with the words "the knower of Brahman" (brahmavit).
Anticipating the question, "What is that Brahman which is to be known?", he says: "consisting of truth and so forth" (satyādi). || 30 ||

The statement of the result is that one attains the Supreme; thus it is called "attained" (āpta) by those who know its power. By implication, however, the knowledge of Brahman is the means for the attainment of the Supreme. (31)

In that very same scriptural passage, he shows the distinction by stating: "the statement of the fruit. How is it understood that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is the means for attaining the supreme Brahman? To this, he says: "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*).
For if [it were otherwise], the connection—that one who knows Brahman attains the supreme Brahman—would not be established. If [Brahman-knowledge were merely] the knowledge of Brahman...
It would not be a means for attaining Brahman; therefore, the meaning is that its status as a means is not established because the literal sense of the scripture is untenable. || 31 ||
Just as a sacrificer would attain heaven by means of the Agnihotra sacrifice, so should the knower of Brahman achieve the state beyond rebirth through the knowledge of Brahman.
He establishes the point already stated—that the attainment of Brahman results from the knowledge of Brahman—by means of an illustration: "To heaven," etc. (32).

In this context, Brahman alone is to be grasped as the supreme;
that knowledge is not for the sake of attaining anything else, because knowledge of one thing never leads to the attainment of another. 49–50.
Since it has been stated that "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavit param āpnoti*), how can it be said that the attainment of Brahman occurs through the knowledge of Brahman?
To this, he says: "Brahman itself. He states the reason for this: "Because that is knowledge.
He establishes that the knowledge of Brahman does not lead to anything other than Brahman by saying: "For knowledge of another... [in some places].
Furthermore, there is a statement in both the world and the Veda [to this effect]. || 33 ||

It is maintained that attainment is preceded by the distinction of place, time, and so forth; how then can there be such attainment for one who is undivided by place, time, and the like? This is explained as follows:
Even for one who possesses everything, there would be non-attainment, as in the case of the tenth [man], born of delusion.
He projects [the attainment of] Brahman—[as indicated by] the word "teaches. In both cases, the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes the object (*vastu*).

He says, "it is stated," meaning that although the primary attainment of that Brahman is impossible, its metaphorical attainment is possible, and that is what is being explained. Just as in the world, for the tenth boy, because of his being the tenth—

The meaning is that, due to the power of delusion caused by false knowledge, reality—which is in fact complete—is perceived in such a way; because non-attainment occurs through the force of ignorance, its "attainment" is merely a figurative designation upon the cessation of that [ignorance]. || 34 ||
For, due to the delusion "I am" regarding the five bodies composed of food, [one remains bound]. || 35 ||

He clarifies the point stated as "non-attainment due to the power of delusion" with the verse beginning "In the five": the meaning is that within the five—consisting of the effects and causes, namely the *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*—there is a non-attainment of Brahman established through the delusion produced by the error of thinking "I am [this]" in each one. || 35 ||
From this knowledge that "I am the tenth," by way of the destruction of ignorance, there arises the realization of the tenth [Self] through the removal of ignorance regarding Brahman. (36)

Having stated by way of an illustration that "the failure to attain Brahman is due to ignorance," he now demonstrates by means of another illustration that "its attainment is through knowledge": "I am the tenth. (36)
Since Brahman is secondary (gauṇa) when the knower, the object of knowledge, and so forth are distinct, therefore,
for the sake of establishing the primary meaning, that in which the knower, the object of knowledge, and so forth are non-distinct must be accepted.
