Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[Brahmavallī]:

Since Brahman is intended to be primarily expressed as the object to be known, it should therefore be understood as the substantive (*viśeṣya*); whatever is other than that would be the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). (45)
He demonstrates the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified among those [terms] with the words: "by way of being the object of knowledge" (vedyatvena) || 45 ||

Just as people distinguish a lotus by saying "it is blue," "it is large," or "it is fragrant," so too the attributes such as "Being" (sat) and the rest reside in a single substratum, which is the Supreme Greatness.

He establishes that Brahman is the substantive and "truth" and so forth are its qualifiers by means of an illustration—namely, the word "blue. In the expression "the great supreme," the substantive "great" refers to Brahman. || 46 ||

When analyzed in this way by means of [the reasons] such as "being real" and so forth, [the subject] would be refuted by those subjects whose own specific qualities are contradictory [to the reason]. (47)

Having explained the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "evam" (thus). By the word "sva" (self), Brahman is denoted; its specific qualities are truth and so forth. When Brahman is qualified by these, it follows that Brahman is established as being excluded from those things opposed to truth and the rest—namely, the unreal, the insentient, and the finite. This is the meaning. || 47 ||

And this being so, that Brahman which is known through its qualities is determined by others, like a blue lotus and the like; it cannot be otherwise, because [otherwise] there would be no determination. (48)

He states the result of this exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) with the words "And thus" (*evañca*). Just as in such applications as "the blue lotus" or "the red lotus," the lotus is understood to be excluded from other individual instances, so too that which is determined to be excluded from others—such as the non-existent (*asatya*) and so forth—is Brahman. Thus, being characterized by exclusion, it is the one essence of Being and Consciousness (*saccidekatāna*).

The meaning is that if it is known as "complete," yet its exclusion [of other qualities] is not known, then because its distinction from falsehood and so forth would not be established, it would not be known as "much. || 48 ||
Surely an object that is subject to deviation may be qualified by qualifiers;
but if Brahman is not distinct from anything else, tell me, how can it possess the status of being qualified? (49)

Regarding the statement that Brahman is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and "truth" (*satya*) and so forth are its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), an objection is raised with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). That which varies from one individual instance (*vyakti*) to another is accepted as being a qualifier and a substantive; for example, numerous individual instances of lotuses, which vary among themselves, are qualified by attributes such as blue, red, and so on. But [Brahman is not like this].
Thus, because Brahman is non-dual, multiplicity is impossible; therefore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is untenable in respect to Brahman—this is the meaning. || 49 ||

The literal meaning is as follows: a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is well-known in the sphere of linguistic usage as that which, residing in a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) that possesses multiple natures and multiple flavors, is colored by that very [qualificand] and excludes [other things] of the same class and so forth. In the *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya— [in the section on the *Brahmavallī*]—

it must be stated that because both the known and the unknown states of an object are to be addressed, other means of knowledge such as inference (*anumāna*) likewise lack the capacity to prove momentariness, since they are no different in their inability to make known an object that has not yet been known; this is further supported by the scriptural teaching that what is seen does not perish.
The meaning is that because Brahman, whose nature is eternal constancy, is non-momentary, a sentence such as "the Real" (satya) and so forth does not have momentary objects as its referent. || 70 ||
When the jar exists, there is no destruction, nor does destruction have that [jar] as its locus. If it exists, the substratum remains as before; if it is destroyed, it remains as before. (71)

Furthermore, because destruction is difficult to define with respect to an entity, momentariness is untenable; thus, it is not established that the statement beginning with "the Truth" (satya) has as its object the meaning of momentariness. For destruction cannot reside in a jar that is non-existent, because it would be purposeless and because of the absence of a substratum; nor does destruction exist in a jar that is existent, since destruction would then be identical to existence itself.

He says "existent" (*satī*) because it is impossible for that [destruction] to have [the jar] as its locus, since existence and non-existence are contradictory in a single substratum without alternation.

If the jar were admitted to exist even when destruction has occurred—as it did in the state prior to the occurrence of destruction—by virtue of having that [destruction] as its locus, then, just as before, the jar would not have perished; thus, prior to the [actual] destruction...
He says, "If it exists," [meaning] that there would be no distinction between the times before and after regarding the bell. || 71 ||
If you claim that the destruction of the desired [destruction] must occur for a hundred lives, let it be so;
my position is that the jar is indestructible, and that [position] is not at all undermined by this.

Even though destruction has already begun while the jar exists, one might suspect that the jar would be destroyed again upon seeing its own contradictory property—existence—and thus [the author] accepts this, saying "it is desired. He provides the reason for accepting the destruction of destruction by stating "the jar," meaning that there is no loss of the jar's imperishability when the destruction of its destruction is accepted. || 72 ||
Destruction does not kill the destroyer, just as motion does not kill the mover;
how could that which is established only when something else exists obstruct that very thing? (73)

Furthermore, destruction does not cause its own substratum, the jar, to cease to exist. Because it is an action, for an action such as "going" is never observed to cause the cessation of its own agent, the goer; thus he says, "destruction does not. He establishes the absence of destruction's power to cause the cessation of its own substratum with the words, "in which... (verse 73).
Since this statement was previously cited for the purpose of defining [the nature of things], emptiness does not follow as a consequence here, because it relies upon specific qualifications. (74)

Having accepted that the statement beginning with "the truths" (satya) serves as a qualification, it was stated that it does not have the meaning of emptiness (śūnya) nor the meaning of momentariness (kṣaṇika). Now, since it has been stated that this sentence is for the purpose of defining its own nature (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa), it is not [empty].

One might suspect that the meaning of the sentence is either "the state of being real" (satyatva) or "the state of being momentary" (kṣaṇikārthatva); therefore, he says: "for the purpose of definition" (lakṣaṇārtham).

Here, the expression "the meaning of the sentence" refers to the mention of emptiness (śūnyatā), and the mention of emptiness is for the purpose of indicating [both] emptiness and momentariness. || 74 ||

Even if these [attributes] function as qualifiers, their status as defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) with respect to the Self does not follow, because in the absence of a subject to be defined (lakṣya), the purpose of such characteristics— namely, truthfulness and so forth— is not established.

Raising the objection that—just as in the passage "Truth, space, knowledge, quality, infinite, earth," the words such as "truth" are seen to function as qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa), so too should they be here—one says: "Even though they are qualifiers.

Since the relationship of qualifier and qualified does not exist with respect to the inner Brahman (pratyagbrahman) because it is not an object of desire to know, the word "truth" and so forth in that context [must be understood differently].

The meaning is: "precisely for the purpose of defining the essential nature of consciousness. Having raised the doubt—"Even if the sentence has the purpose of providing a definition, why could emptiness itself not be the object defined?"—he says: "If the object defined does not exist" (lakṣye 'sati). || 75 ||
Therefore, because it expresses a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), this statement does not have emptiness as its meaning;
even if it were the qualificand (viśeṣya), it would not be so, because there is no reason for it to abandon its own primary meaning.

He concludes with "Therefore," stating that there is no suspicion that the sentence has emptiness as its meaning, because the sentence serves the purpose of definition, and that which is non-existent cannot be defined simply by virtue of its non-existence. Having accepted that Brahman is defined by "truth" and the other attributes, it was stated that the sentence does not have emptiness as its meaning; now, regarding Brahman’s [nature of] truth and so forth—

He says—“Even though it is the qualified object”—in order to show that even when [the Brahman] is the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), the sentence does not have emptiness as its meaning, because words such as "Real" (*satya*) restrict the meaning of the qualified object without abandoning their own respective meanings. || 76 ||
If its own referent does not exist, then [a term] such as "real" (satya) cannot function as a qualifier for the meaning of the qualificand;
the capacity to qualify a restricted object is only possible when its own referent exists. (77)

He establishes, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), that a word such as "truth" (satya), when restricted to its own primary meaning, serves to determine the meaning of the substantive (viśeṣya); this is stated in the verse beginning with "svārthe'sti. || 77 ||
In this context, the word "Brahman" possesses its own intrinsic meaning as well as other [qualifications];
therein, "infinite" (ananta) is a qualification precisely by way of excluding finite things. (78)
The two remaining [words] are qualifiers by means of the very channel of surrendering their own meaning;
the abandonment of meanings incompatible with that occurs through implication (sāmarthya), not through the word itself. (79)

Furthermore, in this sentence, the word *brahman* is seen to be meaningful as denoting a vast reality when used together with words such as *satya* (truth), which convey its ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) and other attributes; therefore, how could the sentence [convey] emptiness (*śūnyatva*)? Or rather, [how could it convey] the state of being void?

If Brahman is made known as something distinct from the nature of consciousness, then tell me, by what can the resulting confusion—where it becomes accessible through a mandatory injunction (niyoga)—be prevented? (81)

Having raised the objection that the identity of meaning between the words *brahman* and *ātman* is not established—since the Śruti passage beginning with "That which dwells within the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*) teaches the Supreme Brahman as distinct from the individual self (*vijñānātman*)—it is replied:

if the Veda, which is accessible through scripture, is accepted as the authoritative means of knowledge regarding what is to be enjoined and what is to be avoided, then it is impossible to preclude its authority; therefore, [the distinction taught therein] is merely an illusion.
He states that because it is a restatement of what is already established, the meaning of the scripture must be precisely their identity: "The self of consciousness," etc. (81).
If this suffering self were not inherently powerful, what difference would its necessity or lack of necessity make? (82)

Anticipating the objection that even if the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is known through scripture, it may nevertheless be removed—either by the force of an injunction such as "one should fix the mind [on the thought] 'That thou art'" (*tat tvam asi*), or by the power of such a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—the author says:
"If not" (*na cet*). If the identity of the self with Brahman were not innate, then that [identity] would not be the object of such an injunction.

The meaning is that it is not possible to produce coldness in fire by any other means; likewise, the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman cannot be removed by injunctions (niyoga) and the like, because it is admitted that this difference is to be known through the scriptures (śāstra). || 82 ||

If one perceives the inner self, having cast aside all other objects,
and possesses the knowledge "I am Brahman," how could that be anything other than the supreme [knowledge] derived from the scriptures? (61, 83)

behold the pure Self, which is the innermost essence of the group of non-self elements discarded by such scriptural statements as "Not this, not this," "neither gross nor subtle," and so forth; behold that [Self] which, according to the scripture "That thou art, this Self is Brahman," is...

The meaning is that if the realization "I am Brahman" were to arise in the self as a result of [the attributes] being fully endowed [with it], then the Supreme Brahman would not be other than the self, or the syllable Om would not be other than Brahman; for the statement beginning with "He who [is] in the self," etc., would otherwise have a different purport, and it would be impossible for it to possess authority when in conflict with the primary statement. || 83 ||

and therefore their identity cannot be established due to their mutual contradiction— to this he replies with the words "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*).

If the attributes of Brahman, such as non-grossness and so forth, are accepted as belonging to something other than the Self— which is the referent of the word "thou" (*tvam*)— then those [attributes] of non-grossness...

Conversely, if non-stoutness and the rest do qualify the Self, then the cognition of a difference between the attributes of the Self and Brahman will be removed, and the identity of the Self and Brahman will be established.
The meaning is that because there is no difference in moments and because there is an absence of contradictory properties, there is no suspicion of difference. || 84 ||

If you accept that the self alone is the supreme Brahman, then because the self is the agent of knowledge, knowledge would have the agent as its instrumental cause. (86)

When it is stated that "Brahman is infinite," the identity of Brahman and the Self is asserted for the purpose of supporting that infinity; accepting this, the opponent objects with the words "the Self alone. On the view of identity, regarding the statement "knowledge is Brahman," the word "knowledge" (jñāna) is derived as "that which knows" (jānāti iti jñānam). Since the word "knowledge" is thus an agentive derivation (*kartṛ-sādhana*), and since the Self is its agent, it follows that the Self, as the agent of knowledge, is what is meant by the statement "Brahman is knowledge. Thus, [the opponent] argues that the Self is Brahman.

If the meaning of the verbal root were [the self], it would follow that the self is dependent and impermanent;

He reveals that the term *jñāna* functions as an agent (*kartṛ-sādhana*) by demonstrating the fault in its being a process (*bhāva-sādhana*) through the words "dependence" (*pāratantryam*). If the word *jñāna* is said to denote the act of knowing (*jñāna-kriyā*), then because knowledge is dependent and non-eternal, Brahman would also be non-eternal due to its identity with that [knowledge], based on the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed as "Brahman is knowledge. Thus, there would follow [the consequence of] non-eternality and so forth.

The meaning is that, by way of incidental discussion, the word "knowledge" (jñāna) functions as a term denoting the agent. He states that the self must be accepted as an agent because of its similarity to the science of logic (tarka-śāstra)—thus [he says] "tarka... || 87 ||
Raising their arms high, those who are skilled in such talk say:

He concludes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— that the Self alone is the agent of knowledge and that there is no Brahman other than it— with the words "aloud" (*uccaiḥ*).
Having accepted that knowledge is an effect, he now weakens the objection regarding the agency of the Self.
Regarding the phrase "as has been stated": since it is impossible for knowledge to be an effect, one asks—"Why?"—to address how there can be a perception of its being an effect. || 88 ||
Although there is no deviation from its own nature, it is called an "effect" by way of metaphor;
here, effects that depend upon the intellect are conceptualized through a lack of discrimination. (89)

He provides the answer—stating that although knowledge, which is synonymous with consciousness (*saṃvedana*), is non-different from the nature of the Self, its status as an effect is merely figurative—by saying "svarūpa" (its own nature). He clarifies the figurative nature of its being an effect by saying "buddhi" (intellect):

for in this case, due to the non-discrimination between consciousness and the modifications of the intellect, the effects such as birth and destruction, which actually belong to the intellect, are [superimposed] upon it.

In reality, however, modifications such as birth and so forth do not exist therein; therefore, the meaning is that the state of being an effect is merely superimposed upon the immutable consciousness. || 89 ||

Knowledge is the very nature of the Self; it is not distinct from it.
The capacity of the intellect to produce cognitions is metaphorically attributed to its witness. (90)

Having stated that the self possesses the status of an agent with respect to its own knowledge, he refutes that by saying "the essential nature" (svarūpam). Since the intellect (dhī) produces mental modifications (vṛtti) that are pervaded by the consciousness of the Self,
all of them are embraced by consciousness, like sparks from heated iron.
He explains what was stated— that the immutable self, which is self-cognizing, assumes the state of being an effect through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the modifications of the intellect—
with the words "The self," etc. Just as sparks from heated iron are seen to have the form of fire,

The meaning is that since you bring about [the world] pervaded by those [mental states], consciousness, conditioned by the modifications of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), appears as an effect. || 91 ||

Seeing that the cognitions produced by the intellect are inlaid with consciousness, the ignorant imagine that even the immutable Self performs the act of knowing, thinking, "Knowledge is being produced. (92)

He establishes that the self-consciousness (ātmacaitanya), which appears as the agent due to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the functioning internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), by means of the verse beginning with "caitanya" (92).
Since the manifestation and disappearance of the intellect of human beings have [the Self] as their witness, on what other basis could the status of being a witness and an agent be predicated? (93)
It has been stated that the intellect's capacity for causal agency is metaphorically attributed to its witness; this is now elaborated upon in the verse beginning with "āvirbhāva" (93).
Just as that nature was previously unconditioned by the states of the intellect, so too, even upon the arising of the intellect, let it be experienced as indeed changeless. (94)

He states that when the agency and the state of being an object of action are superimposed upon the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidātman*), its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*) results; thus he says: "Intellect," etc. For just as previously, before the arising of the intellect as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the Self remains in a single uniform state—unconditioned by that [adjunct] and establishing the very absence of the intellect—so too, upon the arising of the intellect, it remains in that same state.

Consciousness must be accepted as being of one and the same form even when there is the presence or absence of mental states (buddhi), because it is impossible to demonstrate any distinction within the witnessing consciousness that serves as their prover.
Therefore, consciousness must be accepted as absolutely immutable (kūṭastha) on the strength of direct experience, since it is the prover of all activities; this is the meaning. || 94 ||

Anticipating the objection that Brahman is not immutable (*kūṭastha*) because it is an object of verbal expression—just like a jar or other objects—the author says: "But [the opposite]" (*tu*). Since Brahman is the illuminator by virtue of being the witness (*sākṣin*) of the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the agent and the object, words such as "Being" (*satya*) and so forth, which denote the agent and the rest, indirectly indicate (*lakṣayanti*) the supreme Brahman; they are not, however, capable of expressing it directly.

The meaning is that, since the grounds for the application of words—such as universals (jāti) and so forth—do not exist in Brahman, the status of being denotable (vācyatva) is therefore unestablished in Brahman. || 95 ||
That knowledge of Brahman which is non-different from all things and changeless is not distinct from Brahman itself, because it is fully realized through the direct perception of everything.
He clarifies the application of the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) to Brahman through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with the words: "But that which...
That which is the knowledge of Brahman is its consciousness (*caitanya*); nor is it distinct from Brahman because of the use of the genitive case, for it is non-different from Brahman.
Were there a separation from knowledge, Brahman would be insentient, and the consequence would be that it would not be Brahman; and that [Brahman] is—

Knowledge is essentially non-different from all things; it is the non-dual Brahman because it is non-different from everything. Therefore, it is changeless due to the absence of any cause for change, and it exists everywhere as the inner self (*pratyak*), since it is fully realized as the Self in each instance.
Consequently, the word "knowledge" applies to Brahman only by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because genus and other such categories are impossible there. This is the meaning. || 96 ||
By the word "truth" (satya), which denotes the reality that excludes all distinctions of a self,
that [ultimate nature] is indicated in that very way, but it is not directly expressed.
It also indicates that the word "satya" (truth) applies to Brahman only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), by stating "is rejected.
This refers to that ultimate reality in which the entire category of unreal things— the various non-self (*anātman*)— has been discarded.

The meaning is that even by the word "truth" (satya), Brahman is indicated just as it is by the word "knowledge" (jñāna); however, it cannot be expressed by that [word], because the absence of a [suitable] causal basis (nimitta) is equal in both cases. || 97 ||

Thus, words such as "truth" (satya) and the like, without abandoning their own primary meanings, indicate another [meaning] by way of the cessation of contradictory objects through the removal of ignorance. (98)

He states that terms such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) and so forth also denote Brahman solely through the secondary function of words (*lakṣaṇā*), just like the terms "truth" (*satya*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*):

"In this way," etc. Indeed, all these words, without abandoning their own primary meanings—namely, that this very object [Brahman] is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), knowledge, bliss, and fullness—[serve to denote it] while [simultaneously] negating the ignorance that is the cause for the perception of contradictory objects.

The meaning of terms such as "real" (satya) and so forth—which exclude meanings such as "unreal" (asatya) and so on—is distinct due to the difference in what is being excluded; therefore, it is established that the Self is not the meaning of a sentence.

If words such as "Truth" (satya) do not abandon their own meanings, then—just as in sentences like "bringing of cows"—the sentence-meaning in this sentence regarding Truth and so forth would be either a relation (*saṃsarga*) or something related (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). Although it is accepted that the meaning [of the Upanishads] is Brahman, as stated by Vārtikakāra, precisely because of the various things to be negated, nevertheless— in order to avoid a contradictory meaning— since those [negations] culminate in Brahman, which is the object of indication (*alakṣya*), the oneness (*ekarasya*) of the Self, which is the meaning of the sentences such as "Brahman is Truth," is established from the word itself, as being distinct from both a relation (*saṃsarga*) and related entities (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
This is the meaning. || 99 ||
From which words turn back, and which is further described as "not this, not this"—this being so, everything is meaningful; otherwise, it would be purposeless. || 100 ||

Since it has been stated that Brahman is not an object of words because it is devoid of specific qualities such as possessing a genus (*jāti*), when that very [position] is accepted, then the collection of statements demonstrating its non-objectivity and its lack of specific qualities becomes consistent in meaning; whereas [statements suggesting] that Brahman is an object or possesses specific qualities become inconsistent in meaning and thus lack authority (*apramāṇa*).
He states the proof for the absence of being an object and so forth in the case of the self with the words "yataḥ" (since). || 100 ||
Immutability is said to be truth; knowledge is declared to have that as its quality.
When consciousness is immutable by its very nature, there is infinity and unity for the knower. (1)

Having established that words such as "truth" (satya) convey Brahman through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he concludes the discussion on the substratum of the word-meanings with the verse beginning "immovability" (*kauṭasthya*). That very immovability is the quality of which knowledge is possessed; thus he says "possessing that quality" (*tadguṇam*) to indicate that truth is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of knowledge. Regarding that which was described as truth:

The Bhaṭṭas, proponents of the theory of denotation (*abhidhāna*), maintain that the mutual relation (*saṃsarga*) of word-meanings is the sentence-meaning itself. The Prabhākaras, proponents of the theory of the connection of the denoted (*abhihitānvaya*), hold that the word-meanings themselves, when mutually related and combined, constitute the sentence-meaning known as "combination" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
Thus, according to the Mīmāṃsaka school, there are two types of sentence-meaning.

Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika— [Brahmavallī]—
Since the immutability of knowledge is established by its own inherent nature, its threefold infinity is proven;

thus he says, "by itself" (*svataḥ*). When it is asked how the infinity of that knowledge—which is the very nature of the knower, the Witness, Brahman—is established, it is said: "oneness" (*ekatā*). || 1 ||
However, because there is no distinction among knowers, that [object] is not the most desired;
since there is no other knower, how can it be said that "he who knows"? (2)

Having thus explained the statement, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," he challenges the subsequent portion of the sentence, "He who knows," on the grounds that there would be a distinction between the knower [and the known]. For that Brahman under discussion exists as the very nature of knowledge; since it is admitted to be non-different from the agent of knowledge, it cannot possess the status of being an agent of knowledge.

The meaning is that since no knower is admitted to exist apart from Brahman, and since the relationship of object and agent is not possible in a single entity, the statement "he who knows" is untenable. || 2 ||

The cognition that negates unreal objects and so forth, arising from ignorance regarding the true object characterized by truth and so on, attains only the path [of worldly existence] due to the loss of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna). || 3 ||

That Brahman which is indicated by words such as "Truth" and so forth— when the cognition "I am Brahman," which is non-objective in form, arises as the negation of that which is "unreal" and so on arising from ignorance, one attains Brahman— which was already attained— through the cessation of ignorance, the cause of its non-attainment; thus it is said here [in the scriptures] that it is attained, since the status of object and agent is not intended to be expressed.
He refutes this, saying "not so," with the words "truth, etc. (verse 3).
Thus, that which was known he knows; being liberated, he is liberated;
that which had ceased turns back, and that which has turned back ceases—this I swear to you three times.

Surely, it may be argued that Brahman which was unknown is now known, and the bound soul is liberated; likewise, ignorance ceases, and it is appropriate that Brahman, though already attained, is now attained. To this, he says: "In this manner. This means: like the attainment of what has already been attained.
"Being Brahman itself, one reaches Brahman; consciousness is Brahman; the liberated is liberated"—thus [it is] one.
Intending to show that the scripture beginning with "Without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) is the authority here, he says: "Three times. (4)
Therefore, due to this ignorance which acts as a cataract obscuring one's nearness to agency,
one does not perceive Brahman— characterized by existence and other attributes— even though it resides within oneself.

Anticipating the objection—"If the giving of commands has ceased eternally, why is there no realization of Brahman at all times?"—he says: "Therefore... This means that although ignorance and the like have indeed ceased, they have not ceased in such a way as to be bound [to the state of non-realization]. || 5 ||

Therefore, by the negation of ignorance, his vision is forever radiant.
One who drinks [the nectar] and so forth perceives the diversity [of objects] as the inner self (pratyagātman). || 6 ||

Since it is established that the non-manifestation of Brahman is caused by the superimposition of proximity—namely, the agency and other attributes falsely attributed through ignorance—he states the resulting conclusion with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). || 6 ||
Since the self's cognition of being an agent and an enjoyer arises from its contact with the mere elements, it is therefore deposited within the intellect (buddhi).

One might raise the objection that while the phrase "who knows thus" (*evaṃ yo veda*) is possible [in this context], the word "deposited" (*nihita*) is not possible; for Brahman, being non-material, cannot serve as a substratum—just as a jujube fruit cannot be in a bowl—and its being "deposited" in the intellect is therefore unestablished. Anticipating this, he says: "consisting of the elements" (*bhūtamātra*). Here, the term "consisting of the elements" (*bhūtamātra*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is composed of the elements. [This is so] because of ignorance (*avidyā*)...

The meaning is that the Self’s own expression is attributed to the intellect because the Self possesses properties such as being a single agent, which are produced by its connection with the intellect. || 7 ||
Freed from darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas), that [Brahman] is perceived through its own mode of functioning;
therefore, the Śruti declares: "Brahman is hidden in the intellect by means of the mind alone. (8)

By means of the sattvic modification of the intellect arising from the statement "I am Brahman," through the vision of Brahman, liberation resides in the intellect of Brahman; thus he states the authority for this alternative position: "That [darkness]... (Verse 8).
Because of the affliction of desire, ignorance, and so forth, they do not perceive that [Self] hidden within this [intellect]; therefore, the intellect is called the "house. (9)
Having thus explained the meaning of the word "nihita" (hidden), he establishes that the intellect is a cave by stating: "nigūḍham" (concealed). || 9 ||
The supreme ether is that which is within the heart, for it is superior to the external;
as the Veda says, "that which is outside," and that [ether] is the support of the intellect.

He states the meaning of the phrase "in the highest heaven" (*parame vyoman*) with the words "the supreme" (*paramam*). He provides the scriptural authority for the statement that the space within the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) is the "highest heaven" by citing the *Śruti*. He indicates the sense of the locative case—that Brahman is eternally present in that cave which is the intellect (*buddhi*) located within the aforementioned space of the heart—with the words "and therein" (*tatra ca*). ||10||

68. Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika:
(Ala)—Whether with respect to the actual state of things in the cave or in the supreme firmament;
Nothing other than that which is characterized by truth and so forth is perceived directly. || 11 ||

He states another meaning for the verse beginning with *parame vyoman*: "In the cave" (*guhāyām*). Within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is the unmanifested space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) which, in relation to its effects, is the supreme space; this is the unknown Brahman. Therein resides the pure Brahman, free from both cause and effect. Thus, the expression is a figurative statement made in consideration of the actual state of affairs. This is the meaning.

The statement regarding the "truth" (satya) and so forth was made with reference to the actual state of things. Since there exists nothing else that is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) other than Brahman— which is the unmanifest cause of the world, distinct from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its effect, and which consists of truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss, being pure and opposed in nature to both cause and effect— therefore, within the cave of the intellect (*buddhi-guhā*), [Brahman alone resides].
The supreme ether is the unknown Brahman; it exists as its very nature. The meaning is that within it, Brahman—distinct from both cause and effect—is established. || 11 ||
The ascetic, whose intellect is perfectly turned away from things contrary to the meaning of truth and so forth,
then enters the intellect inwardly and beholds the true Self.

Regarding the cause of the intellect (*buddhi*), he states the purpose of describing the abiding of Brahman—which is free from both cause and effect—once that Brahman has been known: "From the unreal, the inert, the limited, and suffering... [and so forth]. This is to eliminate doubt concerning [Brahman] as being anything other than these.

— The supreme candidate for knowledge, whose intellect has turned away from error (*viparyāsa*), having entered into the inner Self, the Cause which is Brahman, by means of the instrument of the intellect (*dhiyaḥ annaḥ karaṇāt*), perceives that the entire effect and its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) do not exist apart from That;
and thus [he realizes] that even the unknown Brahman, the Cause, is [identical with] the effect...

The meaning is that, having realized the non-existence of anything apart from Brahman—which is distinct from the world of phenomena—one determines that Brahman alone, whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, infinity, and bliss, is the reality of the witness of the intellect. || 12 ||
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing the means [to liberation], the Śruti has thus instructed us to cause the intellect to enter within, into the cave and the supreme ether. (13)
Since it has been stated that Brahman is thus deposited in the cause of the intellect (*buddhi*), the status of Brahman as the witness of the intellect is established;

therefore, the scripture beginning with "deposited in the cave" (*guhāyām*) teaches that the entry of Brahman—which is distinct from both cause and effect—into the inner self, which is the cause of the intellect, serves as a means for the realization "I am Brahman. Thus, the scripture instructs [the seeker].
He states that the scriptural passage beginning with "He who knows this" has a logical meaning: "Therefore," etc. (13).

1. First Section] Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
"I am that Supreme Brahman, for the purpose of removing the notion of duality."
In the cave of the heart, within the supreme ether, that which is to be known remains as the Knower.
Now, following the first explanation alone, he states the meaning of the sentence—beginning with the words "of the knower" (jñātuḥ).
When it is said that the object of knowledge for the Self, who is the witness of the intellect, is the Supreme Brahman, a notion of difference between the two arises.

To prevent that [misconception], it is said that Brahman is placed in that space which is superior to external space as perceived by the intellect; thus, when the Brahman to be known is realized in the Witness, only that much remains, and since even that Witness is nothing but Brahman, there is no possibility of suspecting a difference between the two—this is the meaning. || 14 ||
For one who follows the very path of the relationship between the means and the goal, the Supreme—which is free from both means and goal—enters into his own self. 15.

Anticipating the objection that if there were non-difference between the knower and the known—the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—then because the *jīva* is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), it would follow that Brahman too is subject to transmigratory existence, and thus the attainment of that [Brahman] would not be the desired goal, he says: "The goal... etc. For a transmigrating being who is engaged in activity by way of the connection between the goal and the means—such as the thought that heaven and so forth are the goal to be achieved through sacrifice and so forth—[the attainment of Brahman would be undesirable].

When that Supreme Brahman, which is distinct from both [the individual soul and the world], is attained as one's own essential nature (svarūpa), then even for the transmigrating being (saṃsārin), the state of being a transmigrator ceases. Therefore, how could it be possible to suspect that Brahman possesses the state of being a transmigrator by way of that [individual]? This is the meaning. || 15 ||

Fearing that it might be impossible for one to enjoy all desires simultaneously while acting as an agent, [the author] says "by Brahman" and "simultaneously, together" (saha). Regarding the point that the knower of the oneness of Brahman and the Self attains the entirety of human goals, [the text says]: "He enjoys all desires... (so 'śnute sarvān kāmān).

He explains the portion of the sentence beginning with "māni" (he thinks) by saying "so'śnute" (he enjoys). Anticipating the objection that the accomplishment of all human goals through agency is not possible, he demonstrates—by relying on the subsequent statement—that for the knower who exists in the form of Brahman, the accomplishment of all human goals is not contradictory, because agency is superimposed by ignorance. This is shown in the passage beginning with "kartṛtve".
He states the meaning of the word *saha* as "simultaneously" (*yugapat*). || 16 ||
That Brahman would not exist in the inward [Self] if its meaning were one of difference;
nor can that which is oriented toward the external (parāgbhūta) be conceived as possessing the qualities of "Being" and so forth, which belong to the Supreme.
Anticipating the objection, "Why should the word *saha* (together) not be taken in its literal sense? he says: "The west... [and so on].

This is because if the word *saha* were taken in its primary sense, there would be a distinction between the Self (*ātman*) and Brahman; consequently, the word *saha* would have the meaning of "distinction" (*bheda*).

It might be argued that the hearing of the word "saha" (together) indeed signifies difference, and thus the word "saha" possesses meaning through the sense of difference; to this it is replied:
in that case, Brahman—which constitutes one's own essential nature—would not be established, and such would be the result for statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

Because it is logical that the word "together" (saha) implies simultaneity—avoiding the contradiction of the statement—the meaning is that in a single moment alone, the knower of Brahman experiences all human goals in the form of Brahman. He states another defect [in the opponent's view] regarding the difference between the Self and Brahman: "It is conceivable," etc. (verse 17).
Nor can it be said that [the word *saha*] does not express the sense of simultaneity because it is a particle (*nipāta*);
therefore, the word *saha* must indeed be the denoter of the meaning "simultaneously" (*yugapad*). (18)
Anticipating the objection that the word *saha* cannot have that meaning because it lacks the capacity to signify "simultaneity," he says:
"Nor... The meaning is that since the word *saha* expresses the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthatā*), it is not at all able to express the sense of simultaneity;
this is because particles (*nipāta*) possess multiple meanings and this [word] is a particle. He summarizes the conclusion:
Therefore, [it is so]. || 18 ||
Since there exists nothing other than the Self from which ignorance and the like are eliminated through knowledge, therefore the wise one enjoys all desires together with Brahman. (19)
Even though the word *saha* means "simultaneously," since simultaneity depends upon difference, there is a concern that it implies a distinction [between the knower and the known].
Anticipating this objection, he says: "from knowledge" (*jñānāt*). Through the knowledge "I am Brahman," ignorance is removed;

by the removal of that [ignorance], its effects—such as unreality and limitation—are also removed. Thus, one who has realized Brahman, the knower of Brahman, [becomes one] with the nature of the Self.

And in the form of Brahman, it experiences all joys simultaneously. The meaning is that during the state of ignorance, because of the limitation by adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is a manifestation as if divided; thus, there is the mention of "many" [joys]. || 19 ||
For the knower, nothing other than the inward-facing [Self] residing within the cave of the heart is found;
for those who know it, Brahman—consisting of truth and so forth—is indeed the innermost Self (pratyagātman).
Anticipating the objection that there might be a distinction between the knower and Brahman because of the statement "by means of the wise one (vipaścit) and Brahman," he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the knower": since it is stated in the verse, "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave," that Brahman resides within the intellect (*buddhi*), and since the Self (*ātman*) likewise resides there, the meaning is that there is not even a scent of difference between the two. || 20 ||
In order to eliminate the possibility that [the Self] is an object of knowledge distinct from the All-Seeing One, [it is taught] through grammatical coordination with the All-Seeing Brahman. (21)

He states another reason for the absence of difference between the knower and Brahman: "Vipaścit" (the All-knowing). By the word "jñeyatvāt" (because of being knowable) and so forth, the fact that Brahman is the object to be attained is understood. || 21 ||

By means of a single [consciousness] that functions sequentially, it pervades those things that function sequentially.
"Having realized all desires, he is one who is desireless," so says the Śruti.

Having restated the meaning of the phrase "he enjoys all desires," he shows the agreement with another scriptural passage (*śrutyantara*) regarding that very same point by saying, "by one [path]. Anticipating the objection that the knower must possess activity in order to attain the pleasure of sense objects, he qualifies his realization as being "occurring without succession" (*akramavartinī*). || 22 ||
In the beginning, at the end, and likewise in the middle, the various bodies of the intellects are pervaded by the one undifferentiated consciousness,
which is of the nature of non-dual experience.
It establishes the immutability (kūṭasthatva) stated regarding cognition with the verse beginning "In the beginning" (ādau). || 23 ||
Since the knower of Brahman enjoys all causes of worldly activity as objects of desire, for that reason there is no activity for the knower of Brahman that is without a cause.

He states the intended meaning of the passage— beginning with "all activities"— to show that even for those who know Brahman, if they desire worldly activity, there would be a contradiction with the aforementioned scripture: "by the knower, [desires] for pleasures termed 'kāma'..."
The meaning is that because he is existent and because desire is absent, the activity conditioned by that [desire] is not established. || 24 ||
Sensual desires have ignorance as their cause; activities have desire as their root.
Both dharma and adharma have those [activities] as their root, and from that, the body arises as the locus of misfortune. (25)
Therefore, upon the cessation of ignorance, there shall be for the wise man a perpetual cessation;
indeed, at that very moment, there is the cessation of all modifications that are the causes of karma.
He establishes that for those who know Brahman, the cessation of desire and other afflictions is accomplished without effort through the removal of ignorance by means of knowledge;
this is shown by the verse beginning with "avidyā" (ignorance). 25–26.
In ancient times, he declared that this is the aphorism (sūtra) for the entire meaning of the Upaniṣads;
and its meaning has been correctly described in brief by means of the mantra. (27)

In order to state the connection of the subsequent section beginning with "tasmād vā etasmāt," [the author] recounts what has preceded: "The whole," etc. The commentator has stated that the sentence "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" is a summary (sūtra) of the subject matter of the two chapters—the Brahman, the knowledge thereof, and its fruit. And that summarized meaning—
The meaning is that [the teaching] has been explained in brief by means of the mantra beginning with "The triad is truth," through the removal of doubt and error. || 27 ||

Now, whatever meaning has been indicated here by this first sūtra, this commentary is stated from that point until its conclusion. (28)

By the phrase "anena" (by this), he demonstrates the connection: that the collection of texts beginning with "tasmāt" and ending with the conclusion is for the purpose of elaborating upon that meaning which was indicated by the aphorism "brahmavidāpnoti param" and which was briefly explained by the mantra. || 28 ||
Truth, knowledge, and infinite—beyond the five elements beginning with taste—is that which is described in the scriptures as "unseen" and so forth; I am that Brahman, free from fear. (29)
Having stated the purport of the collection [of verses], he declares that which was spoken in the mantra: "It is true," [verse 29].
Now, one might ask: how can that which is true and infinite be correctly understood?
This is now being analyzed, given that [understanding] depends upon causes such as place and time. (30)

When the mantra declares the identity of the Self and Brahman—stating that the Self is Brahman, which is distinct from the five sheaths (*kośa*), consists of truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss, and is without distinction or fear—an objection is raised with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). [The objection is: Since all objects of words are delimited in three ways, and since Brahman, being a real entity, is likewise differentiated like a rope-snake...
The meaning is that because [the mantra] lacks the possibility of being real, and precisely because it is unreal and insentient, the stated meaning of the mantra is not established.

Since Brahman is the cause of the entire universe, its threefold infinity is established; consequently, reality and consciousness are logically possible in it. Furthermore, that infinity—which is produced by its being the cause of all—must be demonstrated immediately hereafter.
He refutes this by stating: "It indicates [the location]. (30)
In reality, Brahman's infinity is said to be threefold—namely, with respect to space, extension, and time; therefore, its existence as well is established as true.

It was stated that "this is now being analyzed," and he elaborates on this with the words "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*). In this sequence, for the body that is being born, the very five elements that constituted the previously acquired body serve as its material cause (*upādāna*), while the instruments (*karaṇas*) belonging to that [previous state] are merely manifested here. This point is stated in accordance with such scriptural passages as "Just as a weaver," and so forth; thus he says: "In the previous birth... (verse 72).
Even though the Virāj, born from the Sūtra, is the self of all,
it undergoes limitation due to the delusion that "I am this much," arising from the conjunction of desire and karma.

Regarding the body produced from food in the manner previously described, that which is its gross portion—though it is the unconditioned Virāj who is the object of the aphorism—undergoes a limitation due to delusion, under the influence of desire and karma, such that one thinks, "I am only this much. To this effect, he says: "Of the Self of all" (sarvātmanaḥ). || 73 ||
Likewise, because it consists of the *liṅga* and possesses both collective (*samaṣṭi*) and individual (*vyaṣṭi*) forms,
the unmanifest (*avyakta*), due to that limitation, exists in a state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatā*).

In the very same way, he states that the subtle portion within that very body which exists as the nature of the seventeen-fold *liṅga* would be a limitation (*avaccheda*) of the *sūtra*, which consists of both the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*). He says: "The *liṅga*... The cause of those two limitations is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); its form during deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) is the limitation here in this body.
He says, "Let it be grasped," [expressed as] "tadavaccheda" (the delimitation of that). || 74 ||
Even though the Self is infinite and beyond [the field], its status as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) arises through ignorance;
thus, it is logically consistent that [the Lord] says, "Know Me also as the knower of the field. (75)

And as for that which is perceived here in the body as the reflection of consciousness called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña), let it be understood as a limitation of the Supreme, who is distinct from cause and effect; thus he says: "even of the Supreme Self.
He supports this with the words of the Blessed One—that the Supreme Self alone is the knower of the field in this body and there is no other—by citing: "the knower of the field..."
And so it is said. || 75 ||

"I do not know"—this ignorance (avidyā) alone is considered impermanent and to have that [knowledge] as its cause;
it would be established by its own very manifestation, like a bat at dawn.

Anticipating the question of what the cause of the aforementioned limitations is, the author explains *avidyā*—which was previously stated to be the cause of being a *kṣetrajña*—by saying "not," and so forth. The meaning is that *avidyā* alone, as the cause of being a *kṣetrajña*, is the cause of the aforementioned limitations; because *avidyā* is to be removed by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it cannot [be established] through such means.

Anticipating the objection that [ignorance] must be established, he says, "by its own establishment," meaning that ignorance is established by the very power of one's own self-evident consciousness (*ātmacaitanya*). He proves the establishment of ignorance through one's own experience by means of an illustration:
"the night. Just as this owl’s night—*aulūkī*—is perceived as darkness during the day, so too...

The meaning is that just as for Rulūka [the world] appears through his own experience, so too does ignorance (avidyā) establish itself through its own experience within the reality that is a single expanse of consciousness (cidekatāna). || 76 ||
He who desires to see ignorance with a vision born of valid means of knowledge will surely behold the darkness situated within the interior of a cave by means of a lamp.
But to one who disregards his own experience and accepts ignorance as established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), he says: "By valid means of knowledge" [verse 77].
To perceive here that "this is not the Self" is the manifestation of ignorance;
therefore, that is called ignorance, while knowledge consists solely in the nature of the Self. (78)

Raising the objection that, although ignorance (avidyā) is not established by the mind, the non-self (anātman) is established by the mind and therefore cannot be an effect of ignorance, [the author]—intending to include that too within ignorance on the grounds of its being an object of perception (dṛśyatva) and so forth—states:
"The non-self... Having raised the further objection, "What then is knowledge (vidyā)?", he states: "Knowledge is consciousness; that is the Self itself."
"Vidyā" means "knowledge. || 78 ||
Apart from the excessive grasping at a self, no nature of that [ignorance] exists;
thus it is always appropriate to regard ignorance as being like an enemy. (79)
However, some describe ignorance (*avidyā*) as the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge; in response to them, he says: "The Self.
Non-apprehension of the Self means its veiling or concealment; there is no form of ignorance apart from that.
Indeed, it is not possible for a non-entity (*abhāva*) to possess the capacity to veil; therefore, ignorance consists in the veiling of a real entity.

The meaning is "its own nature. Regarding the term *avidyā* (ignorance): anticipating the question of what the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) might be, [the author explains it as follows]... In the case of "friend," "dharma," and so forth, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is either otherness from that or opposition to it; likewise, [the meaning of the negative particle in the context of knowledge is] otherness from knowledge.
Alternatively, he states that the meaning of the negative particle is "being contrary to knowledge" rather than "the absence of that," by saying "as if it were [actually] present. (79)

Therefore, the conceptual construction of "existent," "non-existent," and so forth, belonging to those of deluded minds, subsides when investigated; it does not persist within the self that is beyond grasping, characterized by the realization "I do not know."

Having thus shown that ignorance (*avidyā*) is characterized by the absence of existence, he concludes what was stated regarding the fact that the entire category of non-self is a manifestation of ignorance: "Therefore... Since the collection of non-selves, consisting of the existent, the non-existent, and so forth, when examined, ultimately resolves into ignorance alone, therefore it is a play (*vilasita*) of ignorance.
The meaning is that it is to be sought after. || 80 ||
With his mind enveloped by that [ignorance], he, having abandoned his former body,
enters a womb as a subtle body (liṅgātman), impelled by the winds of karma and other factors.

Raising the objection—"Even though ignorance of the Self (ātmāvidyā) conceals the reality, what is established regarding the present birth of the body?"—he says: "By that" (tayā). By the word *citta*, discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) is understood; the *liṅgātman* is the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by the subtle body (*liṅga*). || 81 ||
Food, water, and fire—each of these, when consumed, becomes threefold;
thus, each single element undergoes transformation into a tripartite state.
Through the portions consisting of feces, flesh, and intellect; through urine, blood, breath, and rays;

and likewise through the parts of bone, marrow, speech, and food—by these, the vital energies [are formed] over time for the soul (jīva) that has entered the womb of a woman and remains there, with respect to its assumption of a twofold body.
He demonstrates the threefold transformation of the food and other substances released by the mother for consumption with the verse beginning "Food," etc. (82–83).
The goddess Bhāratī [is the presiding deity] of the mind, the intellect, and the sense organs, as well as of the power of karma;
and Prāṇa [is the deity] for the purpose of characterizing the various divisions of the vital breaths. 84.

In the passage "That which is most subtle is the mind," the word *manas* indicates the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*). In the passage "That which is most subtle is speech," the word *vāk* indicates the remaining organs of action (*karmendriya*).
In the passage "That which is most subtle is the vital breath," the word *prāṇa* is intended as an indication of the various functions such as *prāṇa* and so forth.
He says "the mind" to indicate that which has been destroyed. || 84 ||

Whichever sense organ is impelled by the mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) arising from karma, [that very organ functions]. (85) [This is] the first section, accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.
From that [ignorance], egoism arises according to one's karma and according to one's learning. || 85 ||

Now, he explains—beginning with the words "arising from karma"—that the birth of the mind and consciousness occurs only when they are permeated by the [primal] matter (māyā), in order to refute the Sāṃkhya position. || 85 ||
For it is from the conceit "I am a hearer" that the faculty of hearing arises;
one should understand the remaining faculties in the same way. (86)

This very point—that from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) associated with *sāttvika* [guṇa] there arises the birth of the respective sense organs—is clarified as follows: "From the conceit 'I am the hearer' the organ of touch is born; from the conceit 'I am the seer'..."

He says "in the remaining [senses]" (pariśiṣṭeṣu) to indicate that one should see [the same principle] applied to such statements as "from pride (māna) the eye-faculty is born," and so forth. || 86 ||
The arising of a body is unarisen, like space, by virtue of the birth of a jar;
therefore, [the categories] such as "existence" (asti) and so forth would also not exist, because they depend upon that very birth.

Having raised the objection that the Self might also undergo birth, just like the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, he states that its birth is merely adventitious through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi): "The body," etc.

Since birth is refuted for the Self by its very nature, he states that the other modifications of being (bhāvavikāra), such as existence and so forth, are likewise negated for it: "Existence, etc. || 87 ||
To the extent that this body of the one dwelling in the womb grows, to that same extent the manifestation of the subtle body (liṅga) also arises. (88)

In the passage "not born after the birth of the body," the birth of the individual soul (jīva) is intended with reference to the birth of the subtle body (liṅga); anticipating the objection as to how the subtle body itself could arise if it already exists through the Veda, he says: "To whatever extent... (verse 88).
Then, in the ninth month of the complete formation of the embodied being, the latent impressions arising from many past births manifest themselves in succession. (89)

He provides a description of the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (*jīva*)— which is conditioned by the subtle body (*liṅga*)— after it has entered the womb and remains therein, for the sake of cultivating detachment. By the words beginning with "samagra," [the author describes] the embodied one (*dehin*),
who possesses the subtle body, having entered the womb under the influence of merit and demerit, lying right there, endowed with all the instruments of perception, in the ninth month.

The meaning is that at the tenth month, or upon the attainment of birth, the manifestation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) set in motion throughout many previous births occurs even before that. The word "atha" (then/now) is intended to indicate an alternative regarding the month. || 89 ||

Sureśvarācārya’s *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*—[In the *Brahmavallī*]: "Having become manifest, yet still ignorant and conditioned by the sufferings of the womb and so forth, he then grieves for his own self, despondent, crying out, 'Alas, what misery! (90)

He demonstrates the arising of great sorrow within his own self as an effect following the production of knowledge consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) while still in the womb, with the verse beginning "āvirbhūta" (90).
In the past, I repeatedly experienced unbearable torments that cut into my very vitals—the heated sands of Karambha which burn those of impure intent. (91)

He restates the manner of his grief with the words "experienced" (*anubhūtā*). This refers to past births prior to entering the womb; the phrase "pains that cut through the vital organs" (*marmacchido vedanā*) is to be supplied as the object. For those very grains of heated sand (*karambhavālukā*), when intensely heated, burn those people of impure intent who have committed evil deeds; and those [pains]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
The connection is that "they were experienced by me as being made of clay. || 91 ||
Scorched by the digestive fire, the drops of the humor known as pitta,
submerged within the womb, burn me most intensely. (92)
He says—starting with "jāṭara—"—that for me, lying within the womb, there is a sensation exceeding those sensations previously experienced. || 92 ||
The mouths of the worms of the Audarya hell, which are equal to the thorns of the Kūṭaśālmalī tree,
pierce those who are being tormented by saws on their ribs.

It is said that not only is there the state of being burned by the digestive fire (*audarya-agni*) of the mother while remaining in the womb, but there is also another unbearable suffering: "By the digestive... (verse 93).
The suffering I experienced while in the womb—filled with pervasive foul odors and inflamed by the digestive fire—is less than that which arises from being boiled in the Kumbhīpāka hell. (94)

Showing that the suffering of dwelling in the womb is greater than the suffering of the Kumbhīpāka hell, he states the desirability of abandoning the womb-residence with the verse beginning "garbhe" (94).
The drinking of pus, bile, and phlegm, the eating of what has been vomited, and the state of becoming a worm within filth—all this was experienced by that which dwelt in the womb. (95)
Lying within the womb exceeds dwelling in many different varieties of hells; therefore, one should strive even more to reject dwelling in the womb—thus he says: "Foul-smelling" (pūti). || 95 ||

Furthermore, whatever great suffering is observed in all the hells does not exceed the suffering caused by dwelling in the womb;

He concludes the description of the soul's stay within the womb for one who has entered it with the verse beginning "asthi" (verse 97).
Desirous of departing and tormented by suffering, he falls headlong below, crying out loudly with his face cast down, like one released from a mechanical device and lying flat on his back.

At that time, the child is ignorant of anything and remains like a mere lump of flesh;

he consumes pus as if it were milk—fie upon this most sinful childhood! 200.

Then, having attained youth, he became arrogant and overwhelmed by the fever of passion;
he suddenly began to sing loudly and likewise began to leap about. (1)
Blinded by lust, anger, and pride, he climbs the tree with speed; though it terrifies those who are at peace, he does not perceive anything at all.
He elaborates on the stage of youth following childhood: "Arrogant," etc. (1–2).
Then, having reached old age—a state of great humiliation—he becomes afflicted with suffering;
his chest is constricted by phlegm, and the food he has eaten does not digest.

One who eats pungent, bitter, and astringent foods develops a sour taste in the mouth, a distorted vision, and suffers from wind-disorders (vāta) that cause the hips and neck to bend; such a person has cracked feet and lacks strength. (4)

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the capacity for grasping what has been heard. Intelligence (*medhā*) is the function of the capacity for not forgetting what has been grasped. Even beyond that, no illustration for the suffering of death can be found;
for living beings tremble in fear of it, even when they have already reached the height of agony.

A living being is carried away by death, even while embraced by kinsmen,
just as a serpent dwelling within the waters of the ocean is seized by Garuḍa.
Suspecting that the suffering of death might be avoided by kinsmen alone, he says— with an illustration— "It is carried away"— verse 11.

Mounted upon the machine of saṃsāra and presided over by the messengers of Yama, he is joined with the noose of Time and afflicted by the suffering of "Where shall I go? (18).
He says that even for one who has emerged from the gross body and is departing for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma, there is no freedom of will: "saṃsāra... (verse 18).
In this world that is like an illusion, whose vow could it be that "mother, father, teacher, son, and kin are mine"?
For when one departs alone, led by one's own karma, [who will follow?]

and every morning they depart from them;

like a water-wheel, man wanders incessantly and without rest.

He concludes the description of the course of transmigratory existence— which has been elaborated for the sake of generating detachment regarding the states of the living being, such as conception, birth, childhood, youth, old age, death, and so forth— with the verse beginning "mṛtau" (21).
In the sky, rain-clouds, the earth, mortals, women, and food— these deities received the oblation known as faith, the moon, rain, and food, which was thus offered.

it is said that for him, there follows in due course the cessation of the great cycle of worldly existence.
Regarding the origin of the person from food as stated [in the preceding verse], he cites the agreement of another scriptural passage: "From fire, rain... and so forth.

From that, a king is born; then those same gods offer Soma into the fire of Parjanya, and from that oblation of Soma, rain is produced. Then, in the third fire characterized as the earth, the gods offer the rain; and from that oblation of rain, food comes into being.
Then, in the fourth fire, which is man, the aforementioned gods offer that food; and from that oblation of food—

The meaning is as follows: "From that, a person is produced"—therefore, when the fifth oblation is offered, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the sacrificer, which are like a woman, pour forth semen; then, being one who is to be called a "male," a person (*puruṣa*) is born.
This refers to the statement introducing the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), beginning with "That very person consists of the essence of food" (*sa vā eṣa puruṣo 'nnarasamayaḥ*).

He states the intended meaning [of the passage] with the word "gradually" (*kramāt*). By means of the subsequent text, which introduces the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) in sequence, he explains that the dissolution of each preceding sheath into each succeeding one is taught; subsequently, the knowledge of the identity of the Self with Brahman—which is distinct from cause and effect—is declared [in passages such as] "Brahman is the tail, the support," as that which removes ignorance along with its effects.
This is the meaning. || 22 || 23 ||
All such transformations as these have their locus in the subtle body (liṅgadeha);
although he does not possess them, through delusion he falsely imagines himself to possess them. (24)
To explain the intent behind the mention of the "person" (*puruṣa*) in the immediately preceding statements, [the author] raises an objection and then refutes it, saying "beginning with 'these'":

although the previously mentioned [states], such as being in the womb, reside in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and do not reside in the Self, it is appropriate to describe them for the purpose of cultivating detachment (*vairāgya*) toward that [Self]. Thus he says: "beginning with 'these'. Even though they were mentioned before... the womb... [is as follows].

Modifications such as dwelling in a womb and so forth reside in the two bodies and do not abide in the Self; nevertheless, although the Self is in reality devoid of modifications such as dwelling in a womb, due to the failure to grasp the distinction between the Self and the two bodies, the Self, through the power of delusion, conceives the notion: "I alone am the one undergoing modifications such as dwelling in a womb."
The meaning is that by means of this, saṃsāra being perceived therein will bring about the cultivation of detachment. || 24 ||
For one acts toward knowledge and action out of the conceit "I am a knower";
then, out of delusion, thinking "I am a thinker," one performs mental activities. (25)

Anticipating the doubt as to how there could be the conceit of "I" with respect to the three bodies, [the author] reveals that the conceit of "I" in the intellect (*buddhi*) is caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*), along with its effects—beginning with the word "known" (*jñāta*). He describes the conceit of "I" in the mind (*manas*), which is produced by non-discrimination (*aviveka*), along with its effects—beginning with the word "thinking" (*mantṛ*). || 25 ||
Through the conceit of being the vital breath (prāṇa), it engages in the activity of action;
and through the conceit of being the eye, it is intent upon the perception of form.

Having introduced the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*)—such as "I shall be the agent of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the downward breath (*apāna*), and so forth"—as well as its effects, which are prompted by ignorance;

Likewise, when the body is burned and so forth, the ignorant person thinks, "I am burned";
and he perceives the darkness of the body as his own, thinking, "I am dark. (27)

He demonstrates the conceit regarding the gross body and its effects arising from delusion with the word "tathā" (so too). Ignorance (*abudhatva*) is the state of being devoid of the grasp of discrimination between the body and the self. || 27 ||
Through ignorance, by means of the conceit regarding cattle and other possessions, thinking "I am the possessor of those," one thinks:
"I am a student, I am a householder, likewise I am an ascetic, and I am a sage."
One regards the consecrations of the body, the liṅga, and the self as being caused by attachment. || 28 ||

He illustrates the effect that arises from ignorance due to one's identification with cows and so forth, even though they are [already] present, by saying "cattle-wealth and so forth. He states that one imagines within the Self those impressions (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the body and the subtle body (*liṅgātman*)— such as being a student (*brahmacārin*), bathing, and sipping water— which are produced by ignorance, solely because of attachment to those two.
"One who practices the holy life" (brahmacārī). || 28 ||
The body is said to be the effect of the elements, which are distinct from the self; through the delusion of "I" and "mine," one encounters misfortune. || 29 ||

What more need be said? The body consists of the five elements; within it, due to the conceit of "I" and "mine," the cycle of worldly existence appears to the eternally liberated Self through the power of delusion—thus he concludes with the words, "of those who perceive the Self as distinct. (29)

Although all beings are equally subject to the necessity of food and are likewise identical in their nature as Brahman, it is only the male person who is understood here, because he alone possesses the qualification for ritual action and knowledge.

Having thus shown the cycle of existence within the self, he states the intended meaning of the mention of "the person" (puruṣa) in the immediately following verse, while omitting the mention of "animals and so forth," with the words "And of all... (verse 30).
Because he desired to transfer [the burden] by means of this knowledge of Brahman to that man who is the innermost Brahman within, from this nest of manifold misfortunes; (31)
He establishes that eligibility for both ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) is the cause for the Self’s apprehension by stating "aneka... [and so forth].

It is intended here that liberation arises from the knowledge of Brahman for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified by ritual actions; therefore, [the text speaks of] "many" [factors].
(Note: *ka*, *kha* read *sthūlade*; *ga*, *gha*, *ca* read *vidyāvi*; *rā*, *gha* read *yoriva*).

The meaning is that since it is desired to lead a person fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra— which is based on what is not the Self— to Brahman, which is the innermost of all, by means of the knowledge "I am Brahman," it is logical that only one who is capable of being qualified for both action and knowledge is to be understood here. || 31 ||
Just as one might point out the moon by first indicating the tip of a tree branch,
so too is Brahman shown in the inward-facing [Self] by first pointing to the sheath and then to that which is beyond the sheath.

Anticipating the objection that if liberation is intended to be taught here through the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), then that alone should have been stated and the presentation of the five sheaths (pañcakośa) would be useless, he says: "Like the branch of a tree" (taruśākhā). || 32 ||
In this beginningless saṃsāra, the mind is colored by latent impressions (vāsanā).
It can be made to turn back through means; therefore, that [means] is taught. (33)

He clarifies what was already stated— that the description of the five sheaths is for the purpose of providing a means to the knowledge of Brahman— with the verse beginning "anādau" (in the beginningless):
"The single inner Self, untouched by duality, appears as if external, just as the interior appears as the exterior."
That which is divided by the distinction between "you" and "I" is false, being devoid of reality.

Fearing that the non-duality [of Brahman] might be lost due to the lack of distinction between Brahman and the sheaths (kośa) in the instruction on the five sheaths—which serve as the means for the knowledge of Brahman—he says: "not touching duality. Just as this inner self (pratyagātman) exists as one within its own interior self without any contact with difference, so too, even with respect to the external sheaths, it does not touch duality.

Regarding the statement "it exists," he states the reason: "yuṣmad" and so forth. The meaning is that because our own fivefold group and yours—constituting the ten-fold aggregate—are divided from the inner self (pratyagātman) by its own ignorance (avidyā), and because every kind of duality is false since it is produced by the self's ignorance, there is no loss of non-duality (advaita). || 34 ||

Just as the Annamaya and the others [are designated] in our division, so too are the inner selves (pratyagātman) of those [others] traditionally known as the "you" (yuṣmad), beginning with food (anna). || 35 ||
He demonstrates the ten sheaths (kośas) indicated by the distinction between "you" and "I" with the word *asmad* ("I"):

Just as for this inner self (*pratyagātman*), in its division as "I," there are five sheaths consisting of food (*annamaya*), vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and bliss (*ānandamaya*)— which are the referents of the suffix *-maya* and are graspable by the notion of "I"— so too are those [of the other].
The meanings of the word *prakṛti*—the inner self (*pratyagātman*), food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss—are conceived as being within the sphere of "you" (*yuṣmad-bhāva*).
Since the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-buddhi*) does not apply to them, the meaning is that there exists this tenfold sheath (*kośa-daśaka*) in this manner. || 35 ||
