Having dissolved the internal [elements] accordingly within their respective inner selves, Śureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[Brahmavallī]: 94. Having dissolved the internal [elements] accordingly within their respective inner selves, [one attains the state of Brahman].
One should indeed worship food and the other elements, as they proceed in an ascending order of form.

Anticipating the question—"To what purpose is the five sheaths divided tenfold by means of the analysis of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*)?"—he says: "The internal ones. Following the previously mentioned method, after the tenfold comprehension of the sheaths, [he enumerates] the internal ones: those consisting of food (*annamaya*), vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and bliss (*ānandamaya*).

Having dissolved each of the meanings of the *tanmātra* suffixes— food, breath, mind, consciousness, and bliss— which constitute the causes inherent within the primary objects, by means of the discriminative intellect that realizes there is no effect apart from its cause; and having known them as being merely that [cause], one should again dissolve food into breath, breath into mind, mind into consciousness, and consciousness...
The meaning is that one should define [it] as being merely the primordial cause designated by the word "Bliss" (Ānanda). || 36 ||

Having thus consumed the nature of the effect and remaining in the nature of the cause, one embraces Brahman through the self; and having consumed even that [nature of the cause] by means of the [great] statement, one [remains as Brahman].

By means of the process demonstrated, the wise person— having withdrawn the state of being an effect into the state of being its cause and remaining in the form of the unknown Brahman— dissolves even that causal state through the knowledge arising from the sentence "I am Brahman," and thus attains Brahman, which is distinct from both cause and effect in its own essential nature; this is what he says:
"Having eaten," thus [it is said]. || 37 ||
Food is to be known as Virāj; it increases from the vital breath (prāṇa).
Therefore, the Self of the Vedas, consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma [Vedas], is internal and composed of mind (manomaya). || 38 ||

He explains the food and other elements mentioned in the instruction "one should worship food and so forth" with the words "Food... [and so on]. Within the Sūtra-self (Hiraṇyagarbha), who possesses both the power of action and the power of knowledge, the portion consisting of the power of action is grasped by the word "Prāṇa";
from that, the production of food occurs, as he says: "from Prāṇa. Furthermore, the portion consisting of the power of knowledge is the mind (*manas*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

And thus it is divided into two; therein, that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which possesses the power to produce conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) is denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*). This he states with the words "Ṛg, Yajus... and so forth. The connection is therefore: "from this prāṇa, within.
By the term "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), the mind itself is understood. || 38 ||
Vijñāna is the cognition whose object is the meaning of the Vedas, characterized by certainty;
bliss (ānanda), produced from knowledge and action, is characterized as the fruit. || 39 ||

Based on the context of the *prakṛti* (primordial nature), he states that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which possesses the power to produce non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)—this is what is meant by the phrase "the meaning of the Veda," etc. Accepting that the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) refers to the cause, he says: [Note: The manuscript variants provided indicate textual differences regarding the preceding words, but the core argument remains as translated above.]

Regarding the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*): therein, the triad of sheaths consisting of breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the *sūtrātman*-sheath; food (*anna*) is the *virāṭ*-sheath; and bliss (*ānanda*) is the causal (*kāraṇa*)-sheath—this is the summary. || 39 ||
These three foods alone belong entirely to Prajāpati:
breath, mind, and speech; thus Virāj attained the nature of food.

And he says that this pentad of sheaths is also mentioned in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* with the words "only three. By the word "speech" (*vāk*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is understood. In the phrase "he will make food smaller," the word "food" (*anna*) refers to the Virāj; the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) is that the cause for that has been stated in the passage beginning with "this [world] was indeed that. || 40 ||
Thus, among the four [sheaths], the innermost self alone is called the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya);
because its nature is a mass of pure consciousness (prajñānaghana), it may nevertheless appear as distinct from the perspective of its effects.

Just as the nature of the four [sheaths] beginning with food (*anna*) is bliss (*ānanda*), so too the nature of the four suffix-meanings (*pratyayārtha*) beginning with *annamaya* is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). This is what he states with the words "of the four.
In that regard, he provides the reason—namely, that the four sheaths do not exist apart from the individual soul (*jīva*)—with the words "consisting of consciousness" (*prajñāna*).

Raising the objection as to how there can be a conceptualization of a head, tail, and so forth, for the individual soul (jīva) which is a mass of pure consciousness (prajñānaghana), he says "It may be so," [implying it is possible] because of the differentiation of the fruits of karma. || 41 ||
The arrangement of the head and so forth is for the purpose of the act of meditation;
therefore, one should explain these mental layers (citīḥ) in this manner. 42.

Having stated the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "That indeed is this person" (sa vā eṣa puruṣaḥ), he states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "This indeed is its head" (tasyedameva śiraḥ) as follows: "The head, etc. He says "Therefore," indicating that even among the elders there is a well-known convention based on the conceptualization of the head and so forth for the purpose of performing meditation (upāsanā). || 42 ||
The head is the crown, the two arms are the wings, and the self is the body in the middle; the remainder is to be known as the tail—thus one should contemplate consciousness. (43)

Explaining the meaning arising from the word *akṣara* in the passage beginning with "of that, this indeed," he reveals that consciousness itself (*cit*)—which consists of five aspects—is what is to be contemplated: "The head," etc. (verse 43).
One who knows this, sitting thus upon these layers in their proper order, enters deeper and deeper by the successive abandonment of each preceding one. (44)
In response to the inquiry as to what fruit is obtained through the worship of the fivefold altar (*cityupāsana*), he says: "Upāsīnaḥ" (worshipping).
Through the continuous contemplation of the fivefold sheaths (*kośas*) which constitute the altar, the intellect becomes purified—this is the purport [of the passage beginning with] "ga.
gha. cha. 'tyādeḥ tātpa'"; [and it serves] for the sake of the meaning [of the word] "ma. gha. nārthe śi°"; [and it serves] for the literal meaning [of the word] "3. ka. kṣarārthe".

The intellect of discrimination arises while one lies [in this state]. By its power, one successively abandons each preceding sheath and attains each subsequent one.
Thus, having dissolved all the sheaths, one attains liberation through the knowledge "I am Brahman"—this is the meaning. || 44 ||

Because the Veda is beyond suspicion, what has been stated may be accepted as possible; for doubt arising from human intellect would only apply to that which is known through inference or direct perception.

One might object: "How then can the results of meditation, such as 'all food indeed comes to them,' be taken literally, given that it is impossible for a single [meditation] to have two results? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Because of the Śruti," meaning that since the two results for a single meditation are established by the Śruti, they are not contradictory; for there is no doubt regarding the matter stated in the Śruti due to its faultlessness.

Anticipating the objection as to where there might be scope for doubt regarding the existence [of the Veda], he says "liṅga" (verse 45): doubt may arise in respect to perception and the other means of knowledge because of the possibility of defects in their instruments due to the influence of human intellect; however, since that is absent in the case of the Veda, it is not so.
Or rather, the Śruti, having restated that which is already attained by its very nature,
enjoins meditation upon the Self as the "Great" (bhūman), just as it enjoins [meditation] upon names and so forth. || 46 ||
He states another intended meaning of the instruction on the worship of the five sheaths (kośas) with the words "or by way of its own nature" (svabhāvato vā).

Just as in the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, after restating the worship established by its own nature— which concerns names and so forth through the relationship of high and low— the knowledge of the Infinite (bhūman) is enjoined, so too [is it here] for those who identify the Self with the sheaths.

The meaning is that by the very practice of the aforementioned meditations, having dissolved each preceding stage into each succeeding one, the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is intended here as the primary goal, even without any desire for the fruits of ritual action (*śrutaphala*). || 46 ||

Or, since [the means] for attaining fruits inferior to liberation are already established through another Vedic revelation, knowledge is here taught by restating that [inferior path] for the sake of attaining the supreme good. (47)

He states another intended meaning for the presentation of the five sheaths with the words, "from another scriptural passage" (*śrutyantarāt*). For it is established that in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* and other texts, meditation upon the Virāj-self and the Sūtra-self is prescribed for the attainment of those fruits which lie prior to liberation and are included within the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); here, by way of restating that, knowledge which has liberation as its fruit is being taught.
This is the meaning. || 47 ||

By the very boat of the knowledge of Brahman, [one crosses] the great ocean of the sheaths and of misfortune.
Then, desiring to lead him to the further shore, she spoke thus: "He indeed [is that]."

Having thus stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he introduces a scriptural passage regarding that very same subject for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the words, beginning with "Brahmavidyā. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the Śruti [desires] to lead [the person]"; [it refers to] the person alone in relation to knowledge and action.
The meaning of the word "atha" (then) is that it follows immediately after the determination that [the agent] is not [the cause] of animals and so forth. || 48 ||
Having touched the fundamental self (mūlātman) through sound, he then enters into the state of being the sheath (kośātmatā) for the sake of remembering that; thus he is designated as "this" (eṣa).

Therein, he explains the meaning of the three words— beginning with "the fundamental Self" (*mūlātmānam*). Having grasped the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which is distinct from cause and effect, by means of the word "self" (*sva*), and having established through the word "verily" (*vai*) that very Self well-known in all the Upaniṣads,
[he shows] that it alone, having attained the nature of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) through its own ignorance, becomes another— [not different from itself].
The meaning is that this [Self] is taught by means of words such as "knower" (kṣatṛ) and so forth. || 49 ||

Indeed, it is as if [the Self] takes pity on that [individual soul], which, though unworthy of it due to ignorance, has entered into the state of the five sheaths—just as a rope may appear to have the nature of a snake. 50.

If the inner self (pratyagātman) is of a nature distinct from cause and effect, then how could it possibly assume the nature of the five sheaths (pañcakośa) through ignorance (avidyā)? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Through ignorance" (avidyayā). || 50 ||
In this context, that [transformation] is denied for the Supreme Self;
however, through both reasoning and scripture, it is understood that the body is the effect of food. (51)

Having raised the doubt as to how the inner self (*pratyagātman*) can consist of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) as previously stated, [the author] says: "The suffix *maya* here... In the present passage, the suffix *maya* is employed in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). And because of the reasoning that the supreme inner self is partless, unattached, and so forth, it is established by such statements as "it is not born, it does not die," and so on, that it is not subject to modification.

Furthermore, it is not established because it has been refuted by the [scriptural] departure [of the self]. Therefore, the meaning is that since the body is perceived as a transformation of the essence of food (annarasa), and the self likewise possesses that as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), the designation [of the self as "consisting of food"] is thus established. || 51 ||
"Let this very head of his not be characterized by superimposition (adhyāsa), just like the sheath of vital breath (prāṇakośa)"; it is from this [statement] that it is determined. (52)

He states "this very one" (*idameva*) in order to show that what is to be grasped in the first sheath, beginning with the head, is indeed what is well-known [in common experience], and not a conceptual construction as in the case of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; thus he says "this very one. Furthermore, since the suffix *maya* is used in the sense of "consisting of" (*tadātmaka*) in the case of *annamaya prāṇaḥ*, it follows that the suffix *maya* is employed in the sense of "consisting of" when applied to the self (*ātman*). Moreover, the suffix *maya* is used in the sense of "made of" (*vikāra*) in cases where there is a distinction between the material cause and its product, as in *mṛnmaya* (made of clay) or *suvarṇamaya* (made of gold); however, in the present context, no such distinction exists between the self and the essence of food. To the question of why the identity of the body with Virāj is stated, he says: "the state of being Virāj. When, through meditation, the body attains the nature of Virāj, the vital breath (prāṇa) residing within that body also becomes Hiraṇyagarbha; consequently, the Self, having that as its limiting adjunct, is established as unconditioned.
The meaning is that just as when a jar is destroyed and has attained the state of shards and so forth, the lamp contained within it attains the state of mere light, so it is in this case. || 54 ||
One should know that by means of the *annamaya* alone,
all those [sheaths] beginning with the *prāṇamaya*, fashioned in the form of a person, are like molten copper in a crucible. 55.

The head and other parts of the *annamaya* (consisting of food) are well known; however, raising the doubt as to how this applies to the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath) and the others, he says: "One should know. Just as molten copper or similar metal cast into a mold takes on the shape of that mold, so too, because the body possesses a head and other such features, the *prāṇamaya* and the rest situated within it should be understood as being endowed with those same features.
The meaning is that this conceptual construction (kalpanā) is for the sake of the true purpose and for the sake of making the discernment of the meanings of words easy. || 55 ||

Furthermore, a verse that restates what has been said above is also recited here, out of a desire for the welfare [of others], on the day of the realization of the meaning spoken by the Brāhmaṇa. (56)
He states the meaning of the phrase "there is also this verse" as follows: "as has been explained," etc. (56).
Thus ends the first section. || 1 ||
From food alone all creatures are born; nourished by it, they grow; and indeed, they dissolve entirely back into food.
He joins the syllables of the verse [beginning with] "From food indeed" (annādeva). || 57 ||

Food, being produced prior to the elements, is the Virāj, the eldest.
He is indeed the first embodied being; such is the ancient traditional teaching.
Regarding the statement that "food is indeed the eldest of beings," how is the primacy of food asserted? To this he says:
"From the beings. He provides the authority for the fact that Virāj was produced prior to the beings: "That indeed...
Because it burns, fire is called *oṣa*; that by which it causes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) to burn is [called] *auṣadha*.
Therefore, those who know the truth of its elevation always call it medicine (*auṣadha*). (59)

Anticipating the question of how it is that food is said by the Śruti to be "all herbs," he says: "Because of burning" (*oṣaṇāt*). This means because of its burning nature. He establishes the burning nature of fire with the words: "the minerals" (*dhātūn*). The meaning is that it burns; that is, it consumes. When food is not obtained, the digestive fire (*jāṭharo 'gniḥ*) burns only the bodily constituents (*dhātūn*); of that—
By the words "from grains" (*dhānāt*), he expresses that food is medicine because it provides nourishment, drink, relief, and satisfaction; thus he says: "from grains. (59)

Since the cow nourishes all beings with her teats— consisting of food to be sucked and so forth— for the calf known as the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), she is therefore the source of all medicinal herbs.
He states the summarized meaning of the verse beginning with "sarvoṣadham" (all-herb) as follows: "of all [things]" (*sarveṣām*). By the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in the phrase "with things to be sucked, etc. (*coṣyādibhiḥ*), the inclusion of things to be licked, chewed, and eaten is intended; "dhayati" means "he causes to drink. || 60 ||
For food is indeed the cause of the world's arising, subsistence, and destruction. || 61 ||
Those who constantly worship for the sake of attaining their goals obtain all food through the self as the deity. 62.
Regarding the statement "those who worship food as Brahman," he states the reason for applying the word "Brahman" to food: "Because it arises.

He states the fruit of the meditation on food as Brahman: "Those, indeed... That food, which consists of the Virāj, those who meditate upon it with the sense of "I" (ahaṃgraha) through long-term practice, devotion, and continuity, they [become] everything in the form of the Virāj-self.
Or they obtain internal food; for the meaning is that the worshiper of Virāj becomes the eater of all kinds of food, just like the Self of Virāj itself. || 61 || 62 ||

Sureśvarācārya’s *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*—[In the *Brahmavallī*]: "This is indeed Virāj," so it is said; for the status of being the eater of food is affirmed by the followers of the *Tāṇḍya*.
Since every effect is pervaded by the cause in the form of the Eater.
Thus, for the purpose of teaching the cause, it is further stated: "For food indeed [is this]. (63)

He states the authority for Virāj’s being the eater of food with the words, "That very [Virāj]," etc. Anticipating the question, "For what purpose is the repetition of the passage beginning with 'Food indeed is the life of beings'? he says, "The effect," etc. This is for the purpose of supporting the worshiper's ability to consume all food by means of the nature of the Virāj-self; thus, it demonstrates the pervasion of the effect by the Virāj-self, which is the object of worship.
The moment [of the argument] is stated again by means of a further statement. For it is observed that every effect is pervaded by its cause;

and since all food is pervaded here in this context by Virāj in the form of *aut* (the syllable *au*), therefore, for one who meditates upon food, the eating of all food becomes possible through the form of the self that is Virāj.
Thus, the passage beginning with "for food" (*annaṃ hi*) is repeated for the purpose of stating this reason.
The meaning is that the speech is appropriate. || 63 ||
Because it is eaten as the primary substance, and because it likewise eats, that is called "food" (anna) by the wise, on account of this relationship between the eater and the eaten. (64)
He states the meaning of the two statements beginning with "is eaten" and "eats": "It is called food (anna) because it is eaten and because it causes eating. || 64 ||
The Virāṭ attains all effects by virtue of being their causal self;
therefore, it is designated as "Tat" (That) for the purpose of entering within them. || 65 ||

He concludes the statement regarding the pervasion of Virāj by means of the relationship between food and the eater of food—stated as being identical with Prajāpati—by saying "he attains. He explains that the section concerning Prāṇa proceeds for the purpose of causing the entry of the intellect into the Self, which resides within, [starting] from the subject under discussion, namely the material cause (prakṛti), which is food, and from the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya), which is the Annamaya [Self]. Thus he says: "Then from that..."
Rapture. || 65 ||
Having reminded [the listener] who stands at a great distance by the word *vai* alone,
one takes up the Vairāja [sāman] which has the form of the inner self (adhyātma-rūpin) by means of the word *tasmāt*;
then, by the word *etasmāt*, the state of being Vairāja is made manifest.

Regarding the meaning of the three words in the sentence thus introduced, he says: "By the word *vai*. By means of the word *vai*, one is reminded of the Virāj-self, which consists of food and constitutes the primary sense [of the root], situated at a great distance; it is precisely there [that the following is stated].

Therefore, having employed the word "from that" (*tasmāt*) and having grasped the *Virāj* as the self, the identity of this [self] with the *Virāj* is demonstrated by the pronoun "this" (*etasmāt*), which refers back to what was previously introduced as the *Virāj* and shares the same grammatical core (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, because the body— which is of internal form and serves as the substrate for cognition— is present here. This is due to the coreferentiality of the two words.
The meaning is that [it] would be impossible without [the quality of] being a single entity. || 66 || 67 ||
In this way, the effect would possess the very nature of its cause; the same would apply to subsequent effects as well.
Thus, Brahman would become infinite, otherwise it would contradict the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhya.

Just as here, by means of the words "that" (tat) and "this" (etat), the identity of the Virāj with the internal body is intended, so too in what follows, by means of the words "that" and "this," the identity of the effects—such as the *prāṇamaya*—with their cause, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is intended. He states this with the words: "of the effects. [The result] follows from the fact that the effect is nothing but its cause.

He says of that: "It is Brahman. The meaning is that, according to the logic already stated, since the phenomenal world of duality is nothing but the unknown Brahman, it is established that its ultimate conclusion is as a mere undivided reality, distinct from both cause and effect. However, if there were a difference between the world and Brahman, then that very duality would be the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) or determination of the Sāṃkhyas and others.
Consequently, there would be a contradiction with the reasonings of various scriptures; thus he says: "Sāṃkhya... (verse 68).
By means of positive concomitance through its own nature and by means of negative concomitance through the exclusion of prior effects, the aforementioned point has been established. (69)
He establishes that the effect has the nature of its cause by means of another reason: "pūrvakārya... (the previous effect).

Because the subsequent cause, such as the *prāṇamaya*, is established as distinct from the preceding effect, such as the *annamaya*, there is the establishment of their difference (*vyatireka-siddhi*).
Furthermore, because the preceding effect is concomitant with the subsequent cause, and through the absence of that [cause] there is the absence of that [effect], there is concomitance (*anvaya*).
Success! The meaning is that, in this way, through both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the identity of cause and effect has been established. || 69 ||

Distinct from this aforementioned self consisting of food (annamaya), there is another, different from it, inner, and inward-facing; this is the Self (ātman) because of its connection with the nature of the Self. (70)
He explains the meaning of the words "another inner self" (anyo'ntara ātmā) with the phrase "as stated" (yathokta). || 70 ||
Just as the food-sheath was previously pervaded by four sheaths, one should understand that the subsequent ones likewise follow from the connection of three, two, and one object respectively. 71.

He extends the principle demonstrated regarding that which consists of food (*annamaya*) to those consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) and so forth, by means of the term "sheaths" (*kośaiḥ*). As [in the case of] 1.
ka. kha. *'jyeta te*; 2. ka. cha. *'rājā.mā*; 3. ka. *'nandaṃ bha*; 4. ga. gha. saṃ. *svātma*.

The *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya—[in the first section of the *Brahmavallī*]: The one established as the *annamaya* (consisting of food) is encompassed by the four sheaths (*kośas*) consisting of *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*; likewise, the *prāṇamaya* is encompassed by the three consisting of *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*.

The mind-made (manomaya) is pervaded by both the consciousness-made (vijñānamaya) and the bliss-made (ānandamaya); however, the consciousness-made is pervaded by the single bliss-made. Therefore, since each preceding layer is pervaded by each succeeding one, the meaning is that the nature of each preceding layer is established as being the succeeding layer, just as a rope is [mistakenly perceived] as a snake. || 71 ||
This [self] is filled by that vital-breath (prāṇamaya), like a serpent by its rope;
the food-made (annamaya) self is fashioned through its effects, according to the scripture which states it is "a mere beginning in speech. (72)
He cites the statement "by that it is filled" as proof for the fact that the *annamaya* (consisting of food) is pervaded by the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath).
Anticipating the objection that this example is inappropriate because the *annamaya* is not established as being merely imagined (*kalpita*), he says:
"In terms of its effect" (*kāryataḥ*). || 72 ||

For it has been stated that this one which is known as the vital-breath sheath (prāṇamaya) is indeed of human form; since it is formless, how could there be anything else [within it], and what can be considered its cause? || 73 ||

He states the meaning of the passage "That indeed is of the form of a person" with the words "sa vā" (that indeed). He raises an objection, saying that because the *prāṇamaya* (sheath of vital breath) is partless, it is illogical for it to have the form of a person characterized by having a head, hands, and so forth; this he does with the words "amūrtatvāt" (because of being formless). He provides the resolution with the passage beginning "tasya puruṣavidhatām" (its state of being of the form of a person), stating that [the description] is based on a cause. [This refers to] the gross body—

Because this [Self] has the form of a person (*puruṣākāratva*), the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) contained within it is also conceived as having the form of a person, like molten copper poured into a mold.
Therefore, the meaning is that the cause for its being in the form of a person is stated by this sentence. || 73 ||
Prāṇa is its head because it is the most excellent; since prāṇa has its abode in the mouth, vyāna is its right wing and apāna is said to be the left.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "His very breath is the head" as follows: "His breath... (verse 74).
The commonality would be vigor, while the other [the opponent's position] lacks that nature;
and here the word "space" (ākāśa) would be used because of its similarity to the sky (ambara). (75)

When it is asked, "What is this vyāna?", [the author] points to the possessor of the attribute (dharmī) by means of the attribute (dharma), stating that the common property of the bodily functions is the vigor of vyāna—thus he says, "sāmānyam" (the commonality). He states "of the other" (itarasya) to show that prāṇa and the rest do not possess such a quality. Regarding the phrase "ākāśa is the Self," by the word "ākāśa"—

The *samāna* [breath] is grasped because, due to its pervasiveness, it is similar to space; thus he says: [This concludes] the third section, accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri. Page 103.
And "space" as well. || 75 ||
Because it is the support of the vital breaths (prāṇas), that Self (ātman) exists according to scripture;
and because of the scriptural vision stating, "The earth is the deity, she is the tail. (76)

This is proclaimed to be the cause of the stability of the internal *asat*; just as [it was taught] regarding the self consisting of food (*annamaya*), he here likewise speaks a verse concerning the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*). (77)

Anticipating the objection, "How can the *samāna* [breath] be all-pervasive?", he provides the answer— showing that the *samāna* is the self (*ātman*) of the vital functions (*vṛtti*), since the scripture, in the passage "On what is the *prāṇa* established?", reveals that the functions beginning with *prāṇa* are all established in the *samāna*— by stating, "Of the *prāṇas*... He then introduces the sentence, "The earth is the tail, the support."

The word "earth" refers to the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*); this is the remainder [of the sense]. By the scriptural text, "This very [earth], having firmly held the downward breath (*apāna*) of the person," he connects the sentence as follows: for the internal breath, this deity Earth is the support—the cause of stability—like a tail.
Regarding the phrase "This very [earth]," he states the meaning of the verse that follows, beginning with "And on this point there is this verse."
"As if in a non-self," [so it is said]. 76 || 77 ||
Thus ends the second section. || 2 ||
Following after that very breath, the gods breathe; they do not breathe by their own power.
He explains the syllables of the verse beginning with "The gods breathe after the breath" (prāṇaṃ devā anuprāṇanti) as follows: "The breath," etc. (78).
When you rain here, then these living beings breathe;
humans, animals, and others live by depending upon their vital breath. (79)
He cites another scriptural passage to show that the activity of the gods and others is dependent upon the vital breaths: "You rain," etc. (79).
The internal organs, the external deities, and the presiding divinities—having attained the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), they abandoned death; so says the Śruti.
Regarding that very point, he shows the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti: "With reference to the self," etc. (80).
All this is consistent because the vital breath (*asu*) is indeed the life-force (*āyus*) of everything;
therefore, those who know that [reality] have repeatedly called it "the life of all" (*sarvāyus*). (81)
The scripture beginning with "Then he carried her beyond death" is what is understood by the word "śruti.

Therefore, he states the meaning of the phrase "it is called sarvāyuṣam" as follows: "That [word] is appropriate," etc. [This refers to] the reference to the vital breath (prāṇa) for the sake of providing a causal basis.

The *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika* composed by Sureśvarācārya—[in the *Brahmavallī*, seventh section]: "All things exist, mutually increasing one another, with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as their cause; therefore, the meaning is that the vital breath constitutes the life-span of everything. (81)
Those who worship this self through the quality of all-encompassing life attain that vital breath which is all-encompassing by means of their diligent application.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "all indeed" as follows: "by the entire lifespan. (82)
Of that one consisting of food (annamaya), this which is known as the one consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya) is the existence within the body;
it is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), and for that reason, [the former] possesses a self through it.

The injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhāna*) is not intended to be taught in this section, because the purpose is exhausted by the demonstration of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikatva*) in both the opening and the conclusion; furthermore, if the middle portion were intended to teach an injunction for meditation, it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, with the intention that the mention of fruits here and there is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), [the author] explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Of him, this indeed... (*tasyaiṣa eva...*) as follows:
The author says: "But for him... (83).
Or rather, the Self characterized by truth and so forth is the primary [Self], while this other one is the secondary Self;
for it is logical that the former is the innermost of all, as the Śruti declares: "He who is within the first. (84)
The initial explanation—that each preceding sheath (kośa) becomes the self (ātman) for each subsequent one—was based on a superficial view;

that is incorrect, as it would result in the word "ātman" being used in a non-primary sense and would contradict the use of the pronoun "this" (etad) which refers back to the subject under discussion.
Therefore, what is intended here by the word "ātman" is the conscious self (cidātman) alone, which serves as the substratum for the superimposition of all the sheaths.

Thus he says: "beginning with Truth" (*satyādi*). Since the innermost Self (*pratyagbhūta*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the primary sense, because He is within all, and because there is no other entity internal to Him; and since the sheaths (*kośa*) are the Self only in a secondary sense, and because this is consistent with the scriptural statement, "Of the former [is the latter]," and by the logic already demonstrated for the word "this" (*eṣa*), which refers back to the subject under discussion.
And because it is logical, the meaning is that here the conscious self alone, characterized by reality and so forth, is intended to be expressed. || 84 ||

For we declare that Self to be one whose characteristic is the qualities such as truthfulness and the like, who has cast off the entirety of saṃsāra, and who belongs to all those who are otherwise possessed by false notions. (85)
And because the five sheaths are merely imagined, he states that the Supreme Self alone is grasped here by the word "Self" in the phrase:
"Of those with false selves. (85)

He states the purport of the third section: "For from breath... By the reasoning stated in the *Bhṛguvallī*—namely, that these beings are indeed born from breath—one sets aside the self consisting of food (*annamaya*).
The commencement of the third sheath is intended to lead that person who has settled on the thought "I am breath" to the self consisting of mind (*manomaya*).

even though it is heard in scripture that "one attains this self consisting of bliss," whereby it is the object of the act of attaining (*saṃkramaṇa*), how can the one consisting of bliss be an effect?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "of those whose nature is effects. (27)
Whether it be passing away, attainment, or transmigration, there can be no such thing for the Supreme Self;
because the Self is of the nature of the Self, nothing whatsoever attains it, nor does anything pass beyond it.

In order to state the impossibility of the transition (*saṃkrānti*) of the Supreme Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), he examines the possibilities of such a transition: "Or is it a passing away? Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-different from the Supreme Self, a transition in the sense of an attainment within the Supreme Self is not possible; thus, he rejects the second alternative by stating, "No, because of its being the Self."

[The opponent] says: "No one whatsoever transcends that Brahman," according to the scripture; therefore, it is not possible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to step beyond Brahman, because of its non-difference from Brahman, and because Brahman is all-pervading. To this, [the author] first replies: "That is not so" (verse 28).
Nor does the Lord, by means of himself, enter into his own self;
for even a skillful practitioner here is not able to climb upon his own shoulder. (29)
He establishes the point already stated—that neither the transgression nor the attainment of oneself by oneself is possible—by means of an illustration: "And not... (29).

Because a form consisting of head and limbs is impossible here [in the supreme reality], it is impossible in the highest principle; this is so because of the scriptural teaching, "Not this, not this" (neti neti).

For this reason as well, he states that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not Brahman: "Because of the head and so forth. Since the one consisting of bliss is established as having attributes through the conceptualization of limbs such as a head, and since no attribute whatsoever—such as form—is possible in the supreme Brahman according to the scriptural teaching "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*), the one consisting of bliss, being possessed of attributes, cannot be Brahman.
The meaning is "you. || 30 ||

"Invisible" and "without self"—thus there would be a contradiction between the preceding and the following;
for if [the self] possessed form, the doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist would not arise. (115, 31)

Furthermore, because it would entail the consequence of contradiction between what precedes and what follows, he states that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not Brahman: "It is invisible" (*adṛśya*).
Since the existence of the one consisting of bliss is well-established as being characterized by distinctions, doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist is inappropriate in its case;
yet such doubt is observed regarding Brahman. Therefore, he states that the one consisting of bliss is not Brahman.
It may be so. || 31 ||

Therefore, this [self] is to be understood as having the nature of an effect (*kāryātman*), due to the weight of the reasoning already stated and because of the cessation of Bhṛgu; thus, its being an effect is also logical. (32)

He states the result of the reasoning already set forth: "The nature of the effect," etc. Regarding the point that—having stated "consisting of bliss alone"—the cessation of the dialogue between Bhṛgu and Varuṇa with the words "This is the teaching of Bhṛgu" leads to the conclusion that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is Brahman on the basis of the authority of its position (*sthāna-prāmāṇya*), he says in response: "Of Bhṛgu," etc. (Verse 32).
During a surge of bliss, Brahmā spoke this with the desire to reveal its means:
"O Blessed One, teach me Brahman," thus Bhṛgu said to Varuṇa.
In order to establish that very point, he states the matter already accepted: "Ānanda... (verse 33).
Since the goal (upeya) has already been explained, the means (upāya) remains to be discussed here;
for since all five treasuries (kośa) are the means, one attains that [goal] by means of them. (34)
He states the reason why the Bhṛguvallī begins for the purpose of prescribing the means for the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self:
"Because [it] has already been explained. He introduces that very means [with the words]: "The means... (34).
For, through both positive and negative concomitance, the sheaths (kośas) are examined as the self;
indeed, it is because of this that their status as a means [to such knowledge] is recognized. (35)
He establishes that the sheaths (*kośas*) serve as a means (*upāya*) by virtue of being the cause for the arising of self-knowledge: "By positive concomitance" (*anvaya*).

In the *Ānandavallī*, the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is stated as the goal (*upeya*); in the *Bhṛguvallī*, by way of teaching the five sheaths—food, breath, and so forth—as the means to that [knowledge], the operation known as positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is prescribed. Thus, [the sheaths] are indeed a means.

Since the two [preceding] verses have already established [the point], and there is nothing further to be said, it is appropriate for Bhṛgu to desist right here; however, one should not suspect that the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is Brahman simply because the five successive stages concern Brahman, for the meaning is that even here the word "bliss" refers to the sheath (kośa). || 35 ||

Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[Brahmavallī]:
Wherever there may be independence for an agent, it is precisely therein that he is enjoined.
Since the fruit does not depend on human effort, it can only be connected [to the action] through its very nature. || 36 ||

One might raise the objection that here no operation known as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is enjoined, because it has already been stated that "Brahman is bliss" (*ānando brahma*) refers to knowledge, and thus that [knowledge] alone is what is to be enjoined. Anticipating this, he says:

"It is of the nature of being" (*syāttarūpam*). This is because, in the absence of the enjoinability of knowledge, [the injunction would be redundant] in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*).

If it is asked for what purpose the knowledge [of unity] is proclaimed, he says in response: "The fruit. For the sake of establishing the relationship between the means and the end—where the operation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) constitutes the means and the knowledge of unity is the end—the fruit characterized as the knowledge of unity is intended in the present sentence, but not that which is to be enjoined.
The meaning is that it is stated for the purpose of proving its non-establishment [as an agent], because it is unfit for injunction precisely due to its lack of dependence on an agent. || 36 ||
Then, for the sake of his comprehension of the meaning of the statement, Bhṛgu ceased [teaching] the remaining five sheaths, since they were already established by himself. || 37 ||

Since knowledge cannot be an object of injunction, Varuṇa taught Bhṛgu the five sheaths— beginning with food and ending with bliss— which serve as the means for realizing the meaning of the sentence; then,
because the remaining knowledge is established by the sentence itself independently of any injunction, Bhṛgu desisted, and not because [the knowledge] was not [attained].

He concludes that Nandamaya has attained the state of Brahman with the words "the five sheaths" (pañcakośān). By the word "tataḥ" (thence), the absence of anything further to be said is indicated. || 37 ||
By whom can the nature of Brahman, which consists of bliss, be denied?
That is the form of the Supreme Self, in which all duality has been entirely eliminated. (38)
In the passage "Ānanda is Brahman," it was stated that the word *ānanda* refers to the sheath (kośa);
now, he says "brahmatā" to show that there is no inconsistency even if it refers to Brahman.
For here, by the word *ānanda*, that bliss which is devoid of all particularities such as pleasure (*priya*) and joy (*moda*) is grasped; therefore, [it is] Brahman...
The meaning is that, because of that [nature], it is precisely that which is denoted by the word "bliss" (ānanda), and not ignorance accompanied by appearance (sābhāsa-ajñāna). || 38 ||

We declare that bliss to be the ultimate state where the distinctions among the forms of pleasure derived from beloved objects and the like cease entirely, and which is utterly beyond the reach of the mind.
He clarifies this very point—that bliss is without distinction and is Brahman itself—with the words "from the beloved," etc. (Verse 39).

When these five sheaths, which have ignorance as their cause, have been negated...
It is not logical that there be a state of being composed of bliss (ānandamayatā) in that which is beyond the reach of the intellect and speech. // 40 //

Anticipating the objection that in the passage "Bliss is Brahman," the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) refers to the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) on the authority of its context, he says: "The sheaths" (*kośa*). Since bliss is devoid of distinctions, it is beyond the reach of speech and mind;
therefore, because it is not included within the five sheaths—which consist of ignorance and its effects—it cannot be "consisting of bliss."

The meaning is that the status of Brahman cannot belong to the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) on the grounds of its location, because that [claim] contradicts the previously cited scriptural passages and other evidence, and is therefore not authoritative. || 40 ||
For the sheaths beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya) are indeed full by virtue of having supreme bliss as their intrinsic nature;
thus, although they are of the nature of effects, they possess the quality of being "consisting of bliss" because that [bliss] is their cause.

By means of the support of the statement "therefore this is full," he states another reason for the fact that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not Brahman: "by the nature of supreme bliss" (*parānanda*). Just as the four sheaths beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), which are of the nature of effects, are described as being filled by Brahman whose nature is supreme bliss, so too is it the case for the one consisting of bliss, because there is no distinction in its being of the nature of an effect.
Because it is filled by Ānanda on account of its cause (the bliss of Brahman), it possesses the nature of being "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), but not because it is Brahman itself;

therefore, just as the self consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) is filled by the one consisting of bliss, so too the one consisting of bliss is filled by the Brahman that is the tail, and is not Brahman itself—this is the meaning. || 41 ||
Therefore, the Śruti has declared that the Self, consisting of bliss and characterized by adjuncts, is the effect of knowledge and action, which is perceived by the intellect as being dear. 42.
He concludes by summarizing the result, given that it is impossible for the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) to be Brahman in the manner described: "Therefore... || 42 ||

For that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya), appearing in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) such as beloved ones, is indeed perceived by those who see their own dreams while abiding in the layer consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya). || 43 ||

He states that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not Brahman because it is perceived by the inner self (*pratyagātman*) during the state of dream: "Because of [the mention of] 'dear' and so forth" (Sūtra 1.1.14).
Affection toward objects such as sons and the like is called the head;
joy arising from the cause of beloved things is proclaimed as *moda* (delight). || 44 ||

6. Sixth Section. Here, regarding this aforementioned matter, a verse is also proclaimed aloud: [The commentary by Ānandagiri follows].
How indeed can one grasp the meaning of a sentence by means of a mantra? || 51 ||
He who knows that which is non-existent becomes equal to the non-existent. But those Brahmins who know that "Brahman exists," they know him as truly existent.

Having introduced the mantra into Brahman—which is the foundation of all, which is self-sufficient, and which has been described by the Brāhmaṇa—he summarizes its meaning with the word "therein" (tatra). Thus ends the fifth section. 5.52.

Even though it exists as the very nature of the Self, if one perceives Brahman as non-existent, that person becomes truly non-existent in this world, being possessed by the conceit of identifying with the sheaths (kośas) as the self.

"He becomes as if non-existent" (asanneva sa bhavati). He elaborates upon the meaning of the verse "If he knows Brahman as non-existent" (asad brahmeti veda cet) with the words "even though it exists" (sadapi). || 53 ||

For indeed, one does not experience Brahman while existing in the form of the sheath; how much less so while existing in the form of a serpent, [failing to realize] the rope whose nature is reality? (54) — Anticipating the objection, "Why is the Self non-existent, since it exists in the form of the sheath?", he says: "For indeed... and so forth.
In the illustration it is the serpent, and in the subject of the analogy it is the Self, that is connected with agency. || 54 ||
If one knows that the single, existent Brahman is indeed distinct from the sheaths which are non-existent,
the Brāhmaṇas know him to be truly existent, because no other form exists for the Seer.

He elaborates on the second half of the verse, "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existent," with the words beginning "asadbhyaḥ" (from the non-existent). The meaning of the reason is that there is no other form apart from the Self, which is Brahman, and it is accepted that Brahman itself is existence. || 55 ||
Therefore, having abandoned the sheaths imagined by ignorance, one should take refuge in the Supreme Self, which is changeless and beyond the reach of the mind. || 56 ||

Since the self exists only in the form of Brahman and not in the form of the sheaths (kośas)—because the sheaths are unreal due to being merely imagined—one should abandon the sheaths through the knowledge of discrimination and know the Supreme Self as the self; thus he says, "Because... (verse 56).

He states the purport of the subsequent text beginning with "Now, therefore, the further questions" as follows: "It has been said. In the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," it was stated that only the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman, and not the ignorant, unlearned person, because the latter has fallen into the notion of the five sheaths being the Self; this very point is now resolved by means of an objection.
The meaning is that there is no purpose for the commencement of the subsequent text. || 60 ||
If the supreme Brahman were common to both the knower and the ignorant, then attainment and non-attainment would be equal for both, since there would be no possible cause for any restriction. (51)

The scripture itself demonstrates the very objection intended: "Common" (sādhāraṇam). If the essential nature common to both the knower and the ignorant were the Supreme Brahman, then it would be logical for both to equally either attain Brahman or fail to attain it; it would not be the case that the knower attains Brahman while the ignorant does not.

The meaning is that, having raised the objection that "there can be no restriction because of the absence of a restrictor," the subsequent portion of the text proceeds for the purpose of establishing such a restriction. || 61 ||

He states another intended meaning of the subsequent section [of the text] with the words "only the effect" (*kāryamātra*). The meaning is that, since the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) have been understood as the Self (*ātman*), there might arise the doubt that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) does not exist at all;
therefore, the immediately following section is introduced both to establish its existence and to provide the resolution to the two remaining questions. || 62 ||
Now, therefore, these further questions will be stated for one who seeks a definitive resolution.
Immediately thereafter, following the teacher’s statement regarding the common nature of the object of knowledge, questions were posed by the disciple in the presence of the guru. (64)

Having thus stated the purport (*tātparya*), he explains the meanings of the words (*padārtha*) with the word "atha" (*atheti*). The meaning of the word "atha" is the immediate succession following the statement regarding the fruitfulness of the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya-jñāna*). The meaning of the word "ataḥ" (*yataḥ... ataḥ*) is that because Brahman is common to both the knower and the ignorant, and because it is immeasurable (*aprameya*), questions arise [concerning it]. [The meaning of the word "anantaram"] is immediately after the teacher’s speech.

Does anyone, having departed this world, enjoy that other world as an ignorant person? Or does the wise person not transcend it? What is the proof for this?
Another question may arise as to whether this is so or not, for she is multivocal due to her triple nature. (65)

He explains by dividing the questions themselves with the word "api" (also). One question is: does a certain ignorant person, upon dying, attain liberation (*kaivalya*), or does he not attain it? A second question is: even though Brahman is the Self, if one thinks that the ignorant person does not attain it due to the absence of the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), then does the knower (*vidvān*) also attain it, or does he not?

Because there is a distinction between the attainment of Brahman and the cessation of ignorance, there is a third [category] regarding whether Brahman exists or does not exist; this is the meaning of the plural number. || 65 ||

And here, the *pluti* (prolonged vowel) signifies an inquiry, since this is the matter to be investigated; indeed, the subsequent scriptural passage is intended as the answer to these very objections. (66)

Since it is preceded by the existence of both, "existence" is stated first. (67)
Whatever effect, such as a jar or a sprout, is observed, it indeed possesses a cause; and since space and so forth are not effects for us, let them likewise be understood in this same way.
Having bypassed the sequence, he states the reason for determining the third question first: "Of the two," etc. (67).

He establishes the existence of Brahman through inference with the words "ghaṭa" (pot), etc. By relying on the worldly pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "space and so forth have an existent prior cause because they are effects, like a pot," it is first understood that there is a real cause; and since that cause is not limited by space and so forth—by virtue of being the cause of space and the rest—it is established as Brahman.
Such is the meaning. || 68 ||
If this effect were non-existent, everything would be permeated by non-existence;
moreover, the causality of a non-existent thing cannot be established because it lacks any essential nature.

Fearing that because the cause of the world, Brahman, is not perceived specifically, it might therefore be non-existent and thus the cause of the world would be non-existent itself, he says: "If [it were] from the non-existent" (asataśced). Furthermore, causality consists in existence at a time necessarily prior to the effect; that is not possible for a void. Thus he says: "Of the non-existent" (asataḥ) || 69 ||
A permanent entity brings about its effect just as a magnet does;
if causality were thus [inherent], how could there be any excellence (atiśaya) on the part of the agent? (70)
Anticipating the objection that even Brahmā cannot be the cause of the world because he is immutable (*kūṭastha*), he says: "being constant" (*dhruvaḥ san*).
Anticipating the objection that something which acts is accepted as a cause, and thus an immutable being cannot be a cause, he says:
"acting" (*kurvataḥ*). If the cause were always acting, then, due to the absence of any excellence or distinction (*atiśaya-viśeṣa*), it would be of a single uniform nature.
Otherwise, the status of being a cause would belong only to that which is immutable (*kūṭastha*). If it is argued that something becomes a cause only when it is acting, then the meaning is this:

the status of being a cause belongs only to that which is not currently acting, because that which has the form of "acting" (*kurvad-rūpa*) does not produce an effect while it is itself not acting. || 70 ||
That individual self (pratyagātman) which was previously described as being without a source (viyoni), he desired; for no one has desire without an object of desire.

Having established the existence of the inner self (pratyagātman), which is the cause of ether and the rest, he introduces the immediately following sentence regarding that very subject with the words "That ignorance" (sāvidyā). He states the reason for employing the word "that" (sa) to refer to the unknown inner self, the cause of ether and the rest, with the words "not [merely] ignorance" (nāvidyām). || 71 ||

Just as a single form of firebrand appears multiform due to something else,
so this multiplicity of the Supreme Self arises from the delusion of forms and names.
"Therefore, the Lord says, 'May I be born' by way of name and form. (72)

Showing that the manifoldness of the Supreme Self through desire is likewise due to ignorance— just as one desires through ignorance— the author introduces the subsequent passage with the words "of a firebrand" (*alātasya*).
When it is stationary, being of a single nature consisting of mere light, its state of possessing many forms, such as length, curvature, and so forth, arises from specific movements.

Likewise, for the other Self, who is by nature uniform, there occurs a state of manifoldness through the power of the delusion produced by ignorance (avidyā) regarding name and form. Therefore, since manifoldness is impossible without ignorance, the meaning of the scriptural text "May I be born as many" is that [the Self] was born in the form of names and so forth. || 72 ||
When name-and-form reside within the Self, they are manifested in many ways from the Self by the Lord, depending on place, time, and the force of karma.
That daily manifestation of the names and forms of Viṣṇu, which belongs to those two, constitutes his repeated becoming, just as the multiplicity of the wielder of māyā [appears]. (74)

Through ignorance, he elaborates upon the manifold manifestation of the Supreme as "situated in the Self. By the word "world" (jagat), the collection of living beings is understood. In both *vārtikas*, the word "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) refers to ignorance. ||73||74||
For multiplicity is not directly applicable to this partless [entity];
therefore, its multiplicity must be figurative, as in the case of the womb [being compared] to jars and the like. (75)
Anticipating the objection that because Brahman undergoes transformation, its becoming manifold is primary and not something created by ignorance, he says: "No" (na hi). || 75 ||
Austerity (*tapas*) is the contemplation of the Lord regarding the subject of creation and so forth as prescribed by the *Śruti*.
Since it is an effect, the impossibility of such a worldly austerity would arise here [in this context]. (76)

Regarding the phrase "he performed austerity" (*sa tapo'tapyata*), he states the meaning of the word *tapas* as "Vedic" (*śrauta*). Why is it that the word *tapas* does not refer to the well-known [physical] penances such as the *kṛcchra* and so forth? He explains: because they are effects (*kāryatvāt*), since those [penances] occur after the creation of the castes, stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so on, and are therefore impossible in the case of Brahmā. (76)
Having reflected according to the sacred revelation, the Lord of the Universe created [the world] in due order,
with its proper forms, its specific functions, and its particular structures.
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "sa sapastaptvā" (having performed penance for his sin) as follows: "yathāśruti" (according to the literal hearing of the text). || 77 ||

The Lord of Lords,

the master of illusion, having produced the world through His very power of illusion (māyā), entered into it just as a magician enters into the imagined serpents and other such things he has created. (78)
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Having created that" (tatsṛṣṭvā) as follows: "The magician" (māyāvī). || 78 ||
Brahman is the causal clay, and the entire universe is its effect; its essence is that alone.
Apart from being comprised of that, no other entry [into it] exists. (79)
Having created the world, the Creator entered into it; this is what is meant by "Brahman. He raises an objection regarding this entry with the words "like clay" (mṛdvat). ||75||
Nor is it heard that anyone other than Viṣṇu entered [the body];
for the Veda declares that after creating the world, He alone entered into it. (80)

If it is argued that entry is not established because the effect is non-different from its material cause (*upādāna*), and thus there is no space for the material cause— Brahman— to enter, then one must accept that something other than Brahman has entered;

anticipating this objection, he says "No" (*na ca*) [verse 80], because such a view would contradict the scriptural teaching that the creator of the world and the one who enters it are one and the same.
If the world had entered [the Self] as clay enters a pot through the nature of the skull, it would be possible;
however, because clay possesses a manifold nature, it is not so for the vision [of the Self], which is unitary. (81)
Just as the very material cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a jar, when entering into the jar-powder and so forth,

is designated as "entering the jar" by way of its identity with it, so too is the designation established that Brahman, the very material cause of the world, having produced the world, has entered into it; thus he objects.
Regarding the phrase "from a potsherd, etc.": he rejects [the objection] by demonstrating the lack of parity, stating "from clay. (81)
How can there be entry for that which is all-pervasive, as if entering a dense forest?
If it is argued that [the self] must therefore be conceived as limited because of the scriptural mention of "entry," [we reply: 82.

He clarifies this very inconsistency with the words "anāpta" (unattained). He raises the objection—"praveśa" (entry)—suggesting that by the scriptural mention of entry, the creator should be understood as being limited in extent. || 82 ||
Furthermore, this entry [of the self] into the mouth and so forth will be possible, just like that of the hand;
however, even for that which is formless, it would not be so, because of the reason that [a formless thing] cannot pervade an effect.
Anticipating the objection—"Even if limitedness is accepted, how is entry possible?"—he says: "In the mouth.
Since entry of one material object into another material object is observed, but the Supreme is immaterial, there can be no entry into the effect [of Brahman].

Sixth Section.

[The objection] that it is logical [for the cause to be omnipresent] because it pervades its effects, and thus there is no location for the effect that is not pervaded by it— this is answered as follows: "amūrta-" (immaterial).
Thus it is said. || 83 ||
Whether the effect is pervasive or non-pervasive, the cause indeed pervades it;
for there is no place devoid of the Self that another living being could enter.
Raising the objection, "Since its limited nature is admitted, how can it pervade the effect? he says:
"Or it is all-pervading. The meaning is that an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) necessarily pervades its own effect, whether it be limited or unlimited;
thus, the claim that [the Self] "having created, entered" would be undesirable even if the Supreme were all-pervading.
Anticipating the objection that because the individual soul (jīva) is not all-pervading, it could not enter into this body, he says: "For not... (84).
Now, if the Lord were to enter the effect by way of the cause, then I would likewise enter the effect by way of the nature of the effect. (85)

He raises an objection: "If it is argued that there is no logical impossibility regarding the entry [of the Lord] because it is accepted that just as an effect culminates in the form of its cause, so too the Lord, having produced the world, enters into it; then [the author replies]: 'Now (atha)'. Just as in the statement 'I am Brahman,' the nature of the Self as Brahman is made known through the negation of the agency of the 'I', so too in the aforementioned [case]..."

If, upon entering [the Self], there were an abandonment of the nature of being an effect, then in that case, entry into the effect would not be established; thus he gives the answer: "I am" (aham). 85.
If it were held that an effect consisting of a living soul passes into another effect, this would not be so because of contradiction; for a jar does not become a water-jug.

He raises the objection again: "The nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the effect of the Supreme Self, consisting of the effects such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, is what is called the 'entry' of the Supreme. He refutes this with the words "this is their view," stating that because one does not observe a jar becoming a bowl, and because it is impossible for one thing to become another, the individual soul cannot have the ego-sense and so forth as its nature; thus he says, "because of contradiction" (verse 86).

Furthermore, the scripture would be contradicted by its restatement of the distinction from effects such as name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and liberation would be extremely difficult to attain if that [distinction] were to perish. || 87 ||

Furthermore, if the individual soul (*jīva*), which is an effect of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), were itself an effect such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), then the Śruti—which states, "Having entered [the world] by means of this living self (*jīva* as *ātman*"—would contradict its own teaching by implying that the individual soul is distinct from effects consisting of name, form, and action. Thus he says: "Name... [and so on]. If the effect that is the individual soul were to undergo the state of becoming another effect, then for that...

[In the Brahmavalī]: Liberation, which is the state of Brahman, would also be difficult to attain without the destruction of one's own nature, since for one thing to become another, there must be a transformation into that other.
He states that even according to our own doctrine, the aforementioned entry is untenable: "And liberation... (87).
"If entry were like that of water or the sun, it would not be by way of an undivided form;
and because it is formless, such an entry is not possible for it. (88)
Anticipating the objection that there might be entry by another means, he refutes it with the words "like water and the sun. || 88 ||
In that case, its inclusion [in the category of inference] is not possible in any way;
nor do we know any other alternative by which the statement could be justified. (89)

If not even one of the aforementioned modes of entry is tenable according to the method demonstrated, then the entry of the supreme Self is not possible in any way whatsoever; thus he concludes: "In that case, then. Consequently, the statement regarding entry must set aside the modes previously mentioned.
Anticipating the objection that it might be established by another means, he says: "And not... (89).
"In that case, let this [statement] be discarded as being useless like the words of a child;
for it is not so with the statement regarding entry, because it relies upon another servant. (90)

Raising the objection, "In that case, how is the authority of the sentence concerning entry [into the heart] to be established?", he concludes the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words, "Because it would be purposeless" (ānarthakyāt). He then establishes the final position (siddhānta) with the words, "It is not so," meaning that the sentence concerning entry should not be discarded, because another possible interpretation for it exists. || 90 ||
Having stated that "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and having described its characteristics such as truth and so forth,
he caused him to enter the cave in order to quell the notion that it is not the Self.

Since the entry—which is not actually to be established—is merely imagined for the sake of knowing the oneness of Brahman and the Self, there is no room for the aforementioned defects; thus, he clarifies this alternative interpretation with the words "the knower of Brahman" (brahmavit). || 91 ||
The qualification "Brahman is the Self" is for the purpose of excluding non-Brahmanhood;
when that [non-Brahmanhood] is excluded, one attains isolation (kaivalya), which is the meaning of the sentence.

Just as it is said that the statement regarding entry into the cave in the verse, "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave," is for the purpose of removing the notion that Brahman is not the Self, so too this statement, "This Self is Brahman," establishes Brahman as the predicate (viśeṣya) in order to remove the suspicion that the Self might not be Brahman; thus he says, "in order to remove the non-Brahmanhood. This is for the purpose of removing Brahman’s status as non-Self.
When the cessation of the individual self's non-Brahman-hood is obtained through the force of the qualification, he states the established meaning: "Upon its cessation," etc. (92).

Since such is the fruit, therefore knowledge is intended here.
The non-dual Brahman is in the cave; therefore, it is said to be hidden. || 93 ||

He states—beginning with "yasmāt"—that since the knowledge of oneness whose fruit is liberation is intended here, the assumption of entry [of the Self] into both the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa is for that purpose. || 93 ||
For [the scripture] indeed states that the effect, ending with the *annamaya*, exists for the purpose of conforming to that [Self]. (94)
Surpassing each preceding one and transcending the three sheaths,
the Supreme has been revealed within the cave that consists of the nature of consciousness.

Anticipating the objection—“How is it that knowledge of oneness (*ekatva-jñāna*) is intended here, since the presentation of the five sheaths (*kośa-pañcaka*) is also seen in this context?”—he says: “tadrūpa... [meaning] “having that as its form. The realization of the nature of the oneness of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikatva-svarūpānugama*), which is the comprehension of that [oneness], is the purpose for which the five sheaths, beginning with the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and ending with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), are presented here; therefore—
The meaning is that it is *jñāna* alone that is intended here, because the statement regarding the five sheaths (*kośapañcaka*) serves as a means to that [knowledge]. || 94 ||
It has been stated that the mention of "entering" is for the purpose of realizing unity; this is now elaborated upon with the words "pūrvapūrva... and so on.

Having grasped the inner *prāṇamaya* as distinct from the outer *annamaya*, and likewise the *manomaya* as distinct from that, and the *vijñānamaya* as distinct from that—having thus transcended these three previously mentioned sheaths (*kośas*)—in this manner...

The cave, which consists of the nature of consciousness and is characterized by the intellect, is where the Supreme Self has entered; thus it is shown that the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme is established—this is the meaning. || 95 ||
In that regard, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is perceived like Rāhu and the moon;
for it is from the human level upward that this happiness reaches its ultimate fulfillment.
As it is being drawn up gradually, one should cause him to realize: "That is Brahman. (96)
He states the reason for the teaching that one should abandon other sheaths and enter into the Buddha alone by saying "therein.

Since it is the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self that is intended here, the Teacher, seeing a fit disciple, would instruct him, "Thou art Brahman"; thus he says, "from the human [sheath]," etc. (96).
In this [reality], which has conceptualization as its source, the non-conceptual is realized; therefore, entry into it is described for him by means of conceptualization. (97)
He elucidates in another way what was already stated—that the conceptualization of entry is for the sake of knowing oneness—by saying "vikalpa" (conceptualization), etc.
For this intellect has conceptualization as its source, because it is the substratum of all conceptualizations; therein [resides] the inner self...

Sureśvarācārya’s *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*—[In the section on Brahman: Only when there is entry into the Self does one become free from all conceptual constructions (*nirvikalpa*), liberated from all ignorance and its effects, realizing "I am Brahman."
The meaning is that because another [person] can be known, there arises the conceptualization of entering into them for the sake of attaining knowledge of their identity. || 97 ||
In this [Self] whose nature is light, we perceive the characteristics of the seer, the hearer, and so forth, due to delusion; therefore, it is conceptualized as having entered [into the body].

And because the specific cognitions of the self, such as seeing and hearing, are modified by the eyes, ears, and so forth through the medium of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), its entry into them occurs; thus he says: "consisting of light" (prakāśātmaka). This—
The word "ripened" (*smin*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Its nature as luminosity arises because it undergoes transformation into the form of cognition;

therein, forms such as "seen" or "heard" are perceived through delusion. Since that [internal organ], when purified, is nothing but the Supreme Self, the conceptualization of its "entry" is intended solely for the purpose of establishing their identity. || 98 ||
By saying, "This very one is his embodied self," the Śruti declares the identity between the two—the one who has entered the heart and the one who has not. (99)

For this reason as well, he states that the identity of Brahman and the Self is intended here: "of him" (tasya). Since the Supreme Self is indicated in the verse beginning with "he indeed becomes the Supreme Self," and because it is possible for the word "this" (eṣa) to refer to Him due to proximity, He alone is the Supreme Self of that aforementioned pentad of sheaths.

When it is said "the embodied self" (śārīra ātmā), the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman alone is established; the meaning is that it is the Supreme [Brahman] itself which, by entering the five sheaths (pañcakosa), becomes the state of the individual soul. || 99 ||
When the faults that cause [the self] to enter into another's soul have been sublated by means of the words "for when... and so forth, then destruction is established as a logical possibility. (400)

If the soul and Brahman were absolutely identical, then the removal of defects such as agency—which are superimposed upon Brahman on account of its "entry" [into the world]—could not be established by the knowledge arising from statements such as "When, indeed...
(Yadā hi). Thus, he states the resulting conclusion in the verse beginning with "praveśa. || 400 ||
The entry of that which has never entered as its own nature is thus conceptualized;
but how could there be oneness through the abandonment of both the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara)? || 1 ||
Since Brahman is non-transmigratory, if the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are one, then by virtue of that non-difference, transmigratoriness must also be attributed to the soul;

however, because transmigratoriness is merely imagined (*kalpita*), liberation is possible through the knowledge of oneness. Therefore, the conception of "entry" [into the body] is for the purpose of attaining that knowledge of oneness.
