He concludes that it is logical [to say] "not having entered": "By that," he states the very reason for the conceptualization of entry. Śaṅkara—
The ascetic [says]: "O Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña). || 1 ||
Having created the effect consisting of both the formed and the formless, the Lord entered it;
just as silver [is superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl, the Self became that very Self falsely. || 2 ||
Having entered into that, it became both the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*tyat*); he states the intended meaning of this as follows: "Formed" (*mūrta*), etc.
Having created the five elements, which consist of the formed and the formless, the Supreme Self entered them;
and having entered, this Self falsely became identified with each of those very things, just as mother-of-pearl falsely becomes silver.
The meaning is that it is just like that. || 2 ||
The three elements (bhūtas) are existent as having form; the other is said to be "this" (idam).
From the unmanifest (avyākṛta) down to the body, this much is reality, and nothing else.

He states a further internal distinction: "The three elements—earth, water, and fire—are *mūrta* (embodied) and denoted by the word *sat*; the two elements—wind and ether—are *amūrta* (unembodied) and denoted by the word *tyat*. Having thus described the oneness of the inner self (*pratīc*) with the five elements, he anticipates the objection that some other distinct effect remains unaccounted for, and therefore provides an explanation: 1. *Mūrtam* (the embodied): This refers to the triad of earth, water, and fire. These are called *mūrta* because they possess form (*mūrti*), consist of parts, and are subject to transformation. They are designated by the term *sat*, as they are perceived through the senses and are substantial. 2. *Amūrtam* (the unembodied): This refers to the pair of wind and ether. These are called *amūrta* because they lack form, are partless, and are not subject to such transformation. They are designated by the term *tyat*. Thus, having established the identity of the Self with the five elements, the author proceeds to show that there is no residue remaining apart from this.
Having understood everything from the "effected" (kṛta) up to the "end of effects" as consisting of the five elements, he says: "from the unmanifested" (avyākṛtāt). || 3 ||
Having distinguished it from other similar classes, this is expressed by means of "this-ness" (idantā).
That which is thus defined is what is meant here by "defined" (nirukta); otherwise, it is "undefined" (anirukta).

He states the meaning of "defined and undefined" as follows: "The common... That specific feature by which a thing is pointed out as "this" after being distinguished from both similar and dissimilar entities is called "defined" (nirukta) by the word *nirukta*.
However, a specific feature that does not differentiate [the thing] from similar and dissimilar entities is "undefined" (anirukta).
The meaning is that he becomes expressible by words. || 4 ||
The manifest and unmanifest forms have been previously described as being respectively perceptible and imperceptible;
those two are further characterized by the nature of being definable and its opposite.
The word "directly" (sākṣāt) excludes the independence of both the manifest and the unmanifest. [This refers to] the three elements...

He states the meaning of "consciousness and unconsciousness" as follows: "Consciousness...
In this context, only conventional truth (vyāvahārika-satya) would apply by virtue of the [speaker's] qualification,
because absolute truth (pāramārthika-satya) is proclaimed at the end of the statement.

Regarding the phrase "truth and falsehood became truth," he states the meaning of the first word "truth" as "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*). He provides the reason for this by stating "on account of the context," explaining that it was spoken as "truth" within the section discussing empirical objects such as Satyadāsa and others, and because of its proximity to "falsehood. He then states another reason for that very point:
"Ultimate" (pāramārthika). || 7 ||
"Like a mirage and so forth, that which is false is here called 'unreal' (anṛta). Thus it was that the Creator, through ignorance, produced [the world] arising from ignorance.

He states the meaning of the word *anṛta* (unreal) as "the mirage and so forth. He concludes the meaning already explained for such statements as "being and non-being" with the words "this, therefore. || 8 ||
For, by the negation of everything consisting of reality, existence, and so forth, that which is devoid of all manifoldness is realized as "I am Brahman. (9)

When it is stated that the inner self (pratyagātman) possesses the nature of the entire world through ignorance, the author explains the resulting implication with the words "by negation" (pratyākhyānena). The meaning is that when the undivided reality, which has become the Self of all, is understood through the passage beginning with "Yā hyeva" by means of the negation of all particularities, then [the aforementioned state] becomes logically established. || 9 ||
"This is not so; this does not exist as 'neither is nor is it not,' because both arise from delusion. Indeed, even the Lord of the Universe has said: 'It is neither existent nor non-existent. (10)

If the world, which consists of reality and so forth, is imagined, then Brahman too must be imagined because it is included within "being" (sat); anticipating this objection, he says: "Not this. For there is no "being" here [in the case of Brahman].

One should know that single Inner Self, which is unchanging, as the witness of the appearance and disappearance of the intellect in this world.
Fearing that if, like the effect, the cause were also subject to deviation from knowledge (*jñāna*), then what could possibly remain non-deviant, he says: "In manifestation... (verse 11).
Therefore, the Supreme Brahman exists, whose [states]—though imagined through ignorance—appear as if they were real, characterized by cause and effect, by relying upon mere existence. (12)

By stating that all conceptualizations of a self are dependent upon the immutable consciousness of Brahman, it is established that the existence of Brahman under discussion is proven; thus he states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 12 ||
Whatever is subject to dispute and is non-sentient, all that is preceded by an intelligent agent, because it possesses that nature, like a jar and so forth. (13)

Regarding the existence of Brahman as the subject under discussion, he formulates an inference as a ground for its possibility: "In dispute," etc. Whatever consists of a specific arrangement is preceded by an intelligent agent, just like a jar, a water-pot, and so forth;
likewise, the world under consideration is also preceded by a conscious being, because it consists of a specific arrangement, as is commonly accepted.
This is the meaning. || 13 ||
In this regard, concerning the matter thus explained, a verse is now stated as before;
it restates the meaning declared by the Śruti for the sake of strengthening the human intellect. (14)

Since the existence of Brahman has been stated through both [scriptural] authority and inference regarding the Brāhmaṇas, he introduces the mantra with the words "In this regard" (*tatra*) [in the phrase] "there is also this verse. || 14 ||
Thus ends the sixth section. || 6 ||
This world, which is perceivable through the cognition of words, was previously non-existent;
and here, by the word "non-existent" (asat), there would be that which is devoid of name and form.

He states the meaning of the phrase "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" with the word "yat. The meaning is that this world, which is currently experienced and is now understood through the cognition of "this," was "non-existent" (*asat*) in its prior state.
He excludes the possibility that the word "non-existent" refers to a void by stating: "by the word 'non-existent'... [The text continues: ...of the void being the source of the world.
The meaning is that it is because of the impossibility of [the self] being a cause. || 15 ||

The effect, consisting of name and form, is indeed non-existent by its own nature because it is not the Self;

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say "from that, indeed, it was born" because the existence of the world arises from itself, he says: "Name," etc. Here, "existence" (sattvam) means the state of being distinct from what is insubstantial (tuccha). || 16 ||
That which is truth, knowledge, and infinite, having been joined with ignorance,

He states the meaning of "Then he made himself by himself" as follows: "Truth," [verse 17].
Since the skillful Lord himself created all this,
therefore great-souled ones declare that it was well-made by the Lord alone.
He states the meaning of the sentence "therefore that is called well-done" with the words "because... (yasmāt). || 18 ||
If an effect produced by Īśvara is called "well-done" (sukṛta) because of the direct hearing of its completion, nevertheless, Īśvara is not called the "doer. || 19 ||
Having explained that "well-done" refers to the Creator, Brahmā, he states another meaning with the words "or if. || 19 ||
In the world as well, they say that the work which is performed with effort by a master himself is truly "well-done," but not so that which is done by his servants.
He shows the worldly consensus regarding the statement "merit is created by God" with the words: "In the world also... (20).
That which is indeed called the "Suta," whose nature consists of truth, charity, and so forth, is remembered as the supreme essence (*rasa*) of this sapless effect (*kārya*). (21)
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That which is indeed well-done" (yadvai tat sukṛtam) as follows: "That which is indeed that... (yadvai tad iti). || 21 ||

Showing the meaning of the word *rasa*, he clarifies what has already been stated: "Rasa... [etc.].

He introduces the subsequent statement in order to justify the previously stated blissfulness of rasa: "of rasa," etc. (23).
For this reason also, one must accept that it exists;
furthermore, the Supreme Brahman exists because its nature as "flavor" (rasa) is well-established.

He states another meaning for the passage beginning with "For [it is] flavor" (rasaṃ hi) with the words "From this" (etasmāt). He elaborates on what has already been stated—that Brahman exists not only because of its being the cause, but also because its nature as flavor is established by scripture—with the words "And from this" (itaśca). || 24 ||
The cause of satisfaction is that which is called taste (rasa), characterized by sweetness, sourness, and so forth. || 25 ||
Just as those who have obtained food and other tastes sit down satisfied, so too do these people,
joyful, free from desire, and devoid of effort, remain for the sake of accomplishing their goal.
By means of explaining the well-known meanings of the words *rasa* (flavor) and *artha* (object), he establishes that the nature of being *rasa* exists in Brahman, thereby proving its reality.

"The cause of satisfaction" means: since that which is non-existent cannot be a cause of satisfaction, and since Brahman is the cause of satisfaction by virtue of being *rasa*, it follows that Brahman exists. || 25 ||
To clarify that very point, he states an illustration: "Food and so forth" (verse 26).
In the same way, those stainless renunciants who have cast off all desires and are free from external acquisitions have attained supreme bliss beyond conceptual cognition.
He shows the illustrative example with the words: "cast aside" (apaviddha). || 27 ||
Surely their supreme well-being greatly delights their minds;
for those very signs belong to those whose hearts are filled with joy.

Since it is established that for the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas—who are devoid of the enjoyment of sense objects and have attained the supreme bliss (paramānanda) that is free from specific cognition—there exists a state of supreme well-being (svāsthya), what is proven by this? With this intention, he says: "Certainly" (nūnam). He provides the proof for this with the words: "From joy" (prahlāda...). || 28 ||
I observe the signs in those who know the Self, like a man with scabies whose mind is intensely attached to pleasure as he scratches his genitals. (29)

He clarifies those very signs by means of an illustrative example: "upāgni" (near the fire). This refers to one who is staying near a fire and is afflicted by a particular disease, especially one involving the heat of the fire.

When one who has previously engaged in scratching a limb or similar act experiences pleasure, the clarity of the senses, intellect, and so forth that is perceived by him as he attains supreme composure with an internally attached mind—
that very same clarity is observed in the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakas, whose minds know their own Self and have never smelled the scent of sensory objects; therefore, it exists.
The meaning is that Brahman is the cause of satisfaction in the manner previously described. || 29 ||
For those who do not know the reality of bliss, this may be an inference;
for those who have directly realized the reality of the Self, it is indeed most immediate perception.

Anticipating the objection that since pleasure which is self-evident through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is accepted as the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*), it would follow that bliss (*ānanda*)—if it were inferable from the previously mentioned marks (*liṅga*)—could not be established as the goal of man, [the author] replies with "Not so" (*na-etat*): because the inference is presented from the perspective of the ignorant, whereas from the perspective of the wise, bliss is directly perceived. (30)

The internal integration of the external sense organs that is observed here is seen to exist in the form of a collective activity toward a single object, even though [the Self] is itself non-composite.

Having thus explained the passage beginning with "rasaṃ hi," he provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to introduce the passage beginning with "ko hi" by stating: "Of the external senses. For that which is observed in the sphere of worldly activity as a collective functioning (*saṃhati*) of the bed, the seat, and so forth, toward a single object called "enjoyment," is [the same] as that of the bed—etc.

It has been observed that when Devadatta—the one who is the residual substratum (śeṣin) not composed of these [elements]—exists, [the body] comes to be; likewise, the composition of the various kinds of air, the sense organs, and the intellect and so forth within the internal body, being observed, must exist only when some non-composite entity exists. This disputed composition has as its purpose a non-composite conscious being, for it is qualified...
Because it is a composite, like a bed or other objects commonly accepted as composites; the meaning is that that for whose sake this composite exists—that Brahman—does indeed exist. || 31 ||
Therefore, with a rebuke, the Śruti says: "For who indeed would breathe?
[Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.11], for if bliss did not exist in the ether, the supreme void, [it would be so]. (32)

He introduces two sentences regarding the point already stated with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). This means that the fact that the aggregate has the unaggregated as its referent is established by inference. Having split the word ending in the locative case, he applies it to the scripture [with the words] "ākāśe" (in the ether): "If [it were] in the ether consisting of the elemental ether, which is delimited by the heart and free from all defects..."

The meaning is that if the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the witness of all mental modifications and whose nature is unsurpassed bliss, were not to exist, then activity would not be accomplished through the conjunction of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) and so forth. Alternatively, [the reading] may be "vāvindra" with the nominative case ending.

The meaning is "no. || 32 ||
In this world, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, there is no bliss greater than that which, according to one’s meritorious deeds, always causes us joy. (33)

He states the meaning of the passage "for he alone causes bliss" with the words "from Brahmā down to... The meaning is that since worldly bliss, which is characterized by degrees of excellence, cannot exist apart from the unsurpassed bliss of Brahman, it must be [identical] with that.
This very worldly bliss reaches its culmination in that abundance [of Being] through the perfection of its means;
that is the supreme bliss, the essence.

He elaborates on that very point with the words "so 'yam" (this is that). Regarding the phrase "the perfection of the means," the word "having attained its own nature" (labdhātmakaḥ) should be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāharaṇīyam*). || 34 ||
Since the reasons for the existence of Brahman have been correctly stated, the Śruti now puts forward the question, "Or is he ignorant? (Uta-avidvān). 35.
In order to state the connection of the immediately following sentence beginning with "yadā hi," he recounts what has preceded: "astitve" (regarding existence).

The meaning is that since the reasons for the existence of Brahman—reasons which are free from sublation—have been demonstrated by the preceding section starting from "so'kāmayata," the answer to the question "Does it exist or does it not exist? is thereby established.
He introduces the subsequent section with the word "uta" for the purpose of resolving two remaining questions. || 35 ||

Only the wise man attains that Brahman which is fear and the cause of fear; for there is indeed nothing else, because of the obstruction caused by the mere quality of darkness (tamas) until its attainment.
In this regard, he states "vidvāneva eti" (only the knower goes) in order to support the point that only the wise person attains that Brahman;
he provides the reason for the claim that "only the knower attains Brahman" by saying "tamomātra" (merely by darkness), because the attainment of Brahman is obstructed only by darkness.
Anticipating the objection that it is well known that even place, time, and so forth constitute an intervention [between the cause and the effect], he says: "Nothing else. (36)
For whatever constitutes an obstruction arises from the cause of delusion;
therefore, it is precisely avidyā that serves as the obstacle to the attainment of liberation. || 37 ||
He establishes that there is no obstacle to liberation other than ignorance with the words: "For an obstacle... (37).

Although it is the witness of ignorance, it is never set nor does it rise;
though veiled by ignorance, it speaks through the power of that very ignorance.

Anticipating the objection—how can even ignorance (avidyā) constitute an obscuration for the Self, which is self-luminous and the very means of establishing [all things]—the author says: "Ignorance. It is precisely for the Self, characterized as described above, that being obscured by ignorance is asserted solely through the power of ignorance itself. Therefore, the attainment of Brahman-as-Self occurs by virtue of the knowledge of the Self.
The meaning is: "only for the wise person. || 38 ||
If it is claimed that its attainment occurs apart from learning, then this objection is appropriate;
however, such being the case, it is not tenable.

Anticipating the objection that since Brahman is the nature of all things, even an ignorant person might attain it, the author raises the following dilemma: is it meant that the attainment of Brahman occurs for the ignorant person through the removal of ignorance—the cause of saṃsāra—or is it meant that the attainment as the very nature of Brahman is equally present for the ignorant person as well? Having thus proposed the alternatives, he refutes the first one.

Regarding the term "learnedness" (*vidvattā*): it is objected that if knowledge were not the cause for attaining Brahman, then even one who is ignorant would attain Brahman. However, the meaning is that if it is accepted that the attainment of Brahman occurs through the cessation of ignorance—the cause of all evil—by means of knowledge, then the objection regarding the attainment of Brahman by the ignorant does not arise. || 39 ||
But as for that attainment which is common to all because of the self-nature of Brahman,
whether one is learned or unlearned, that is not restricted by us.
He accepts the second [alternative] with the words: "But that which... (40).

Therefore, by the negation of ignorance, there is the attainment [of that which] always consists of the nature of being already attained; for it has its cause in the Self—thus I have stated previously. (41)

He cites the scriptural passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavidāpnoti param*), as authority for the fact that the attainment of Brahman through the removal of ignorance—the cause of what is undesirable—is unique to the wise. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) refers back to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) by means of the ablative case. As for the phrase "because it has the Self as its cause": this is because Brahman is the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*) of all.
This is the meaning. || 41 ||
Therefore, this is now being examined with effort through the Śruti, by means of such passages as "For when one who knows [attains], not one who does not know. (42)

Since the attainment of Brahman through the cessation of ignorance is possible only for the wise and not for the ignorant, that very point is established by means of an investigation into the nature of reality in the immediately following sentence; thus he introduces the subsequent passage with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). || 42 ||

But that vision which follows after objects and rests upon all the sense organs is here designated as "perception" (dṛśi), because its object is worldly.
While explaining the words in that statement, [it is noted] because the invisible object depends upon the visible, and of that...

Since the word *dṛśi* (seeing) is based on the act of seeing, he states its meaning as "the object" (*viṣaya*). In the phrase "not seen" (*adṛśya*), by the word *dṛśi*, all knowledge produced by the eyes, ears, and other senses regarding objects is meant. The meaning is that because the referent of the term is worldly, it cannot be something previously unknown (*apūrva*). || 43 ||
That which possesses specific qualities is perceptible, for it is capable of being seen;
but that which is eternal or non-existent is never capable of being seen. (44)

He states the meaning of the term "visible" (*dṛśya*) with the words "possessing distinctions" (*viśeṣavat*). Having stated that an object possessing distinctions is fit for perception by all, he provides the reason for this point with the words "for that [is]... (*taddhi*). He shows the portion to be excluded—the part to be set aside—with the words: "neither immutable consciousness nor the void is the visible, because they lack the fitness for common perception."

Regarding the word "eternal" (*nitya*): the meaning of the term "invisible" (*adṛśya*) refers to that Brahman which is invisible, being devoid of the aforementioned visible objects. (44) For whatever entity is associated with the visible is called "identity" (*tādātmya*). And because it is naturally destitute of its own self, it acquires [the nature of] "worthiness" (*arha*) through that [association]. (45)

He explains the meaning of the word *ātman*—with the words "as being seen" (*dṛśya*). That which is denoted by the word *ātman* is the universal (*sāmānya*); because it is dependent upon individuals (*vyakti*) and lacks its own essential nature apart from them, it is called *ātmya*, meaning that which "deserves" the self.
He states the meaning of the suffix *-ya* with the words "for by itself" (*svato hi*). "Anātmya" refers to Brahman, which is devoid of universals; in that [Brahman]...
This is the meaning of "eternal" (nitya). || 45 ||

Or rather, this may be the waking state, because it is well-known as that which is perceived; here, the triad of sheaths constitutes the Self, due to their connection with being for the sake of the Self. (46)

By the word "the visible" (*dṛśya*), the Virāṭ-self, which consists of the five gross elements (*pañcīkṛta-pañcamahābhūta*) and is denoted by the term "waking state," is understood as the sheath composed of food (*annamaya-kośa*). Then, he states another position—that everything that is an effect, being gross, is denoted by the word "the visible"—with the words "Or it may be so" (*syād vā*). Furthermore, by the word "the self" (*ātmya*), the sheaths composed of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), mind (*manomaya*), and consciousness (*vijñānamaya*)...

The Sūtra known as *Mayā* is intended here to consist of the five great elements in their unevolved state (*apañcīkṛta*). Thus, he says "the three sheaths" (*kośatrayam*), meaning that every subtle effect is denoted by the word "self" (*ātman*) because it is subordinate to that Self. || 46 ||

The fifth here, by the principle of remainder, would be that which consists of the fruit;
it is Brahman consisting of supreme bliss, the unutterable, supreme state. (47)

The "unutterable" (anirukta) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), which—being delimited by the two bodies and consisting of the reflection of consciousness that is the fruit of knowledge and action—is denoted by the word "unutterable" here by process of elimination; thus he says, "the fifth.

He then states that pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is free from cause and effect and is the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpada*), is what is denoted by the word "not unutterable" (*anirukta*).
"Atyānanda" (supreme bliss) refers to that Brahman which is the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpada-lakṣya), consisting of pure consciousness (cinmātra), and is inexpressible (anirukta);
this is the meaning. || 47 ||
We call that the Supreme Abode, the cause of the five sheaths, in which the world dissolves and from which it arises when dissolved. (48)

He states that Brahman, which is unknown to the entire world, is the cause and the abode denoted by the word *nilaya* (abode): "it is dissolved (*nilīyate*) therein. By the term *anilayana* (non-abode), the referent of the word *tat*—Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free—is expressed as being the very essence of the referent of the word *tvam*. In that which is indefinable and non-abiding...

The meaning is that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Brahman," the identity of the two referents (*tattvam-artha*), which are the indicated meanings (*lakṣya*), is intended.
Or rather, this negation is stated here with reference to truth, falsehood, and so forth;
for it has been said that what was previously attained is now non-existent, and thus the negation of what was attained is well-established. (49)

He states another meaning for the passage beginning with "aṣṭau" (eight): "And 'sat'. By the passage beginning with "It became both *sat* and *tyat*," the attainment of the entire world—which consists of both manifest (*sat*) and unmanifest (*tyat*)—is declared in Brahman. And regarding that which has been so attained, a negation is performed in the passage beginning with "aṣṭau," because the nature of the sentence is negative and because it is a negation of what has been previously established.
The meaning is "because it is logical. || 49 ||

For two aggregates, the formed and the formless, consisting of the "consisting of being" (sat) and the "consisting of non-being" (tyat), are taught in another Vedic passage; therefore, the subsequent mention [of these] must indeed refer to those very two. (50)

He states another advantage— namely, the establishment of syntactic unity with other scriptural passages such as "not this, not this" (neti neti) within the context of the negative position— in the verse beginning with "mūrta" (50).

Since the intellect, consisting of existence and non-existence, deviates from the Self,
it is therefore established in the Inner Self by negating both existence and non-existence. || 52 ||

Now, one might object: "Since the fulfillment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) is possible through the realization of the inner self alone, the negation of the manifold expansion of cause and effect is redundant. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that because the non-self-manifold is the cause of misfortune for the self, it must be negated;
thereby, the intellect must be made firm in the self alone. Therefore, the negation of the non-self is purposeful.

Nityāha says: "Existence and non-existence... The meaning is that when the internal organ has entered into the inner self (pratyagātman), the fulfillment of the human goal occurs through the realization of its identity with Brahman. || 52 ||
By the negation of the visible and so forth, Brahman is made known as the inner self (pratīc);
it is not other than that, for how could anything else possess the nature of the ultimate reality? 53.

Raising the objection as to how a statement such as "Not this, not this" (neti neti), which appears to have negation as its primary purport, can have reality as its purport, [the author] replies: The identity of the Self and Brahman, which is established by its own nature, is made known through the medium of negation;
therefore, since negation serves merely as a gateway for the establishment of reality, the sentence does not have negation as its purport, but rather has reality as its purport. Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "the visible, etc.": since it is taught that Brahman is to be realized within the inner self (*pratīci*), one might suspect that Brahman is something other than the Self; therefore, he says, "Not that. For that Brahman cannot possibly be other than the Self, because anything other than the Self is false (*mithyātva*). Since the same consequence would follow if Brahman were also other [than the Self], there is indeed only the identity (*aikya*) of Brahman and the Self.
Such is the meaning. || 53 ||
Neither the meaning of the negative particle nor conceptual construction can attain accomplishment anywhere else without entering into the non-conceptual ultimate reality. (54)

Fearing that there might be a distinction between the imagined and the non-imagined because it has been stated that nothing other than the Self possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) due to being imagined, he says "No," and so forth. [This refers to] the imagined void.

The author states the intention of the Śruti, which begins with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavidāpnoti param*) and concludes with "He finds fearlessness as his firm foundation" (*abhayaṃ pratiṣṭhāṃ vindate*), by means of the verb *vindati*: "Because [Brahman] is the nature of the Self... He explains that since Brahman, as described in the passage beginning with "the unseen" (*adṛśya*), is by its very nature the essence of the Self, it cannot be attained apart from the knowledge of It.

The meaning is that since the two verbs "knows" (*vetti*) and "finds" (*vindate*) have the same sense, there is no defect whatsoever in beginning with "he knows" and concluding with "he finds. || 55 ||
When one directly knows this [Self], which is devoid of qualities such as the visible and is free from sorrow and fear, then indeed he attains supreme fearlessness. (56)

He states the meaning of "this one finds" as follows: "from the visible, etc. When, with reference to Brahman which is without distinctions, one realizes the non-difference from the inner self (pratyagātman) directly, thinking "I am this," at that very moment the knower, being free from ignorance, attains this absolute liberation (kaivalya) and becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; such is the meaning. || 56 ||
Because it was previously stated once that "Brahman is the tail, the support," for the sake of syntactical unity with that, it is understood here as "the support. (57)
In the application of the term "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*), the intended demonstration is that the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is Brahman alone and nothing else;

thus he says, "Brahman. The meaning is that it is well-known. || 57 ||
Now, it is clearly explained by the passage beginning with "When indeed," how the wise man does not go to the supreme state after departing.
Regarding the question "Does the knower attain it or not?", it is determined that the knower indeed attains Brahman.
Now, he answers the question of whether even one who is ignorant attains Brahman or not, beginning with the word "atha" (now). || 58 ||

Since ignorance, even for one who has eternally attained the Self, causes the state of non-attainment;
Therefore, having heard this from afar, the learned man approaches with respect. (59)

He establishes that the attainment of Brahman is impossible for one who lacks knowledge, because it is ordained that knowledge alone is the cause for attaining Brahman, by stating: "Always... (verse 59).
For this very reason, the wise person does not "attain" that Lord;
for, due to the veil of ignorance, He who is already attained is not perceived as such. 60.

Since the attainment of Brahman by one who possesses knowledge is established, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "because": [the verse begins with] "avidyā. One might object that it is improper to say "the ignorant person does not attain Brahman," because Brahman is always attained as one's very self; anticipating this doubt, he says:
"avidyā" || 60 ||
For when this Self alone—which is devoid of visibility and other such attributes—is present, one is indeed deceived by ignorance itself. (61)
For when he [says] "yadā hyeva," he connects it by supplying the words of the sentence "etasmint" which were required;
thus, the ellipsis is: "he sees his own nature as if it were not attained. || 61 ||
Even wealth that has come into one's hand is regarded as if it were not obtained;
through delusion alone, there may be such non-attainment even of one's own self by one's own self. (62)

He clarifies this with an illustration: "Like [the hand]," etc. The connection is as follows: although Brahman is my very self, being the innermost reality, it remains unattained due to delusion (*moha*). || 62 ||
Then, having extracted that [notion] by means of ignorance— just as one might extract a rope from a rope by oneself—
the non-dual consciousness, through its own nature, creates [the world] as agents and enjoyers by way of non-existence.

To the question, "What would happen if one were thus deceived by ignorance? he says: "By ignorance. When this Self exists deceived by ignorance according to the reasoning previously stated, then—just as a rope, through its own ignorance, makes itself out to be a snake—so too this Self, through its own ignorance, [makes] its own Self non-dual...
The meaning is that [the Lord] acts by separating [the individual soul] from Brahman through its awakening, [presenting it] in the form of an agent and an enjoyer. || 63 ||

He explains the meaning of the phrase "they make a distinction" with the word *aram*:

when one perceives by superimposing agency and so forth upon the Self through ignorance (*avidyā*), then, because one considers there to be a difference between Brahman and the Self, one becomes a possessor of false knowledge (*mithyājñānī*). This is the meaning. || 64 ||

"He is the Lord, distinct from me, and therefore I am not the Lord"—for one who perceives this distinction, that which is without distinction becomes a fissure; in that fissure, misfortune and fear arise. (65)
Now, explaining the fruit of false knowledge, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "tasya" (of that) as follows: "anyo'sāv iti" (that other one...). || 65 ||
Even though he is naturally fearless and wise, by imagining his own self—which is one—to be manifold through ignorance, he incurs fear for that very self. (66)

He elaborates on this very point—that for one who perceives a difference between the self and Brahman, there arises the fear of saṃsāra—by saying, "even though he is fearless. He refers to the self perceived through differentiation by the word "that" (tat). || 66 ||
For, by including the second [cause] through the word "hi" (for), the Śruti has loudly declared: "Indeed, fear arises from a second. (67)

He explains the meaning indicated by the word *hi* in the phrase "for when" (*yadā hi*) as follows: "because of the cause of fear. It is stated here that for one who perceives a second [entity], fear necessarily arises; he says that this very point is also shown in another Vedic text with the words, "from a second. Since a second entity is the cause of fear, the Śruti instructs in this manner.
Such is the meaning. || 67 ||

For one who imagines that the Lord is distinct from that which is subject to his rule—thinking, "From whom the Lord is a source of fear"—fear arises from that very [Lord] for whom he seeks fearlessness. (68)
He provides the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to introduce the passage beginning with "in that very [state]" (*tattveva*), starting with the words "from that which is to be ruled" (*īśitavyāt*):

Since the Lord, being perceived as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the object of his rule—due to the severance of the two—he becomes the cause of fear for one who perceives such a distinction; therefore, Brahman itself, having been conceptually divided through differentiation, becomes the source of fear.
The meaning is that fear arises for one who sees that very [duality], because perceiving difference is the cause of fear. || 68 ||

Oh, there is nothing that surpasses the power of ignorance!
She who is terrifying even to Brahmā on account of the cause of fear from fire and other such things.
If Brahman alone is the fearless Self, from where could fear arise for it? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Aho! [verse 69], meaning that it occurs through the power of ignorance (avidyā).
"Free from fear, the god of fear, the lord even of lords—he too would produce fear; for there is nothing that is not within the scope of ignorance.
(70) He elaborates upon the power of ignorance: "Free from fear," etc. (70).
"I have declared that by knowing which the wise man attains fearlessness;
that very Brahman is indeed the source of fearlessness, yet from delusion, fear arises regarding the Self. (71)
Regarding the meaning already stated, he analyzes the portion of the sentence beginning with "yaj jñātvā" (having known which), namely "tattvam eva bhayam" (that very reality is fear). || 71 ||
That which is one, free from fear, and devoid of the prohibited [duality] of the seen and so forth, exists through the concealment of delusion;
for one who remains under the sway of ignorance, there arises fear of that very [reality].
He clarifies that very point with the verse beginning "niṣiddha" (72).

Or rather, due to the delusion that Brahman is distinct from the wise inner self even by as much as the tip of a hair, the self itself becomes a source of fear for him; or else, this [verse] provides an explanation for the "gap" mentioned previously. (73)
He connects the phrase "of the one who considers himself wise" with the word "api" (even).

The meaning is that for one who perceives Brahman as even slightly different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), being under the sway of delusion, fear arises from the very self due to that delusion. This is because there is nothing impossible for ignorance; thus, [the text] says "in that very [state]" (*tattveva*).
Having explained the first interpretation, he states another explanation: "Or else, the explanation... (verse 73).
Even for one who knows that Brahman, it is terrifying as long as he does not contemplate it.
Because it is devoid of the state of being a benefactor, even his learning is composed of darkness;
therefore, he would be like one who perceives silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. (75)

He clarifies the very manner of this explanation with the words "of one who does not perceive": just as silver-ness and the like in mother-of-pearl and such things do not exist in reality as consisting of darkness (*tamas*), so too, even "learnedness" (*vidvattā*) in the Self, which is Brahman, does not exist in reality as consisting of darkness; for the Self, which is Brahman, is devoid of the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower. Therefore—

Regarding the statement that Brahman is devoid of the state of being a knower of objects, he cites another scriptural passage: "Of whom... (verse 76).
For that [Reality] is indeed other than the object of knowledge; it is indeed other than the absence of the object of knowledge;

He states the intended meaning of another scriptural passage that has been cited: "It is indeed other," etc. (77).

Since the nature of being the object of cognition and the cognizer follows after objects such as sound and so forth, the state of being the knower and the known is likewise [dependent on them], for otherwise that [relationship] would be inconsistent. (78)

Having cited scripture to show that the Brahman-Self possesses neither knowability, unknowability, nor the state of being a knower, he now adds a logical argument for that very point established by scripture, beginning with the words "vedya" (knowable): "Upon the arising of knowledge, the nature of being an object of knowledge enters into and persists within insentient things, which are the referents of words; and upon the non-arising of knowledge, their state of being an unknowable self—that is, not being its object—persists in those very same things."

It remains. In this very way, the state of being a knower and the agency of knowing with respect to objects of knowledge belong only to the insentient internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which undergoes transformation and is accompanied by the appearance (*ābhāsa*). Since it is not possible for the Self—which is non-insentient and solely intent upon consciousness—to be an object of knowledge or the like, it is established that the Self, whose nature is immutable perception (*kūṭastha-dṛṣṭi*), is not an object.

This is the meaning. If the self were admitted to be an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) and so forth, then its status as Brahman—established by the scriptures as being immutable, non-dual, and pure consciousness (*kūṭasthādvayadṛṣṭi*)—would result in being inconsistent; therefore, he clarifies the very reasoning already stated regarding its not being an object of knowledge with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). || 78 ||

Having emerged from that which is imagined through ignorance—namely, from the knowledge [of the world], from the knower, and from all other things—one should know "I am Brahman" by means of the sacred word. (79)

"having raised [the question]" (*vyutthāpya*). Anticipating the objection that this would entail a distinction between bliss with a superior degree (*sātiśayānanda*) and unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*), he refutes it by citing the Śruti: "Other beings subsist on only a fraction of that very bliss," stating:
"Brahmā, etc. That same bliss of Brahman, when delimited by a modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) produced by auspicious karma, is [bliss] with a superior degree.

Thus, through a progressive increase starting from the human state, we directly attain that bliss which abides within one's own self. (87)

He presents the relationship between the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*)— namely, that the unconditioned, unsurpassed bliss is realized through the conditioned, surpassing bliss— in the verse beginning with "uttarottara" (higher and higher). The meaning is that, by means of inquiry, we realize through direct perception—that is, as our own essential nature—the unsurpassed bliss which culminates within the self; thus, there arises the realization of Brahman, who is the innermost self and unsurpassed bliss. || 87 ||
Or this [bliss] might arise from the connection between the sense objects and the senses;
or it might be like worldly bliss, though devoid of desire for any means of attainment. (88)
He shows the nature of *vicāra* [investigation] with the words "the object," etc. (88).
In that regard, worldly bliss (*laukikānanda*) is that which is seen to have external and internal means as its causes; it is this very thing that is referred to here. (89)
Regarding the phrase "this very [bliss]," he explains the meaning of the word "bliss" (ānanda) therein: "In that context" (tatra). || 89 ||
1. *vipluṣa* | 2. *śayamāna* (in versions ga, gha, ṅa, ca) | 3. *taṃ svasva* (in versions ka, kha) [page 152] Eighth Section.
Indeed, by this [knowledge] being elevated while remaining within the sphere of our own experience— 14.7. Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.
We declare that bliss to be without means of attainment and beyond being attained. || 90 ||

Anticipating the objection—namely, that why the fruit of karma is called "bliss" (*sukha*) by the word "joy" (*ānanda*), since what is intended is precisely the realization "I am Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss"—he says: "By that which is being elevated," etc. (90).
Since the ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā*) reaches its highest excellence within that which is by nature devoid of excellence, let us therefore undergo initiation; thus may bliss be perceived. (91)

He clarifies the very apprehension of unsurpassed bliss through the example of surpassed bliss by means of the verse beginning with "niṣṭhām. The phrase "sātiśayam" implies "surpassed magnitude" and so forth. The second word "yasmāt" (from which) should be understood in the sense of "tasmāt" (therefore). || 99 ||
This very number, which possesses excellence and culminates in the object to be numbered—just as by this means our bliss may become established in supreme bliss. (92)
He supports the very point already stated in the form of the illustration and its application with the words: "yeyam... (92).
Therefore, the Śruti itself will reveal this matter, because it perceives that those whose vision is directed outward lack the capacity [to understand it] by their own nature. (93)

He introduces the scriptural passage beginning with "He should be young" (*yuvā syāt*) as a means of establishing that very unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*) which has already been mentioned, stating: "They will reveal... Since unsurpassed bliss is understood through bliss that possesses degrees of excellence, therefore, this very object called unsurpassed bliss [is revealed] by means of bliss possessing degrees of excellence.
The construction of the sentence is as follows: the Śruti, intending to reveal [the Self] by way of this door, says, "He should be a youth," and so forth. Now, one might object:

since the unsurpassed bliss that constitutes the self-luminous inner Self can be understood through its own inherent nature (*svārasyena*), the mention of "surpassable bliss" is redundant. To this he replies: "Externally," etc. (Verse 93).
One who is young and in the first stage of life would be [called] *yuvan*; why then [is it said] "a virtuous youth" (*sādhuyuvan*)?
One who is twenty-five years old and virtuous is called a "virtuous youth. (94)

Having thus stated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he explains the meaning of the word "yuvan" (young man) with the words "yuvā" (the young man). Regarding the expression "sādhuyuvā" (a virtuous young man), he asks:

"What is the purpose of the qualification 'of a young man'? To provide the answer to that, he first clarifies what was previously mentioned regarding being in the first stage of life by saying "pañcaviṃśa" (twenty-five years old); [he means] one who is both virtuous and young.
He first states that "sādhu" is an adjective qualifying the aforementioned youth, according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) [of the word *sādhu*], as follows: "It is 'sādhu'... (94).
1. ga, gha, ca. read ‘pattire’; 2. hṛ. reads ‘śayasyā’na’; 3. ga. reads ‘sātmakaḥ’; 4. ka, kha, ga. read ‘prathamava’. [page 153] 4.
Sureśvarācārya’s *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*—[In the *Brahmavallī*:
"Because 'being virtuous' and 'being young' are mutually deviant, therefore this qualification [is added]; for that reason, it says again, 'one who is both virtuous and young'. (95)]
Now he states the answer to the question with the word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*): having abandoned youthfulness, goodness (*sādhutvam*) is seen in the elderly;
and having cast off goodness, it is found in one who is twenty-five years old, intoxicated by passion and characterized by unrestrained behavior.

Goodness is perceived [in the young man]. Therefore, because goodness and youth are not invariably concomitant with one another, the qualification "the good young man" (sādhuryuvā) becomes meaningful. Thus, the objection regarding the lack of purpose for the qualifier does not hold; this is the meaning. || 95 ||
Because he studies everything that is to be studied, he is called an *adhyāpaka* (teacher);
because he performs his duties with speed and excellence, he is therefore the most skillful (*āśiṣṭha*). || 96 ||
He states the meaning of the word *adhyāpaka* with the words "he studies" (*adhyeti*). He states the meaning of the word *āśiṣṭha* with the words "swiftly" (*kṣipra*).
This means that among those who act swiftly, he himself possesses an excellence [of speed]. The word *ataḥ*, however, is connected with the ablative case. || 96 ||
He whose limbs are entirely beautiful and complete is proclaimed to be most firm;
for he exists having surpassed all others in strength.
He is proclaimed by the learned of far-reaching fame to be the most powerful. || 97 ||
He states the meaning of the word *ḍhiṣṭha* with the words "complete" (*samagra*). He applies the word *baliṣṭha* [in the sense of] "having overcome" (*abhibhūya*);
that is to say, by means of that excess of power. || 97 ||
Whatever internal [means] are required by men anywhere for the enjoyment of what is seen, heard, or desired—he is endowed with all of that. (98)
Having stated the literal meaning of the sentence beginning with "yuvā," he states its intended meaning [tātparyārtha] with the words "yāvad" || 98 ||
"Even if this entire earth were filled with wealth for him"—thus has the means been described for action whose purpose is both seen and unseen. (99)

He demonstrates that [the seeker] is also endowed with external requisites by relying on the immediately following sentence, beginning with "tasya" (of him). The meaning is: if there is the aforementioned perfection of wealth, then there is the perfection of external means. He summarizes the meaning of the three sentences with the word "iti" (thus). "Sādhana" (means) refers to both the internal and the external; thus, both constitute the means.
It is grasped. || 99 ||

A person endowed with both external and internal means of accomplishment [attains the goal]. 149 [End of] the eighth section, accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.
He who attains that joy is called a "delighter of men" (narānanda). || 500 ||
He states the meaning of the phrase "that one human being, Ānanda" with the words "by external [means]," etc. || 500 ||
Whatever hundredfold joys of human beings are gathered together, that same amount, by measure, would constitute a single joy for the Gandharvas of men. || 1 ||
He states the meaning of the two sentences beginning with "those who [know] a hundred" as follows: "Those who... (verse 1).
Fragrant, able to assume any form at will, and possessing powers such as invisibility,
these Gandharvas— skilled in dance, song, and other arts— are inhabitants of the human world.
To state the reason why the bliss of the human *gandharvas* is a hundred times that of human beings, he describes the nature of the human *gandharvas* with the word "sugandhinaḥ" (fragrant). || 2 ||
Through the excellence of the means for counteracting many pairs of opposites, the bliss of a gandharva is far greater than that of a human being. (3)

He states the reason for their superior bliss: "bhūyodvaṃdva... etc. It means that it is due to the abundance (*sāmagryā*) of both the capacity (*śakti*) and the means (*sādhanāni*) for the warding off—that is, the rejection—of numerous pairs of opposites (*dvaṃdvānām*). || 3 ||
Thus, from Brahmā (Virinchi) downwards,
each subsequent one is superior to the preceding one by a tenth part of a thousand, in progressive order.
Just as the bliss of a human Gandharva is a hundred times greater than the bliss of humans, so too [is the increase] due to the excellence of the means.

Having thus explained up to Hiraṇyagarbha, the author extends this principle by stating "and so on" (*āniriva*): according to the order of the text, bliss increases hundredfold at each successive stage compared to the preceding one; this progression proceeds solely by making the abundance of means the determining factor. || 4 ||
He should be a *śrotriya*, one who has studied the Vedas, and be renowned for virtuous conduct;
though his soul may be subject to desires, he should likewise be one whose desires do not overwhelm him.

He states the meaning of the phrase "of the Śrotriya who is not overcome by desire" with the words "the Śrotriya. Anticipating the question of where the qualification "possessing virtuous conduct" for him is obtained, he says "from common renown," because among the elders it is well-known that one who has studied the Veda and possesses good conduct is a Śrotriya. || 5 ||

By a ten-thousandth part of the qualities of a human being, he would come to be.
The mention of "at the beginning" was made for the purpose of establishing this [point], namely that the increase of bliss is due to the cause of being "unstruck by desire. (7)

Regarding the first sequence, he states the reason for not mentioning qualities such as being a *śrotriya*: "Because of [disgust with] the human" (*mārtyāt*). This refers to one who is disgusted by the enjoyment of pleasure associated with humanity—like food vomited up—and who, out of that disgust, desires to attain here and now the bliss of human *gandharvas* in the subsequent stage, even without performing the means of attainment required for that.

In order to convey the meaning that the bliss of a human *gandharva* is equal to a hundred times the bliss of humans, the state of being "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*) and so forth was mentioned in the first instance; thus,
for one who has become detached from human enjoyments due to the cause of such detachment and has attained a bliss equal to that of a human *gandharva*, [the subsequent stages are described].

In order to establish the increase of happiness relative to human beings, it was not stated in the passage beginning with "of the learned one who is untouched by desire" that if one were taken as being "untouched by desire" in the very first instance, then his bliss would be equal to the bliss of the universal sovereign (*sārvabhauma*). Consequently, there would be a contradiction: [the text says] he is detached from human bliss... [and yet... human bliss.

And [the phrase] "possessing the enjoyment of Nanda" means that, in order to show that the bliss of one who is not detached from human bliss is equal to the bliss of a human *gandharva*, the qualities such as being a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) are not mentioned in the first instance. || 6 || 7 ||
Both Vedic learning and freedom from crookedness are equal in every respect;
yet, when the state of being unimpaired by desire increases, one's joy increases accordingly. (8)
Being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*), being free from crookedness (*avṛjinatva*), and being unhindered by desire (*akāmahatatva*)—these three are the means for the attainment of happiness.

Regarding these, he states their internal distinctions, beginning with "the learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*). The word "also" (*api*) is to be connected with the words "twice-born" (*dvi*) and "all" (*sarva*);
however, the word "only" (*eva*) is to be connected with the word "equal" (*sama*). How, then, does happiness arise?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Desire," etc. (8).
Since the state of being untouched by desire leads directly to the attainment of a happiness that surpasses all else, therefore that alone should be considered the highest excellence.

He clarifies that very point with the words "yataḥ" (because). Since the state of being free from desire (*akāmahatatva*) is the cause for attaining unsurpassed bliss, therefore even the intermediate excellence of bliss must depend upon the intermediate excellence of that very state of being free from desire; such is the meaning. || 9 ||

Therefore, for the attainment of the bliss described above, there is a triad of means. 151. Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri.
Being learned in the Vedas and being free from crookedness—these two, as well as having a self that is not overcome by desire. || 10 ||
Having stated the specific distinctions among the three qualities beginning with *śrotriya*-hood, he describes their common nature with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

This means because there is no difference in their being explicitly mentioned in scripture (*śrutatva*). Although "freedom from crookedness" (*avṛjinatva*)—which consists in acting according to what has been taught—is not mentioned here, it is included as it is established by other scriptural passages. || 10 ||
While [the means] up to Brahman are equal, there is a superiority of the latter;
therefore, being untouched by desire is the supreme means compared to the two preceding ones.
He clarifies what was stated previously—that both being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and being free from evil (*avṛjina*) apply everywhere—in the verse beginning with "tulye.

Since it is established that there is equality between being learned in the Vedas and being free from evil, while superiority belongs to being undisturbed by desire (*akāmahatatva*), he states the resulting conclusion in the verse beginning with "akāmahatatā. || 11 ||
Those worlds in the realm of the ancestors where one remains for a long time are known as the Ciraloka-worlds; those who perform ancestral rites such as the śrāddha shall also attain them.

"He alone is the bliss of the ancestors who dwell for long in their worlds"—here, the phrase "dwell for long in their worlds" (*ciralokalokatva*) is an epithet of the ancestors, which he explains with the words "for a long time" (*cirakāla*). He asks: who are those who dwell in the worlds of the ancestors for a long time? He answers that with the words "they too" (*te’pi*). || 12 ||
The world of the gods is known as Ājāna; those born there are remembered as Ājānajāḥ.
Those who perform the rites prescribed by tradition are born there in the realms of the gods.

Regarding the phrase "He alone [is the lord] of the Ājānajā gods," etc., he explains the meaning of the word *ājāna* with the words "Ājāna. When it is asked of whom there is birth in the world of the gods, he says—referring to those who perform meritorious deeds such as digging wells, ponds, and tanks—that they are "those mentioned in the Smṛtis. || 13 ||
But those who, being ignorant, are born in the abodes of the gods solely through their ritual action—
one should know them as "karma-devas," whereas the [other] gods travel by the northern path.

Regarding the passage beginning with "He alone [is among] the *karmadevas*," he explains the meaning of the term *karmadeva* with the words "by action alone. By the word "action" (*karman*), mere ritual action such as the *agnihotra* and so forth is understood. Regarding the passage beginning with "He alone [is among] the gods" (*devas*), he explains the meaning of the word "gods" (*deva*) with the words "the gods. The gods are those who perform the combined practice [of knowledge and action] and travel by the path of the gods (*devayāna*).
The connection is that the gods [arose] from Vidyā and Aditi. || 14 ||

One who is thus free from desire is called "one devoid of ignorance" (niravidya);
when that [desire] is absent, that Brahman is experienced by oneself. || 24 ||

In the final section, "of the Śrotriya who is untouched by desire," because the inner self (pratyagātman)—from whom ignorance has been dispelled through knowledge—is present [as the subject], Brahman is the very self; thus, he states that this very inner self is indicated by the word "this" (*ayam*):
"‘Untouched by desire’—thus. If it is said that one is free from ignorance through knowledge, how [is this so]?
Regarding the statement "the establishment of Brahman is certain," he says there: "In that [establishment]... (24).

Where that which was unknown is known through the concealment [of the self] for the sake of subjectivity, there is dependence on another means of knowledge; it is not so in that which consists of self-evident realization.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to say "Brahman is established by itself alone," because—as a real entity—it must depend on other means of knowledge (māna) like a pot or similar objects, as inferred from its nature; [the author] replies, "It is not so, because of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of insentience," stating: "The unknown... (verse 25).
That which consists of the nature of pure consciousness, whose essence is non-dual experience, has no dependence on other means of knowledge;
it alone is that which is neither set nor risen.

In order to avoid the charge that the means of knowledge lacks pervasion, it was stated that [the Veda] does not consist of an awareness [of its object] by itself; he elaborates upon that with the words "it is indeed valid cognition" (*pramaiva*). The Śruti, making known its own object—the Self—precisely by way of its being non-objective, [removes] the ignorance regarding it.
The sense is that it enters therein by way of being a cause of cessation. || 26 ||
This locative case following the word "puruṣa" has as its primary meaning that which is to be contained;
likewise, this scriptural statement beginning with "yo 'yam" is prone to error. (27)

Even if [the two] were arranged together, since the seventh case (locative) lacks the status of being primarily the substratum (*ādhāra*), it does not have the purpose of enjoining meditation (*upāsanā*); rather, because they refer to Brahman as the object to be contained (*ādheya*), they have the purpose of establishing their identity. Intending that the mention of "the person" (*puruṣa*) is an illustration for the sun, he says: "ādheya... [etc.]. Thus, having set aside the sense of being a substratum, [the text] makes the object to be contained the primary focus.

Anticipating the objection that the locative case is not seen [elsewhere], he states "yo'yam" and so forth, showing that here in the passage "yo'yam vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu," the locative case is indeed observed as having the substratum (the Self) as its primary sense. || 27 ||
That which is perceivable by an intellect not struck by desire, which is the constant witness of the intellect—this very thing is designated here as the "Puruṣa. (28)
He concludes the explanation of the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (you) in the sentence "And he who is this person," with the words beginning "akāma" (free from desire). || 28 ||

Furthermore, the mantra "The Sun is the Self" (Sūrya ātmā), as well as the witness-verse beginning with "He who... (yo'sau), testify that [the sun] is radiant and devoid of any division from us. 155–29.

He states that the sentence "And he who is that Āditya" has as its object the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of the word *tat* (That), saying: "He is. He provides scriptural authority (*śruti*) and traditional authority (*smṛti*) for the claim that the Supreme Self is present within the solar orb, saying: "The Sun... (29).

The reality is divided by ignorance through the distinction between the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara); therefore, upon the abandonment of that [ignorance], there is oneness, just as between a jar and the space within it.

He states the intended meaning of the sentence "That is one" as follows: "The Knower of the Field," etc. Since the single reality, which is in fact undivided, appears as divided into the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Lord (īśvara) due to ignorance (avidyā), the meaning is that the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is to be understood here by means of the removal of ignorance, just like the identity of the space within a jar and the great space (mahākāśa). || 30 ||
For the sun is the supreme excellence of this [universe] consisting of the formed and the formless;
its unification with that which is within itself is the negation of its causes.

Having explained the referent of the term *tat* (That) as having the sun as its substrate, and having taught the referent of the term *tvam* (Thou) as having the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its substrate, he states the result of declaring their identity in the verse beginning with "mūrta" (the formed): the primary effect of the five elements is the subtle body (*liṅga*), and along with that subtle body is the solar orb; therein resides Brahman, the referent of the term *tat*.

In this context, identity with the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha) as the witness (sākṣin) is made known through the removal of ignorance, which is the cause of superimposed excellence and deficiency;

therefore, one should not entertain the doubt that the referent of "that" (tadartha) is superior because it has the sun as its substrate, while the referent of "thou" (tvamartha) is inferior because it has the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as its substrate and is thus defiled by passion and other afflictions.
This is the meaning. ||31||
Having thus withdrawn [the individual soul] which is accessible to the human intellect by means of the word "that" (sa),
he then distinguishes it from the exalted Lord, like two ropes [tied together].
He clarifies the intended manner of communicating the identity between the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam* with the words "having restated" (*anūdya*).

Just as it is said, "That which is the serpent is the rope," so too, having restated the referent of the word *sva* (the individual self) as it is conceived within the intellect in its inferior state, [one establishes] its identity with the referent of the word *tat*, which is conceived as superior and residing in the solar orb.
The meaning is that, in this way, only that reality which is devoid of increase and decrease, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, remains as the residue. || 32 ||

156 Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[In the Brahmavallī]: That which is superior, in relation to which [another] is called "Lord" (īśa), is first forcibly sublated; subsequently, it abandons its superiority, for it is dependent upon that which is inferior. (33)

He clarifies the purpose of the qualification with the word "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*). For the Lord (*īśvara*) is designated as excellent only in relation to the inferiority inherent in the individual soul (*jīva*). And that inferiority of the soul is excluded when the soul is qualified by Brahman through a restatement (*anuvāda*). For Brahman is indeed the qualifier of the soul.

The inferiority residing in that [jīva] necessarily sublates [the excellence of Brahman], because it is impossible for the superior to function as a qualifier for the inferior; and since the inferiority of the jīva has not been removed, Brahman must relinquish its own inherent excellence, because that [excellence] is dependent upon the existence of inferiority—this is the meaning. || 33 ||
Just as there is no increase or decrease in the sun when it stands in the sky, so too there is no excellence or deficiency in the Self;
having abandoned both, one finds the meaning that lies beyond words through the realization "not this, not this" (neti neti).

Since the identity of the Self with Brahman and the identity of Brahman with the Self are established through the cessation of excellence and deficiency, the text states the result of that cessation by means of the passage beginning with "not" (*na*) and so forth. The state in which the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman stand in the relationship of qualifier and qualified is what is being referred to here. (34)
The distinction between the superior and the inferior does not exist here within one's own self for those whose vision is obscured by darkness; [only] they perceive such a distinction. (35)
Anticipating the objection—"If superiority and inferiority are real entities, from what could they cease?"—he says: "Superiority... (verse 35).

Since the cause of excellence and so forth is indeed non-differentiation and not a real entity, when that [non-differentiation] has been realized through knowledge, multiplicity does not cease to exist. (36)
He states the conclusion regarding the fact that excellence and so forth are effects of ignorance: "Ignorance alone... (36).
Since it surpasses all joys by virtue of its primordial pre-eminence,
there is a unity between the two states of one's own self and the sun, due to the turning away from the plane of conceptual construction.

The fruit of knowledge is not merely the cessation of undesirable states such as decline; rather, it is also the attainment of unsurpassed bliss. Thus he says: "It excels. Since it stands above all those joys—beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha (the elder-born Brahmā) and extending to whatever other joys exist—that are produced as the fruits of karma, it excels them all without exception.

The unsurpassed bliss of Brahman belongs to that which is indicated by the word *tat*—Brahman abiding in the solar orb—and to that which is indicated by the word *ātman*—the Self abiding as the witness within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, [the two are] identical. (Note: Variants in the manuscripts include *niratiśayaḥ*, *tathātmā*, and *dṛṣṭaḥ*.)

The meaning is that, from the statement consisting of bliss, oneness must be accepted; and through the knowledge of that, ignorance—which is the substratum of all conceptual constructions—is removed, whereby unsurpassed happiness, characterized by the cessation of what is undesirable, becomes manifest. ||37||
For by the words "Truth" and "Knowledge," there is the exclusion of unreal objects and the like;
through the removal of that which depends on duality, there is the unity of the self and the radiance [of consciousness] abiding in its own nature. (38)

He establishes that very identity of Brahman and the Self which was stated: "It is true. From the scriptural passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," because it prescribes that Brahman has the nature of truth and so forth, it excludes objects such as the unreal; because it prescribes that [Brahman] is knowledge, it eliminates ignorance, which is the cause of duality and the like; thus, [Brahman is established].
The meaning is that the identity of the two selves is logical. || 38 ||

The authors of the Bhāṣya themselves have stated that its existence is established through its function, the attainment of aesthetic flavor (rasa), and the occurrence of vital functions such as breathing. (39)
Since the two questions regarding "existence" and "non-existence" have now been explained, the refutation of the question, "Does the knower [go] to that world? is now stated.
Now he restates the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra [Śaṅkara] with the words "by the effect" (kāryeṇa).

Since the existence of Brahman has been established in accordance with the arguments previously stated in the passage beginning with "He desired" (so 'kāmayata), and since the question "Does it exist or does it not exist? has already been explained and resolved, the remaining two questions—[which follow immediately after]—are addressed.

When the occasion arises, the refutation of that [objection] must be performed; thus, the second question beginning with "Or is it the wise one? is answered by the passage beginning with "He who is this...

When it is stated that "only the wise one attains Brahman," it follows by implication that the ignorant one does not attain it; therefore, the question beginning with "Or is it the ignorant one? is also addressed.
"The meaning is determined," so says the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself; such is the construction of the words in the two *Vārttikas*.
When my mind,
which was dense with ignorance, was scorched by the sun of his speech,
I believe that the determination of [the meaning of] "yadā hi" and so forth occurred. (41)

He clarifies the method of exposition with the words beginning "having gone" (*gatvā*). Here, in all instances, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of "being in such a state. One skilled in the discernment of categories explains that the abiding as the self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the existence of that *ānandamaya* as nothing other than the Brahma that is the tail. Since there is the scriptural hearing (śruti) that "one who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and because it is accepted that the individual soul (jīva), being distinct [from Brahman], attains Brahman through knowledge, the position of difference (bhedapakṣa) having been reached, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "Not of another. For indeed, [Brahman] does not perish...

It is not logical for that which has perished, or for one thing, to become another. Since a cloth is never perceived when a jar has perished, nor when it has not perished, the meaning is that the Self is always Brahman itself and does not become something other than that. || 54 ||
If the wise one were non-different [from Brahman], then since he already exists as that reality, what would it mean for him to "become"?
Indeed, it follows that the supreme Brahman is not attained by one who is a separate self, through which means he might reach it. (55)

He raises the objection that if the individual soul (jīva) were always of the nature of Brahman, the scriptural statement "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" would be untenable—this is expressed in the words "If [it were] non-different" (ananyaśced). To this, he accepts the non-difference on the grounds that it is impossible for one thing to become another thing—this is expressed in the words "Certainly" (bāḍham). || 55 ||
Thus,

He dispels the apprehended contradiction with scripture by means of an illustration—namely, "the tenth": just as the tenth boy appears as if separated from his own true nature due to ignorance, and its attainment is said to result from knowledge, so too the individual soul (*jīva*) appears as if separated from the nature of Brahman due to ignorance; thus, its becoming that [Brahman] results from knowledge.

The meaning is that it is described by the scripture. He clarifies what has already been stated—that non-attainment of Brahman is caused by ignorance, while its cessation through knowledge is itself attainment—with the words "by knowledge" (vidyayā). || 56 ||

Raising the objection that the attainment of Brahman might also be a primary attainment— just like the attainment of a village or the like—

Just as knowledge of the path to a village is the means of attainment only by way of traveling along it, so too is the knowledge of Brahman.

One might object that even through the means of one's own practice, the attainment of Brahman is accomplished as the primary realization of Brahman; thus, he raises this doubt with the words, "tatprāpti" (its attainment). He refutes this by presenting the disparity in instruction with the words, "na vaidharmyāt" (not so, because of the difference in nature). When even those factors that serve as auxiliaries, such as *adharma* and so forth, exist as causes for the state of being a living being (*jīvatva*) and the like pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*), [the existence of] *sattva*...

He raises an objection—that because the nature of *saṃsāra* is independent of any external cause, it cannot be created by God—by stating "without a cause" (*nirnimittam*). He then refutes this by stating "not for him," meaning that if it were so, the fear of *saṃsāra* would exist eternally.
Furthermore, if fear is admitted to be inherent in the Self, its cessation can only occur through the cessation of that Self.

"Furthermore, the cessation of the self is not accepted by the followers of the Veda; therefore, he states that under the view of difference, liberation itself is impossible: 'Or by destruction' (dhvaṃsena vā). The word 'vā' (or) has the sense of 'ca' (and)."
But in the case of their identity, none of these faults would occur;

Regarding the position of non-difference (*abheda*), he states that it is free from all the aforementioned defects: "In the case of oneness," etc. [This means that] there would always be the state of being a transmigrator (*saṃsāritva*) and never the state of liberation (*muktatva*); furthermore, there would be the futility of the causes of bondage and the causes of liberation, as well as contradiction with the scriptures.
This refers to "of these" [as mentioned previously]. In that regard, he indicates the reason with the words "of fear. || 72 ||

Fear could arise from another cause or from itself; however, it cannot be from either, because there is no independence in the other, and the destruction of one's own self is not admitted [in the case of fear arising from itself]. (73)

Thus he says, "by another" (*anya*): if another cause of fear is admitted, then because the self lacks independence, the fear of saṃsāra caused by that other would necessarily exist forever.

In the view that fear has another as its cause, he establishes the cessation [of fear] through dread with the words "svātantrya" (independence). But if ignorance alone is the cause, all this is consistent;
