Anticipating the objection that "all that has been said applies equally even to your own position," he reminds us of what was stated regarding the theory of unity with the words "avidyā" (ignorance). || 75 ||
From the knowledge of that from which fear arises due to ignorance, how could that [fear] possibly exist?
Therefore, like the snake in a rope and other such illusions, fear originates solely from nescience (avidyā).

Fearing that even for the wise there might be no cause for fear other than ignorance because they perceive danger, [the author] says: "Because of which there is ignorance. Although fear may appear to persist in the wise due to the persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), he states the resulting conclusion regarding its impossibility in reality: "Like the snake in the rope," etc. (Verse 76).
If it is argued that power consists of both knowledge and ignorance, that is not so, because of their mutual contradiction;
furthermore, they are perceived as distinct from the self, just like a jar and its form. (77)

Having raised the objection that if one accepts the perception of fear in the self due to ignorance (*avidyā*) and its cessation through knowledge (*vidyā*), then both knowledge and ignorance would have to be admitted as existing therein, he considers the alternatives— whether these two are the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the self or its attributes (*dharma*)— and refutes the first by stating "knowledge" (*vidyā*). This is because they cannot be the self.
He states another reason: "And separately," [verse 77].
For knowledge and ignorance, which reside in the mind, are perceived by direct perception;
therefore, they do not have the self as their inherent property, but rather belong to name-and-form (nāmarūpa). (78)
He states another alternative: "by perception. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is occasional cognition; ignorance (*avidyā*) is false knowledge and non-apprehension.
Since these two are experienced as residing in the mind, their material cause is that which is beginningless.
He states that both knowledge and ignorance, along with their respective substrates, reside solely within the indefinable ignorance (*anirvācya-ajñāna*), by saying "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
By the term "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), beginningless ignorance is denoted. (78)

Those [states] which exist between name-and-form and that which is outside of Brahman belong to those two; they do not exist in Brahman, just as rising and setting do not exist in the sun. 167–168.99.

He states the evidence for the mutual difference between name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and Brahman with the words "between" (*antareti*). The meaning is that those two, name-and-form, are distinct from and external to Brahman, and that Brahman is likewise distinct from within those two, name-and-form. Even though they are distinct, he [now] explains their connection within Brahman:
He says "they do not exist" (verse 79) to show that it is not so, because such a doubt would contradict scriptural passages concerning non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*).

If it is argued that there would be the fault of a single entity being both the agent and the object of the action, we say no; for that [transformation] is merely a cognition, and as such, it dispels for us the notion of difference.

As for the objection that if there were non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, there would be a contradiction regarding the relationship of object and agent in the statement "he reaches this self consisting of bliss," [the author] refutes that by citing the word "karma" (object). For in this sentence,
"reaching" (saṃkrānti) is merely the knowledge "I am Brahman," and since that [knowledge] consists of the superimposed effects upon the Self that is Brahman—

He elaborates on the refutation itself—namely, that once knowledge has been attained, there is no longer any suspicion of a contradiction regarding the agency of action—by stating: "Because of the transition," etc. (80).
If the self does not know itself as being connected with pleasure, pain, and so forth, then for what reason do you have the desire for liberation? Tell me this out of confidence. (81)

Raising the objection that since the transmigratory world (*saṃsāra*) does not exist at all within the eternally liberated Brahman-Self, how could its cessation be the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*), [the author] replies with the verse beginning "sukha" (verse 81). He states this because, if there were no transmigrator distinct from Brahman and thus no transmigratory state for Brahman, there would be no seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*),
and consequently the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) would be rendered purposeless.

In accordance with the actual state of things during waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the Self knows itself through its own inherent manifestation as "I am dark," "I am happy," or "I do not know. (82)

He states that the establishment of transmigratory existence within Brahman is not only due to the logical inconsistency of the scriptures on liberation, but also by virtue of one's own experience—beginning with the words "jāgrad" (waking). The connection [of the phrase] is: "in accordance with the actual state of things" (*vastuvṛttānurodhataḥ*) and "by way of common renown" (*prasiddhitaḥ*).

The "actual state of things" (*vastuvṛtta*) is consciousness (*caitanya*), which constitutes its very nature; it is in conformity with that that there is "common renown," which is one's own experience.
That is to say, "on account of that very thing. || 82 ||

Having explained that the superimposition of transmigratory existence upon the Brahman-Self is due to reasoning and experience, he states another reason for the absence of contradiction between the action and the agent—beginning with the words "kārya" (effect). Anticipating the question, "If there is no division of action, agent, instrument, and so forth within the Self, what remains? he says: "abhāvāt" (due to non-existence). || 83 ||
The causal factors are destroyed by knowledge, just as ignorance is destroyed by wisdom;
the state of being a causal factor arises from ignorance, while its true nature is that of non-causality.

Furthermore, since agency and the like are adventitious to the immutable Self (kūṭastha) due to being produced by ignorance (avidyā), there is no possibility of a contradiction between action and the state of being an agent, because [agency] ceases upon the cessation [of ignorance]. Thus he says: "The causal factors...
For that which is the intrinsic nature of something does not depend on an action for its attainment, since action has other causes; thus, dependence [on action] implies the denial of an agent. (85)
Fearing that immutability (*kūṭasthatva*) might be considered a property of the Self itself dependent upon action, he says: "For that which...
He provides the reason: "Because it is the cause of modification," meaning modification in the form of arising and so forth.

Then, fearing that the scripture on ritual action (*karma-śāstra*) would be rendered useless under his view, he states [the purpose] by way of purifying the intellect for the sake of the entire world...

He states that the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) is not purposeless because, for the attainment of the knowledge that removes ignorance regarding the cause of manifestation, there is a dependence upon ritual action—thus: "Dependence" (verse 85).
Since another [self] does not transition here into this self consisting of food like a leech, the transition is held to be figurative. (86)

"Why is it that approaching [the Lord] has been explained as mere knowledge by means of a figurative sense? Why should it not be understood as the well-known act of physical approach?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not at all. (86)

If it is thought that there is a transition from external activity back [to the self], it is not so; for, as in the case of the mind-made body (manomaya) and others, an action directed toward oneself is not contradictory.
Just as the mind or the intellect, having gone out to the objects by way of its own functions and then returning from them,
enters back into itself, so too the Self, having gone outward into the body and other such things by way of the mind and then emerging from them,
enters into itself; thus, a primary transition (*saṃkrānti*) is possible here.

Since it is improper—according to the reasoning already stated—for there to be a primary transition, transcending, or reaching [the Self] within the Self, "transition" here refers only to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence; nor is that [knowledge] performed by the five sheaths, because the five sheaths are insentient and thus incapable of being agents of knowledge. The meaning is that when agency—which is [in fact] ignorance—is ceased through knowledge, the agency arising from it is also necessarily ceased; thus, the establishment of the Self abiding in its own undifferentiated nature is achieved. || 89 ||

Free from "mine-ness" and free from egoism, we worship Brahman alone as the Self—
those [qualities] which have been attributed to objects such as substances by their users.
Therefore, words cease precisely upon the cessation of their own purpose. || 98 ||

He shows the distinction—that through the function of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*), by virtue of the word "awakening" (*bodharka*), and from the knowledge thus produced, Brahman is realized precisely as the inner self—by the phrase "free from 'mine'" (*nirmamam*). The words employed by the elders who use them for the sake of establishing cognition are understood to turn back from Brahman precisely by ceasing their application toward their own referents—such as the genitive case and so forth—which are the causes for engagement with objects; therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is not denotable by words. || 98 ||
Since the conditions that produce cognition do not proceed from a mother [but rather depend on causes], they cease upon its cessation;

He explains the meaning of the section beginning with "manasā saha" (along with the mind) by means of the words "na" and so forth. Since all modifications (*pratyaya*), which are transformations produced by the intellect (*buddhi*), are unable to reach the Mother— the witness of the intellect and its functions— therefore, upon the cessation of those modifications from their witness, the sounds that produce them [also cease].

They cease together with those very cognitions designated as "mind," which constitute their own effects. Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is not an object of either word or its corresponding cognition. || 99 ||
For all verbal designations, when employed for the sake of apprehension, turn back without having expressed [the ultimate reality], even after having brought it to awareness. (600)

Even in the absence of a direct denotative power (*vācakatva*), there is no loss of the status of scripture as a means of valid cognition, because the word ceases its operation precisely after producing understanding through indication.
This is the remainder [of the verse]. || 600 ||

In this case, there is no non-difference between the two actions, because of the distinction between the action and its fruit;

Since knowledge is the cause and the destruction of ignorance is the effect, and since the temporal sequence of cause and effect is firmly established, there is no room for this fallacious objection; thus he says, "No," and so forth. 6.
From the word that destroys ignorance, the realization "I am Brahman" arises;

Furthermore, since it is [the state of] Buddhahood, there is no requirement even with respect to other means of knowledge (*māna*); this is the meaning established therein. || 8 ||

Anticipating the question, "In that case, where then is there dependence? he says, "For [it is] in the object of cognition," etc., meaning that dependence exists in that which is fit for other means of knowledge (*māna*) and which lacks self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). || 9 ||

Just as fruits on the bank of a river [are perceived] without depending on perception and other means of knowledge, why do you have any need for other means of knowledge here regarding the scripture of the word? (10)

He clarifies the absence of dependence on other means of knowledge regarding the object already stated by means of a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta), beginning with the words "of the river": Just as in the case of a worldly verbal statement uttered by a reliable person, such as "There are fruits on the bank of the river," a dependence on an original source of knowledge (*mūla-pramāṇa*) is observed, it is not so in the case of the verbal statement of the Śruti, such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

It is appropriate for you to have regard for the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), because it is impossible to state that there is dependence on perception and the other means for the sake of that [knowledge]; therefore, the meaning is that both the object and its means of cognition are independent. || 10 ||
The knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and likewise the ascertainment—all these are established through its presence; what else does it require for its own establishment? (11)
Furthermore, because the previously mentioned entity is the establisher of everything, it has no dependence on other means of knowledge; thus he says: "And the knower," etc. (11).

In the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there is no interruption whatsoever in the consciousness that perceives "this is a jar," because it is the witness of both the existence and non-existence of those states.

Just as there is an intervention— characterized by space, time, knowledge, and the activity of the intellect— for the cognition "this is a jar," no such intervention is perceived in the realization of the inner self (pratyagātman) within the three states beginning with waking; therefore, because the self is the witness of both the presence and absence of intervention, it is always established therein.
He says that it depends on another means of knowledge: "jāgrad" (while awake), etc. || 12 ||
The cognition that "this is thus" and "this is not thus" possesses differentiation;
since it is here devoid of a self yet appears as having a self, what does it depend upon? (13)

Furthermore, that conscious self (cidātman) by which this kind of cognition— such as "this is to be done" or "this is not to be done"— which partakes in division and is devoid of its own intrinsic nature when in its own state, is instead characterized as possessing its own intrinsic nature; that Self is not capable of depending on any mental construction (bhāvanā), injunction (niyoga), or any other means of knowledge (mānāntara), because it is the very existence of all forms of cognition.
Having given [this], he says: "This," [as in verse] 13.

Prior to the activity of the agent and other factors, experience—unmixed with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), undisturbed, and not yet dormant—what indeed does it require? (14)

He states—beginning with "kartrādi"—that since the existence of the self is perceived even prior to the operation of causal factors such as the agent, as in the case of deep sleep, there is no need for other means of knowledge regarding its establishment, such as injunction (*niyoga*) or creative effort (*bhāvanā*). ||14||
How can one perceive that object which is not denotable and does not present itself through the means of cognition, even if one is enjoined by an injunction? (15)

Furthermore, it is not logical for the Self to require an injunction (*niyoga*) for the sake of establishing its own existence, because its existence is eternal; nor is it possible for it to require an injunction for the sake of perceiving itself. Thus he says: "The denotable object" (*abhidheyam*). || 15 ||

Furthermore, it might set aside a factual state of affairs already established by another means of knowledge, if the object were understood merely in accordance with the requirements of the injunction. (16)

Furthermore, if the establishment of a real entity is desired by following the authority of an injunction (*vidhi*), then the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and so forth would be a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) compared to sentences such as "It should be seen. Consequently, this proponent would have to reject that Brahman which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as understood through that [sentence], because the sentence "That thou art" and so forth would be intended merely to convey a real entity in accordance with an injunction.

Since that [scriptural statement] too is exhausted merely by the accomplishment of the injunction, it cannot be authoritative regarding a real entity when there is a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, as its primary intent lies elsewhere; thus he says: "Even by another means of knowledge... (verse 16).
Even an object that does not exist here is meditated upon due to worldly convention, like fire [in the analogy of the heated iron];
however, because Brahman is not well-known in such a way, it is extremely difficult to achieve here.

He states another reason for the impossibility of an injunction regarding the knowledge of Brahman: "It is cultivated" (*bhāvyate*). Although even here the meaning characterized by the eating of the heavenly world is cultivated—since the two entities, the heavenly world and fire, are well-known in this context from the Śruti text, "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire"—nevertheless...

The meaning is that because Brahman—characterized by eternal purity and so forth—is not well-known, unlike fire which is known in common worldly experience, the injunction for the knowledge of Brahman is extremely difficult to achieve and logically untenable. || 17 ||

Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[In the Brahmavallī]: "Even a worldly object is established through the connection of word-meanings; yet, Brahman, whose nature is beyond the scope of sentences, is likewise extremely difficult to establish here. (18)
And for this reason, he says "it is performed" (*kriyate*) to show that it is impossible to enjoin the knowledge of Brahman.

Although an extraordinary matter such as a mandate (*niyoga*) or a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) can be accomplished by means of the syntactical connection of word-meanings because it possesses a composite form, nevertheless, since Brahman consists of the sentence-meaning itself and is an indivisible single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*), there is no injunction regarding its knowledge.
The meaning is that the procedure is easy to perform. || 18 ||
Where valid cognition, invalid cognition, and even the semblance of valid cognition all produce valid knowledge, how can there be any doubt regarding its possibility? (19)

Having raised the doubt that Brahman cannot exist because it has been stated to be "not consisting of the meaning of words," he says: "It is the means of valid knowledge" (pramāṇa). The meaning is that since Brahman—which is by nature eternal perception—is established as the very ground that makes possible the means of valid knowledge and so forth, there is no such impossibility regarding it. || 19 ||
Why is it that the scriptural statement [of an injunction] does not have its authority based on this [perception]?
Even the validity of an injunction (niyoga) does not exist without depending upon this means of valid cognition (pramā).

Anticipating the objection— "If injunctions regarding knowledge are not accepted in the Vedāntas, how can they possess authority?"— he states "prāmāṇyam" (authority) to show that the authority of the Vedāntas is established without contradiction even without an injunction, by virtue of their being the cause of that knowledge which removes ignorance and its effects, which abide in the previously mentioned immutable experience. Furthermore, as for the injunction...

Since you maintain that the validity of that [scripture] is due to its power to exclude the association with the *ga* (the suffix), and since it is impossible to accept the authority of an insentient *niyoga* (injunction) without the aforementioned experience (*anubhava*), one must therefore admit the previously mentioned experience as the means of establishing the *niyoga*. With this in mind— that there is no point in accepting a *jñāna-niyoga*— he says:
"Ha—of the injunction. || 20 ||

The sentence beginning with "One should perceive the Self" (paśyed ātmānam) and so forth is an injunction regarding the necessity of performing the act of knowledge, directed toward the person who is to be enjoined. (21)

Furthermore, regarding the acceptance of injunctions (*vidhi*) in the Vedāntas, one might argue that the establishment of Brahman results either from an injunctive sentence or from another type of sentence; having thus raised the alternative, [the author] refutes the first position—that an injunctive sentence has its purpose fulfilled by the injunction alone and thus possesses no authority regarding the reality of the thing (*vastu*)—with the verse beginning "paśyet" (he should see). || 21 ||

Since speech, without even depending upon its own function, directs a person toward the actual state of things, therefore the actual state of things is very difficult to attain. (22)

Since an injunctive sentence impels a person to action by means of its own operation, without depending at all on the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*), it does not establish the reality of the object; this very point is proven by the words "its own operation" (svavyāpāre). || 22 ||
If a task is beyond one's own capacity, even if one is enjoined by hundreds of words, it cannot be accomplished; for he alone is the master over what is possible. (23)
Having granted for the sake of argument that knowledge is something to be performed (*vidheya*), he states that this is not actually the case with the words "by its own power" (*svaśakti*).
For regarding that effect called knowledge— which cannot be done, not done, or done otherwise by the person—
even if a person is enjoined by numerous statements such as "it should be seen," he does not attain independence in the accomplishment of that knowledge.

Since knowledge, which is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object (*vastu*), lacks dependence on a person, a person is indeed independent and autonomous regarding sacrifices and the like; therefore, because knowledge is incapable of being conjoined with an injunction (*vidhi*), there is no injunction in that regard—this is the meaning. || 23 ||

One should diligently inquire about the denotation, the scripture, and what is established thereby; for, by following the injunctive sentences, it [the word] does not touch upon the object independently.

He raises the second alternative—that the reality [of Brahman] is established from statements such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), which are distinct from injunctive sentences—by the word "abhidhā. He refutes this by stating "vidhi," [meaning] that even the scripture of denotation (abhidhā-śruti) follows an injunction and thus lacks independent power to establish the reality. || 24 ||
They even eat their own flesh, never transgressing their commands.

Indeed, for the sake of what is possible, they may even give up their dear lives; for even one enjoined to perform an impossible task [is not required to do so], as in the case where it is said, "one should offer kṛṣṇala-berries. (26)

Because knowledge does not depend upon a person, a person is unable to produce it; regarding this, he provides a counter-example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta): "one's own flesh. Just as when one is enjoined to "cook the kṛṣṇala berries"—a cooking of kṛṣṇalas that results in softening which is entirely impossible—even an intelligent person does not proceed to act, so too [in the case of knowledge].
Furthermore, when even the cooking of a *kṛṣṇala* seed is impossible, the discerning person, being directed toward that knowledge, [desists] through the cognition of its impossibility.

Therefore, since one is not able to engage in that [knowledge] by one's own power, an injunction is not appropriate with respect to knowledge that is not dependent on oneself.
He clarifies this by means of an example based on similarity: "From that too," [verse 25] [verse 26].
Even if he were to do so with his whole being, he would act like the bulb of a *taskara* plant. || 27 ||
The arising of the knowledge of Brahman depends upon the grace of the Guru;
for this is established by the logic of "as that, so that," as well as by Śruti and Smṛti. (28)

If, however, this person to be enjoined were to perform even that knowledge which is impossible to accomplish in its entirety solely by the force of the injunction, then— acting in accordance with the injunction alone while disregarding his own capacity—
he would become a mere vessel for suffering and would not attain the human goal (puruṣārtha) he desires; thus, he states [this] with an illustration:

Regarding the phrase "with his whole self": a certain man, having committed a theft, entered a nearby gambling house (*kandugṛha*) in order to conceal his own crime. He was then appointed by the master of the house, the gambler (*kandu*), to perform the work of a gambler. Because he was assigned to a task for which he was unskilled, while performing that work, the king’s men—who were searching for the thief—suddenly arrived there.

The meaning is as follows: just as one who, having observed unskillfulness in the act of stealing and knowing "this man is a thief," is seized and comes to experience futile suffering—becoming like a "thief's pit"—so too, even though one is engaged in the knowledge of Brahman, because that [knowledge] cannot be produced by him, he would become a partaker of futile suffering while attempting to do so. || 27 ||

Anticipating the objection that knowledge may arise from meditative worship (upāsanā) even in the absence of an injunction regarding knowledge, he says "And not..."—meaning this is not so—because scripture and tradition declare that the fruit of meditation is distinct from knowledge, as it is heard [in those texts]. By the word "nyāya," the principle of "that for which something is done" (tatkratu-nyāya) is intended. || 28 ||

If the cultivation [of the idea] that does not crave for the object were not to produce the cognition of Brahman, then even a well-practiced cognition would not manifest itself to produce the cognition of mother-of-pearl. (29)
Furthermore, if meditation were to accomplish its object, it would not differ from knowledge, and thus one must admit that it does not touch upon the object;

consequently, its status as a means to knowledge is not established. To this he says: "Not the object... Having raised the objection that even if meditation does not touch the object, it may still become a cause for right cognition through the excellence of practice, he replies: "...well-practiced... (29).
If the Self were something to be seen, then there would be an injunction regarding the Self;
however, because seeing [the Self] is here prohibited, there is therefore no injunction concerning that which is beyond [the senses].

Anticipating the objection that there might be an injunction (*niyoga*) regarding the knowledge of the Self or its meditation based on the scriptural mention of "it is to be seen," [the author] states, "Not from seeing" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*),
etc.; since the status of being an object of seeing and so forth is denied, there is no injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self or its meditation.

The true nature of reality is awakened through the entry into injunction;
for that which merely restates [what is already known] lacks authority if it does not depend on an injunction. (31)

He raises an objection, stating that if an injunction (*niyoga*) is not accepted, the Vedāntas would lack authority as they would become mere restatements (*anuvādaka*); therefore, it is only by means of an injunction that they can convey the reality of things. (Verse 31)
It is not so, because here it is action alone that is enjoined by the injunctions;
for by means of them, a person can be directed toward their own specific activity.
Since the intrinsic nature of a substance is not something to be accomplished, how can it be set in motion by those [causes]? || 32 ||
Is an injunction intended with respect to the Vedāntas, the Self, or the knowledge thereof? He says:

The meaning is that since injunctions express only action as something to be performed within the sphere of injunctive practice, there can be no suspicion of an injunction regarding the Self. This is because the scope for a mandate (niyoga) exists only in the case of an object to be accomplished.
He establishes that [the objection] lacks any scope when the object [of knowledge] is established within itself, as follows: "In its own operation," etc. (Verse 32).
Nor is the knowledge of the Self enjoined here by scriptural injunctions, for that is established by the rule: "One's own Veda is to be studied. (33)

He says "nor" [to show] that the second [alternative] is not the case. Is it the knowledge of the Self derived from the word that is to be enjoined, or some other kind of knowledge? Just as the realization of ritual action does not depend on another injunction, so too the realization of the Self does not arise from another injunction. (34)

The capacity to fulfill the goals of man is attained by men, yet it is not attained. || 35 ||

Since the effect of knowledge is to be understood solely through injunction (*niyoga*), this [duty] cannot be established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor even by verbal expression. (36)

If the knowledge of the Self were not something to be enjoined, it would lack fruitfulness; yet its status as an injunction cannot be established without its fruitfulness, nor can its fruitfulness be obtained without its being an injunction. Therefore, he proposes another alternative for the sake of establishing its fruitfulness: "It might be thus," etc. (vv. 35–36).
This is not so, because here, apart from the mere pervasion of the object of knowledge, not even the slightest further result of awakening can be conceived. (37)

He refutes [the objection] with the words "Not so," [arguing that] since the ascertainment of the object of knowledge is the fruit of knowledge, and since that [ascertainment] is inseparable from the arising of knowledge, there can be no injunction regarding knowledge for the sake of that fruit. || 37 ||
Since the realization of one's own self is established even without an injunction, tell me: what would be the purpose of the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied"? (38)
If knowledge arises, then let the fruit—which consists in the manifestation of the object of knowledge—be established even without an injunction;
however, raising the doubt as to how the very arising of that [knowledge] could be established in the absence of an injunction, he recalls what was stated at the point "na cāpi" (nor even...
with the words "antareṇa" (without...). || 38 ||
It is not so, because this other cognition within the self is indeed distinct;
it is merely urged that the supreme [Self] possesses a means for its realization as an effect. (39)

"We do not say that the knowledge of the word is what is to be practiced; rather, it is another kind of knowledge, accompanied by means such as tranquility (śama) and self-control (dama), that is to be practiced"—thus he raises an alternative view with the words "not so" (naivam). || 39 ||
[It is] distinct from the cognition produced by words, and it pertains to another self. (40)

Being unmixed, having as its object a thing beyond the senses, and being absolute—by clarifying that it is indeed a distinct cognition, [the author] reveals its otherness with the words: "from the word" (śabdāt) || 40 ||

For Brahman cannot be determined by knowledge arising from words, because it is not of the nature of the meaning of a sentence, unlike a jar or similar objects. (41)
Anticipating the objection that "since Brahman is already established by verbal knowledge alone, the injunction of another form of knowledge is useless," he says: "Not so" (na hi). || 41 ||

For this meaning of a sentence is traditionally held by those learned in the science of sentences to be characterized by the connection of various word-meanings; yet that [connection] is not our [accepted] sentence.
And because that [Brahman] is not an object [of cognition], Brahman does not bear the form of the meaning of a sentence.

Anticipating the objection as to how Brahman can be of the nature of a non-sentential meaning (*avākyārtha*), [the author] states "not other" (*nānyā*) because he accepts that Brahman is an indivisible, single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*).

Anticipating the objection that its status as a non-sentential meaning is unestablished because it is admitted that the sentence is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, [he proceeds] while accepting that the sentence is indeed the means of valid knowledge regarding Brahman.
He refutes its status as the meaning of a sentence with the words "pramā" (valid cognition). || 42 ||
That [Brahman] must necessarily be admitted as cognizable by another cognition;
for if Brahman were not admitted to be graspable by the cognition arising from the [Vedic] sentence, [it would be unestablished].
If that were so, then the meaning of the sacred tradition would not exist, nor indeed would the meaning of the Veda.

Since it has been established that Brahman is not the meaning of a sentence, it follows by necessity that it is cognizable through a knowledge distinct from verbal knowledge; this is the point he states with the words "by another cognition" (*vijñānāntara*). He raises an objection: if Brahman were not the object of the knowledge arising from sentences, then the acceptance of Vedic sentences as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding it would be contradicted.

Regarding the phrase "if not": he refutes [the objection] by stating "it is not so," on the grounds that it is established that Brahman is the object of the doctrine, which is to be known through the knowledge characterized by direct realization—realization being achievable through the practice of knowledge arising from Vedic statements. || 43 ||
How can this [word] have the meaning of the Veda if it is not accepted as the meaning of the sentence? (44)
Because it does not depend upon human activity, this [result] cannot be a mandate (niyoga);
nor can the cognition arising from a sentence pertain to the Self through the connection of word-meanings. (45)
He restates the objection raised by the Siddhāntin—namely, "How so?"—as already explained. || 44 ||

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) offers this rebuttal: "By human activity" (*puṃvyāpāra*). He argues that because this meaning is to be accomplished through human effort—namely, the thought "this is the meaning of this sentence"—it cannot be established by your injunction (*niyoga*) or by the force of your command, since it is not something that can be brought about by such an act. [This applies to] the dharma arising from the sentence...

Anticipating the objection that Brahman might also be the meaning of a sentence because it is accessible through knowledge (*jñānagamya*), he says: "padārtha... (regarding the word-meaning).

The meaning is that because a word cannot be related to itself as its own referent, and because Brahman is not the referent of a word, it is distinct from dharma; therefore, Brahman is not accessible through knowledge produced by a sentence. || 45 ||

Even in that sequence, this [sentence] does not attain the status of being the meaning of a sentence, because if words were to denote only universals (sāmānya), there would be a total loss [of specific meaning]. (46)
Even if Brahman is connected [to other words] as the referent of a word (*padārtha*), it does not follow that it is cognizable through a sentence (*vākya*).

This is because a word has only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, whereas a sentence has the particular (*viśeṣa*) as its object; and although Brahman is a universal, it lacks the nature of a particular. Thus he says: "Even in its connection with that" (*tadanvaye 'pi*). In reality, however, Brahman by you— [The text ends abruptly.]
The meaning is: since it is accepted that [the object] is devoid of any specific state (viśeṣabhāva), how can there be the application of words to it? || 46 ||
And since there is no denoter of the sentence-meaning apart from the word-meanings, this certainty that "I am Brahman" does not have the form of a sentence-meaning. (47)
Furthermore, since Brahman is not the meaning of any word because it transcends the meanings denoted by words, and since that which is not the meaning of a word cannot be the meaning of a sentence,
there is no word that denotes or makes known Brahman, which is not the meaning of a sentence. Nor...

A word conveys Brahman through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Since that which is entirely devoid of being denotable cannot be the object of indication, he says "padārtha... [etc.]—meaning that because Brahman is thus not an object of verbal knowledge, it is therefore not the meaning of a sentence; rather, it is a different kind of non-verbal knowledge, having the form of an unmediated, non-referential intuition.

And since that [realization] is to be accomplished through the means of the practice of verbal knowledge, characterized by immediate (aparokṣa) cognition, he concludes—stating that Brahman, though distinct from that, is "authoritative based on the Veda" in a figurative sense—with the words "Therefore": "I am Brahman. Although the certainty arising from practice, which has the form of an unconditioned immediacy, is indeed a verbal cognition (*śābda-bodha*), [it is nevertheless so called].

Nevertheless, because it is produced from the accumulation of the practice of such awakening, it can indeed be said that the scripture is the authority regarding the duality within Brahman; this is the meaning. || 47 ||

It has been stated that the true nature of reality is [grasped] through the entry into the injunction (*niyoga*); therefore, the verse has been cited by us as previously explained in order to refute that view. (48)

He states the established conclusion (siddhānta) as the response to your objection— that the establishment of the reality [of Brahman] results from the force of logical necessity (niyoga) and not from the grace of the Veda— by means of the verse beginning with "from which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1):
"niyogeti" || 48 ||

Ninth Section.
As long as there is the constant perception of the distinction—
"this is the object of knowledge," "this is the means of knowledge," and "I am the knower"—
ignorance does not exist in relation to these. (49)

Anticipating the question of how this verse serves as the reason for resolving the aforementioned objection, [the author] establishes the fact that the manifold of non-self (anātma-prapañca) is merely imagined (*kalpita*) in order to prove that point—beginning with the words "This" (*idam*). [He refers to] the triad beginning with the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

The meaning is that because this Self always shines forth in its unmixed nature, there is an absence of ignorance regarding it; since ignorance cannot exist toward that which is [thus] known, its status as an object of valid cognition is not established, and therefore it is a manifestation of nescience (*avidyā*), just like the [illusory] snake and so forth. || 49 ||
Apart from pure consciousness alone, no other form is possible for the witness of all cognitions;
likewise, there is no praise [of it] apart from the appearance of valid knowledge.

Raising the objection that since the conscious self (*cidātman*) is likewise always established and not accessible through the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible for it to exist apart from being unknown, and thus its being a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*) is equal [to that of the objects], he says: "The pure consciousness alone" (*cinmātra*).
Because the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the substratum of all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*), it is impossible to conceive of any other form for it as being imagined by ignorance.

This is the meaning. Having raised the objection, "If the Self is consciousness, how can there be a lack of manifestation as it truly is?", he says "due to the appearance of valid cognition" (*pramābhāsāt*), implying it is due to ignorance (*ajñāna*). By the word "non-manifestation" (*asphūrti*), a lack of clear perception is meant. || 50 ||
This [Self] is devoid of abandonment and acquisition; it is inherently eternal because it is their witness.
Its status as the witness of the seer and so forth also arises from its dependence on those causes.

By stating that the world is imagined (*kalpita*), it has been asserted that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is unimagined as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and is self-luminous (*svayaṃ-prabha*). Now, he declares its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*): "Neither loss... and so forth. Having raised the objection as to how that which is immutable can be a witness (*sākṣin*), [the text] states that it is the cause of duality consisting of loss, acquisition, and so on.
He states that ignorance, along with its appearance, constitutes its status as a witness by virtue of being supported by it, in the verse beginning with "draṣṭrādi" (51).
The cognition "I know this" or "I do not know this" undergoes transformation;
it must have recognition as its basis, for the seer alone possesses both forms.

If it is said that the self’s status as a witness arises from ignorance, then—since knowledge and ignorance must have a single locus—one would have to admit that the self is connected with knowledge just as it is connected with ignorance; this would result in the loss of its quality of being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "This [is the intellect]. The intellect is the *ahaṃ-vṛtti* (the function of "I-ness"); it is that very thing which appears in the form of both knowledge and ignorance. Thus, [the self remains] unattached.

The meaning is that the state of possessing distinctions (saviśeṣatva) is established for the enjoyer (rāmaṇaḥ). Having raised the objection that because the mental modification of "I" (ahaṃvṛtti) has the Self as its locus, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the Self possesses distinctions, [the author replies] that because the modification of recognition (pratyabhijñāvṛtti) has the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as its locus, [the Self remains free from such distinctions].

Since it is accepted that the mental modification (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*) has its locus in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as determined by [the reflection], there is no suspicion of the Self possessing attributes (*saviśeṣatva*).

To this he says: "Excessive over-extension" (*atyabhijñā*). Since the function of the ego-sense (*ahaṃvṛtti*) has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its locus, it follows that the internal organ itself must be admitted as the substrate for experiences consisting of both knowledge and ignorance; thus he says: "Just as in the case of the defective [organ]" (*duṣṭeva*). || 52 ||
But because it is of an indivisible nature and transcends all sheaths,
it is not logical for its form to be manifold like that of the self, as it is the basis for recognition.

Anticipating the objection that knowledge and ignorance must be admitted to have the self as their locus because they appear as residing in the self, he says: "Nirvibhāga... [The self is] without parts; for the self, like the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), does not possess manifold forms.

This is not tenable because it transcends all sheaths; therefore, the meaning is that only that which is the internal organ (*antahkarana*) in its collective sense, designated as "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*), is subject to the distinction between knowledge and ignorance. || 53 ||
One who possesses mindfulness recognizes a transformed form obtained from another source, being refined by the perception of the object. (54)
He clarifies that it is devoid of reason to claim that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the locus of the alternatives of knowledge and ignorance by stating:

"By recollection... The agent of the ego (*ahaṃkartā*), which is subject to transformation and is a composite, is called the "knower. It is conditioned by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of objects produced from the experience of previously arisen cognitions; as the perceiver of objects, it attains a state of transformation—

Having recollected a form, preceded by that recollection, one recognizes it as "this is that" or "I am that. Furthermore, just like the cognition of synthesis residing within the internal organ along with its appearances, even ignorance and the rest—because they reside therein and do not abide in the immutable experience—are perceived there through conceptual construction; this is the meaning. || 54 ||
This conformity to external objects may be a defect of the intellect;
however, because of its immutability, this [defect] does not exist in the Self, which is inward-looking and of the nature of consciousness.

However, regarding those who assert that the inner self (pratyagātman) alone is the knower, he says "of the intellect" (buddheḥ). The transformation into the form of the object and the form of the self is established as belonging to the intellect alone; a transformation in the self is not tenable, because it is immutable (kūṭastha)—this is the meaning. || 55 ||
By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep,
one should exclude the external form of the intellect and illuminate the Self as pure consciousness alone.
One should always discern the meaning of the sentence through the intellect, because it is never subject to deviation.

[Page 188] 9. The Ninth Section. Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
"And because there is sublation of that which is subject to deviation, [the cognition arising from] the form of 'That thou art' and so forth..."
It burns away all ignorance and indeed brings about pure awakening. || 57 ||
By refuting the idea that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is accessible through injunctions (*niyoga*), and for the purpose of establishing that it is accessible solely through scripture (*śabda*),

[the text] demonstrates its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), its quality of being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*), and its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*), [showing that] the duality of the knowable and so forth is merely imagined (*kalpita*).
Its second nature has already been stated. Now, he establishes that the inner self (*pratīc*) is cognizable solely through words, beginning with the verse starting "anvaya" and so forth.

Because it is subject to deviation throughout the three states, all external non-self entities—which are graspable by the intellect and take on the form of the intellect—are [excluded] by relying upon the scriptural reasoning known as *anvaya* (positive concomitance) and *vyatireka* (negative concomitance), which is denoted by the term "reflection" (*manana*).

Having set aside [all else], because pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is eternally non-deviating, the seeker of liberation— who has become established by grasping that very pure consciousness as the referent of the term *tvam*, which is of the nature of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), consisting of the non-verbal meaning (*avākyārtha*), and incapable of syntactic connection with other sentence-meanings— possesses a cognition arising from sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) in the form "I am Brahman."

The meaning is as follows: it is accepted that the function [of the Mahāvākya] burns away the ignorance residing within the self and its effects by virtue of being inseparable from its own arising; thus, it brings about the realization of the identity of the "Thou" (tvam-artha) with Brahman and the identity of Brahman with the "Self" (ātman), which is devoid of all distinctions. Therefore, it is correct that Brahman is accessible through verbal testimony alone. || 56 || 57 ||

Just as in the case of "the pot" and "that which is other than the pot," there would be no sentence-meaning arising from grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth due to their mutual exclusion;
likewise, for us, there is no direct sentence-meaning between the referents of *tat* and *tvam*.

Lest it be argued that if the mutual inherence of Brahman and the Self were to be understood through words, there would be no cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) from the words alone, [the author] says:

"Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), etc. Just as in the case of "The pot-space is the great space," where by the removal of contradictory elements only "space" itself is understood, so too in the case of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), "That" and...

The meaning is that, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words, and because of the relationship of qualifier and qualified between their expressed meanings, as well as the relationship of the indicated and the indicator between the words and their respective meanings, the sentence-meaning— which is characterized as a partless, single essence resulting from the exclusion of the contradictory portions of the referents "That" (*tat*) and "Thou" (*tvam*)— is directly realized from the sentence itself. || 58 ||
Since the meaning of a sentence is established directly from the sentence itself, [the claim that] "this is something entirely different" and so forth would be nothing but mere threshing. (59)

Since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs in this manner from the word alone, it is improper to state that another cognition—distinct from the verbal cognition—is what is to be enjoined; this is the conclusion stated in the verse beginning with "vākyāt" (from the sentence). || 59 ||

Ignorance, erroneous knowledge,
and even doubt are observed only in relation to objects such as a jar, and not in relation to the knower, the act of knowing, or the witness-consciousness.

Anticipating the objection that even if the meaning of the sentence is established through verbal knowledge alone, another form of knowledge must be enjoined for the purpose of removing ignorance and so forth, he says: "Ignorance... (verse 60).
To begin with, the triad beginning with ignorance does not exist even in the cognition itself;
for that [cognition], being immediate, has no means of knowledge other than direct perception.
"Since neither doubt nor certainty regarding the knower arises as a cognition without mediation, no other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is required. Thus,
in the Vārttika, it is stated through both summary and detail that the triad beginning with ignorance does not exist within knowledge.

He shows this by means of two [verses]: "due to ignorance, etc. The word "api" (also/even) is intended to indicate the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the maxim of "how much more so") which will be explained later. || 61 || 62 ||
To begin with, even in the knower, the triad beginning with ignorance does not exist;
how much less so in the absolute Self, whose vision is never impaired? (63)

He says, "The triad beginning with ignorance," because even in the case of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the triad does not exist, since that too is directly perceived by the witness (*sākṣin*) through immediate proximity. Now, he establishes the proposition that "the triad does not exist in the witness" by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic: "What need be said... Since even for the knower and so forth [the triad does not exist] solely by the grace of the Self...
Since [the Self] is established even there, the triad beginning with ignorance is not possible; how much less so in the case of the Self, which is the witness?

Therefore, no further knowledge need be enjoined for the purpose of removing ignorance and the rest; rather, the meaning is that through the very knowledge arising from the authoritative word (śabda), the illusory ignorance and so forth are removed from the Self. || 63 ||

This [state], in which all differentiation has been shaken off and which consists of that which is not the meaning of words, is likewise apprehended by us in deep sleep; it is not unreal, owing to the authority of the Veda.

Furthermore, since the Brahman-Self—which is devoid of distinctions and consists of that which cannot be expressed by words—is experienced during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), no other knowledge need be enjoined for its realization; thus he says: "Nirdhūta... (It is shaken off). Nor should it be said that the aforementioned reality of deep sleep is false, for its perception is established by such scriptural passages as, "When one does not see there... and so forth.
He states that this is because it is rooted in the Śruti: "Not untruth" (64).

Because it is always of the nature of the Self, it is free from deviation and is eternal.
That knowledge which is self-established in the Brahman-Self and which dispels delusion—|| 65 ||
Having raised the objection that another cognition must be enjoined with respect to the Self for the purpose of removing ignorance and so forth, [the author] refutes it;

and in that very context, he states another reason: "And always," etc. Since it is the consciousness that is the very nature of the Self, manifested by the mental modification (buddhi-vṛtti) arising from the [great] sentence, that serves to remove ignorance and the rest, how could there be any need for an injunction regarding another cognition?
The meaning is "he dwells. || 65 ||
In this [Self], there is the distinction between the known and the unknown, as well as the nature of knowledge and ignorance;
likewise, the state of being a knower and not being a knower is established by itself, and not by a witness (sākṣin).

If it is argued that since the world—consisting of the known and the unknown, and knowledge and ignorance—actually exists within the Self, there is a need for the knowledge of its distinction (from the Self) in order to bring about its cessation, [the author] says "no," stating: "The known...
Since the world, consisting of the known and the unknown, and knowledge and ignorance, is established by the Witness Himself from His own perspective, its existence [is self-evident].

Since the two [the world and the knower] are dependent upon the Witness (sākṣin) and are therefore merely imagined, duality is not established therein in an ultimate sense. Likewise, even the status of being a Witness does not possess any real existence for the Witness itself. Consequently, in reality, an injunction for knowledge cannot exist for the purpose of removing the world—which consists of the means and the end of action.
Such is the meaning. || 66 ||
Even an injunction regarding one's own activity compels a person by force;
however, the fact that cognition possesses its object as it truly is is a reality of things themselves, not something produced by human effort.
Regarding the statement that there is no injunction (*vidhi*) in the case of valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*), he states another reason: "In its own operation" (*svavyāpāre*).

For an injunction impels a person toward an action by virtue of its own efficacy; however, valid cognition, being dependent upon the object of knowledge (*prameya-vastu*), is not fit for an injunction. Therefore, it cannot be something to be enjoined—this is the meaning.

Anticipating the objection that knowledge must be treated as something to be enjoined (vidheya) in order for it to convey its object as it truly is, he refutes this with the verse beginning "yathābhūta... (67).
"Endurance" means:
why does one not understand the meaning [of "That thou art"] through the scriptural statement alone, just as one understands it even without a formal ritual procedure? //68//

Furthermore, just as from the Karma-kāṇḍa knowledge of the meaning of ritual sentences is possible apart from an injunction, so too from the Brahma-kāṇḍa knowledge of Brahman is possible apart from an injunction, since there is no difference between the two cases; thus he says: "This... (68).

The application of an injunction regarding an action does not result in the establishment [of the action] within the agent and so forth;
nor is it accepted that a single sentence possesses multiple meanings. (69)

He states another reason for the fact that neither the self nor the knowledge thereof can be objects of injunction, beginning with the words "In an action" (kriyāyām). Furthermore, if knowledge were an object of injunction, the sentence would be intent upon enjoining knowledge; consequently, since the reality [of the self] could not be established from that very [injunction], one would have to accept a separate sentence to convey that reality. Thus he says: "And not... (na ca) || 69
This distinction between the expression and the injunction is established through direct perception itself;
if that [perception] were subject to error, then the teaching of the Omniscient One would be rendered useless. (70)
Anticipating the objection that every sentence is merely injunctive and none is capable of making known an existing reality, he says: "From perception alone," and so forth.
By the word *niyoga*, an injunctive sentence is understood. [This refers to the fact that] sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*)...

that very same non-dual supreme knowledge, which dispels delusion, has now been explained.
He recites a verse to proclaim the connection between the preceding and the subsequent sections: "Truth," etc.

That Brahman, whose nature consists of truth, knowledge, and so forth—which was described in the passage "he who knows it as abiding in the cave of the heart" as being the very essence of the inner self (pratyagātman)—is non-different from and unified with that supreme knowledge which has become the inner self.

And it has been stated that "that very [knowledge] is the remover of delusion. The meaning is that it is the knowledge of the true nature itself, as delimited by the mental modification (buddhivṛtti) arising from the sentence, which removes ignorance. || 1 ||

Now, desiring to explain [the means], the Śruti proceeded toward the attainment of that which is the most effective instrument for achieving the aforementioned knowledge. (2) Having restated the purport of the Ānandavallī, he states the purport of the Mṛguvallī: "Desiring to explain," etc.
The meaning is that the *Bhṛguvallī* proceeds for the purpose of presenting the means for the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, which removes ignorance along with its effects. || 2 ||
"Our sacred tradition (śruti) declares that [the knowledge] must be imparted by the Guru alone, from the Teacher;
therefore, this narrative is told in the form of a disciple and a sub-teacher."
Why is this creeper presented in the sequence of disciple and teacher? To that he says: "By means of the guru... (Verse 3).

206. Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[In the section on Bhṛgu]: "Recite, O Blessed One, Brahman"—this is what is expressed by this mantra; for the word "recite" (*adhīhi*) contains within it the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). (Verse 4)

Having shown the purport of the narrative and stated the intention of the two preceding sentences, he says "Adhīhi" to indicate that the third sentence is for the purpose of presenting the mantra for approaching the teacher (*upasadana*). He explains that the word *adhīhi* occurs in the sense of "teach" (*adhyāpaya*), because the literal meaning [of "study"] is impossible in this context. Thus he says: *antarṇī-*...
Thus [ends section] 4.
Desiring to know the Supreme Brahman, preceded by faith and devotion, one of purified intellect should approach a venerable teacher with this mantra: (5)
He shows the application of the mantra regarding the meaning already stated: "The seeker," etc. (5).
Having turned away from worldly enjoyments that fall short of liberation, Bhṛgu asked his teacher Varuṇa, "Teach me the Supreme Brahman."
Just as mental purity is a qualification for the seeker at the time of approaching the teacher, so too is dispassion; thus he says, "from liberation.
"Teach" means cause to remember, that is to say, cause to know. || 6 ||
"Food is life," and so forth— Varuṇa told Bhṛgu that food is the cause of the body, while life-force (prāṇa) is the cause of the vital breaths and so on.
The eye, the ear, the mind, and speech are the instruments for perception.

He introduces the two statements beginning with "Therefore, this... with the word "Food" (anna). He explains the distinct meanings of the terms "food," "prāṇa," "eye," and so forth, with the word "Body" (deha). The meaning is that the air alone, possessing various functions, is the cause of the fivefold modifications such as prāṇa and the rest; thus it is the "maker of prāṇa and the rest" (prāṇādikāraṇa). || 7 ||
Positive and negative concomitance serve to perceive either the agent or Brahman. (8)

Or rather, for the sake of bringing about the manifestation of the characteristic of the ineffable *bhūman*, the attributes of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) are taught in such passages as "Food is breath" and so forth. (9)
Anticipating the objection—"Why is there a mention of food and so forth for Bhṛgu, who asked, 'O Brahman, instruct me'?"—it is said:

The mention of food and so forth is made for the purpose of explaining that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as a means to the knowledge of Brahman; namely, that because food, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the rest are subject to change, they are not the Self (*anātman*), like a garland and such, whereas the Self is that which is invariable.

Thus, the scriptural text "the life-breath of the life-breath" would be properly relied upon;
and the scriptural passage concerning ritual action, beginning with "speech," is likewise appropriate for Brahmanhood. (10)

Alternatively, objects such as food and so forth are mentioned here through positive and negative concomitance for the sake of engaging [the listener], so that there might be ease [of understanding]: "How indeed might this be? (11)
He concludes the first position with the words: "food and so forth. (11)
That which, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects, does not transcend the nature of Brahman during origination, persistence, and destruction—let that be recognized as Brahman. (12)

He states the purport of the passage beginning with "He said to him" as follows: "In [the section on] origination. The definition of that Brahman which was asked about is stated in the passage beginning with "from which," etc. The meaning is that the definition of Brahman, in its state of being the goal (tārthya), is that Brahman is the cause of the origination, maintenance, and dissolution of the world. || 12 ||
Desire to know that Brahman which has such characteristics:
it is unarisen and undecaying, despite the arising and passing away of the world. (13)
He states the intended meaning of "desire to know that" and so forth: "Desire to know. || 13 ||
Having heard that, Bhṛgu performed penance for the sake of attaining Brahman;
he undertook an unmentioned austerity because of the reason for what had been left unsaid.

He states the meaning of the phrase "he performed austerity" with the word *tapaḥ*. He gives the reason for accepting the austerity—which was not mentioned by his father—as being equivalent to knowledge with the word *pratipede* || 14 ||

208 Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[Bhṛguvalli]: Even after defining Brahman by way of specific illustration as "that from which food comes forth," [it is further explained: "Brahman is that from which food comes forth."
The father said: "Therefore, Bhṛgu himself practiced ascetic penance. (15)

He elucidates what was stated [in the previous verse] regarding the reason for the statement being incomplete with the words "the horn," etc. Although Brahman was directly declared as the inner self (*pratyaktvena*) through the passage beginning with "Food is life" (*annaṃ prāṇam*), [the author] nevertheless stated the definition of Brahman, "From which indeed these... (*yato vā imāni*), as a defining characteristic (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the means for its realization as the inner self has not yet been stated.
The meaning is that Bhṛgu himself understood even this austerity. || 15 ||
Since Brahman was not explicitly specified by the statement of its definition,
Bhṛgu certainly expects a suitable means for the knowledge of Brahman.

If Brahman had been pointed out directly as the Self by the father in the passage beginning with "Food is indeed life," then the statement of its definition in the passage beginning with "From which indeed these... would have been unintended. Therefore, the father generally seeks a suitable means for the purpose of attaining the direct realization of Brahman as the Self.
He states that Bhṛgu conceived [this] at the time of practicing austerities: "Brahman... (verse 16).

From a particular kind of austerity, there may arise a desire for that which is not the ultimate reality as its means; for it is taught in the Smṛti: "That which is difficult to cross and that which is difficult to attain. (17)

Although the father may desire a means suitable for the attainment of Brahman, one might still wonder how that could be achieved by Bhṛgu through a particular austerity (*tapoviśeṣa*) in a single year; anticipating this doubt, he says: "by a particular austerity. He demonstrates, with supporting evidence, that austerity is the most effective means: "that which is difficult to cross... (Verse 17).
Austerity of the mind and of the senses—such is the internal austerity;
it is appropriate here, well-known, and indeed assists us from afar. (18)

He states the meaning of the word *tapas* (austerity) with the words "of the mind" (*manasaśca*). By the word "here" (*iha*), the context of the internal self (*adhyātma*) is understood. He excludes the notion that [austerity] refers to practices such as the *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* penances by saying, "but it is well-known" (*prasiddhaṃ tu*). || 18 ||

Alternatively, the contemplation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and so forth may constitute austerity (*tapas*), since this [austerity] is sufficient for the realization of the meaning of the statement "I am Brahman. (19)
— He states another meaning for the word *tapas* because it is relevant to the subject at hand: "By the connection," etc. [The state of being] a sentence—
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the thorough investigation of the intended meaning, the pursuit of specific means, and the reflection on specific results are included. || 19 ||

"Who am I? To whom do I belong? From where have I come? Who shall I become, and how?"—one who is in the stage of life dedicated to liberation (mokṣāśramī) should always possess such an intent regarding the purpose of existence.
Vyāsa has declared that from this very point on, austerity is for the sake of liberation for one who desires liberation.

He states the proof for the fact that the operation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is an internal means toward the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence: "Who am I? (verse 20).
And because it begins with "yato vā," this very thing has been declared as the supreme austerity. || 21 ||

Having performed austerities with diligence, endowed with the characteristics already described, [one realizes] that "Food is Brahman," because it is connected to the origin and other states of all beings. (22)

Since the elements (bhūtas) possess non-selfhood due to their participation in birth and so forth, whereas Brahman possesses selfhood due to its freedom from those [characteristics], this definition statement is also set forth because it intends to express that very point through the method of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Thus he says: "Because... (yataḥ). || 21 ||
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "Having performed austerity" (sa tapastaptvā) by saying "It has been said" (uktā).
Thus ends the first section (khaṇḍa). || 1 ||

The meaning is that Bhṛgu, having determined that austerity known as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the means for the knowledge of Brahman, and perceiving that the definition stated by his teacher applies to food, concluded that "food is Brahman.
He establishes the fulfillment of the definition of Brahman in food with the words: "Of beings... (22).

Those [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) have been described; their causes, however, such as food and so forth, must be understood, for the definition of a cause does not reside in its effect.
He states that the causes of the meanings of the suffix *mayaḥ* mentioned in the Ānandavallī are denoted by the words "food" (*anna*) and so forth, saying:

"They have been stated. He provides the reason for the point already stated—that because the *annamaya* and the others are effects, they cannot possibly be the cause of the origin of all beings and so forth—saying: "For not... (23).
For this [bliss] consisting of food is indeed pure, arising from food and so forth;
therefore, through the dissolution of the effect according to the Śruti, one attains the bliss of the cause.

He establishes that the food-sheath (*annamaya*) and the others are effects by means of the word "sprout" (*śuṅga*). "Sprout," "effect," and "product" (*kārya*) are synonyms. He states the conclusion regarding the fact that the food-sheath and the others are effects as described: "Because they are effects," etc. (24).

Having thus dissolved all effects into their respective causes, and those causes in turn into each subsequent one, one should proceed to the supreme bliss that is beyond the reach of speech. (25)

Fearing that one might object—namely, that by stating "the knower reaches bliss which is the cause through the dissolution of effects," the reality that is distinct from cause and effect and is to be approached by the liberated has been overlooked—he says:

"The effects... [referring to the passage beginning with] "annamayāt. The suffix *mayaṭ* in *annamaya* and so forth signifies the material cause (*prakṛti*), and thus food (*anna*) is to be dissolved within its own causes.

Having dissolved the vital breath into the vital breath, the mind into the mind, and the intellect into the intellect— which is the cause of the entire universe— into that Bliss which is Brahman; and having, by the power of knowledge, dissolved that [intellect] into the inner Self, which is Brahman, the unmanifest cause distinct from both cause and effect, characterized by eternal purity and other such attributes, the knower culminates in that very form.
This is the meaning. || 25 ||

Having realized that food is Brahman and having observed its nature as something produced, Bhṛgu went again to his teacher to ask for the sake of dispelling his doubt. (26) He states the purport of the passage beginning with "tadvijñāya" (having realized that): "annam" (food). (26)
Having thus observed the defect of being subject to causal production in both food and Brahman,
he questioned the Supreme Brahman again and again until his thirst for knowledge was extinguished.

Just as, even after the knowledge that food is Brahman, because its nature as a body is still perceived and there is no cessation of hunger and thirst, [Nārada] again approached Varuṇa and asked, "Venerable Sir, teach me Brahman," in the very same way, although he had known the nature of breath, mind, and consciousness as Brahman, because their nature as effects was still perceived in each respective case—

Since it is impossible for [the student] to be free from desire due to the coolness [of the teacher's instruction], he went again to the Guru and asked about Brahman in order to pacify his longing for the deer; thus [the author] says "annādeḥ" (from food, etc.). The meaning is "from the vital breaths, etc. In this way, he illustrates the first section with an example. || 27 ||
As long as one who lacks the desire to know does not perceive the Supreme Brahman directly—as clearly as a bilva fruit placed in the palm of the hand—he does not turn back [from saṃsāra]. (28)

Anticipating the objection that the question would then never reach a conclusion, he states "as long as" (yāvat) [in verse 28], meaning that the completion of the inquiry occurs because the desire for further knowledge ceases immediately after the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra).
"Desire to know that Brahman through austerity"—by saying this again and again, he makes us understand here that the vision of the Self is attained by austerity alone. (29)
Even through the practice of questioning until the cessation of desire for deer and jackals, one seeks to know Brahman through austerity.

In this manner, through both positive and negative concomitance, Bhṛgu gradually came to know the Supreme Brahman within his own inner self by means of austerity alone.
He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Ānanda is Brahman" as follows: "By means of positive and negative concomitance," etc. (Verse 30).
Therefore, for this reason, those who desire to abandon the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) must always practice stainless austerity (tapas) for the sake of realizing the Supreme Brahman. 31.

Since it has been established that Brahman, which is established in the inner self (pratyagātman) through the austerity known as positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka), can be known through the [great] sentence, he states the resulting conclusion: "Because... (yasmāt). || 31 ||
Now, after that [section] which took the form of the narrative called "Vyutthāna," the Śruti itself explains the meaning with its own form and with great effort.

Since it was known by Bhṛgu, it is therefore called Bhārgavī;

Wherein this distinction between "you" and "I" immediately ceases—that is the Self, that is the supreme ether; therein knowledge is established. (34)

Raising the objection that because the word "bliss" (ānanda) refers to the cause— as seen in passages such as "From bliss alone [it arises]"— it cannot be established that it refers to Brahman, which is distinct from both cause and effect, he replies: "It is not so," because in the phrase "established in the supreme ether" (parame vyoman),
the word "ether" (vyoma) refers to the inner self (pratyagātman) which is free from both cause and effect.
"From you," [it is said]. || 34 ||

Wherein the selfhood of Brahman and likewise the Brahmahood of the self [are realized], the meaning of the sentence "I am Brahman"—which is indeed beyond the literal meaning of words—is thus understood from the sentence. (35)

Anticipating the objection that the unity of Brahman and the Self as previously described cannot be established because it is beyond worldly experience, he states— beginning with "The Self" (Ātma-tas)— that the nature of the Self as Brahman and the nature of Brahman as the Self are established solely from the Vedānta texts. || 35 ||
And he says: [page 215] 212 Sureśvarācārya’s *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*—[in the section on Mṛguvalayā]—*ga*. *gha*. "Because of the pervasion... [fragmentary].
Anyone else, too, by performing asceticism characterized by single-minded devotion like Bhṛgu,
casts out all five sheaths and attains supreme stability.
He states the meaning of the phrase "he who knows thus becomes established" as follows: "Another also," etc. (36).
Regarding that which was stated previously by the *Vallī*—namely, "the tail of Brahman is the foundation"—the wise man becomes firmly established in that very foundation. || 37 ||
He reveals the supreme foundation itself as Brahman, which is distinct from cause and effect—thus: "Brahman" ||37||
Or rather, this fruit is said here to belong to those householders who worship food;
for it is not logical to proclaim food and such as the fruit for those who have already attained their desires. (38)

By means of the passage beginning with "He who possesses food," etc., [the author] states another result—accepting the mention of the fruit of saguṇa-vidyā for the sake of praising the very knowledge under discussion—saying "food and so forth. That which is the fruit of possessing food and so on for those who meditate upon food and the rest is stated here for the purpose of praising this knowledge of Brahman; it is not by means of the fruit of saguṇa-vidyā.

The meaning is that praise is possible for knowledge devoid of qualities (*nirguṇavidyā*). Anticipating the objection—“Why should there not be a primary proclamation of fruits such as food and so forth for the knower of Brahman?”—he says: “It is logical” (*nyāyyam*). || 38 ||
One who possesses luster becomes further endowed with food, a blazing digestive fire, greatness, and progeny;
indeed, luster is said to be the cause of tranquility, self-restraint, and the like, as well as spiritual splendor (brahmavarcasa).
He explains "annavān" and so forth with the words: "furthermore, one who possesses food. (39)
Thus ends the sixth section. 6.
Food alone is to be held in high esteem, because it is the cause of higher knowledge;
one should not revile food, for by that means the vow of its worshipper is fulfilled from the very beginning.

He states the meaning of "one should not revile food," and so forth, with the words "food. The meaning is that since food, once consumed, serves as the cause for the knowledge already described and yet to be described, it is necessary for the worshiper of food to refrain from reviling it, just as one would a teacher. ||40||

Because they are the cause of each other's existence, the relationship of eater and food is spoken of; this same determination applies to the body and the vital breath, and likewise to all subsequent pairs.

The reason is stated by the passage beginning with "the body is established," etc. The meaning is that the mention of "consisting of food" and so forth is to be understood everywhere as before. Water indeed is food; light is the eater of food. Earth indeed is food;
space is the eater of food. Thus, in both these pairs of alternatives, the aforementioned principle is extended.

"Thus"—it should be determined that fire (abjyotis) exists in earth and ether as the eater of food and the food itself, because they are the causes of each other's stability. The meaning is that the mention of the fruits, such as possessing food, is to be understood there as well, just as in the previous cases. || 41 ||

One should not reject what has been obtained; this shall be the vow regarding food.
One should prepare a great abundance of food, and likewise observe the subsequent vow here.

He states the meaning of the two sentences beginning with "one should not reject food," which concern the vow of the meditator who views the body and the vital breath as food and eater—that is, the non-rejection of food obtained—by saying: "obtained."
