Regarding the passage beginning with "One should make food abundant," he explains its meaning as follows: "Food... [Verse 42]. This means that for one who meditates upon water and light as the eater of food, the vow is to make food abundant.

One should never refuse such a person who has arrived for the purpose of lodging;

He states another position—that the state intended [to be distinguished] is threefold—with the words: "the state of age" (vayovasthā). || 44 ||

These two are intended to be expressed. Therefore, the meaning is that yoga and kṣema are to be meditated upon through the vision of Brahman as established in the prāṇa and apāna. By the word "karma," he indicates the meaning of the phrase "in the hands. || 51 ||
Likewise, Brahman is always to be meditated upon as "Gati" (the Goal) in the feet;
and as "Vimukti" (Liberation) in the anus—these are remembered as the human [mudrās]. 52.

He states the meaning of "the feet" as "the goal" with the word *tathā*. He indicates the meaning of "the anus" as "liberation" with the word *vimuktiḥ*. Liberation (*vimukti*) is the discharge of urine and feces; the sense is that Brahman, in that form, is established in the anus, and thus it is to be meditated upon. This is the meaning of the passage beginning with "human [functions]" (*mānuṣīḥ*).
The speaker provides the statement: "It is known as the Samāja. || 52 ||
Since this command of Viṣṇu pertains to the domain of human beings, the wise always describe it as a "human command" (mānuṣī ājñā). || 53 ||
He explains that very point: "By a human being," etc. (53).
Then, having invoked the goddesses, one should worship them in due order;
during the rain, one should meditate on "satisfaction," because satisfaction is consequent upon rain.
Now he explains the meaning of "daivīḥ" with the word "atha"; and he explains the meaning of "vṛṣṭau" (in the sense of "tṛptau ratim," i.e., delight in satisfaction) with the word "vṛṣṭau. || 54 ||
In that same manner, one should contemplate the subsequent [limbs] as well;
one should worship Brahmā in the organ of generation (upastha) as consisting of qualities such as procreation and the like.
With the word "tena" (by that), he extends the aforementioned principle to the passages beginning with "strength in lightning.

The meaning is that meditations should be performed on Brahman as it is established in lightning in the form of strength, in cattle in the form of fame, and in the stars in the form of light. He explains the passage beginning with "procreation" with the words "brahma" (Brahman). || 55 ||
Procreation—consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth—is immortality for the father; bliss is the human goal in this world, and that too has its basis in the organ of generation. (56)

He explains the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*): "procreation" (*prajāti*). Through the non-interruption of the lineage, by means of purity and other such qualities, and through the arising of knowledge in the father, immortality (*amṛtatva*) comes to be. Furthermore, it is well known that sensual pleasure (*ānanda*) arises from the power of the organ of generation (*upastha*). Thus, Brahman characterized by the qualities of procreation and the rest resides in the organ of generation.
The meaning is that it should be meditated upon as "established. || 56 ||

"Everything is in space"—thus should Brahman be meditated upon by those who are composed.
For one who meditates on that space as the support of all, only that remains. (57)

He states the meaning of the phrase "all is space" by saying "space. Because space is the substratum of all, for one who meditates on Brahman as established in space in the form of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), the very fruit is the state of being the self of all; this is established by such scriptural passages as "in whatever manner... He says "the substratum of all" [to indicate this]. || 57 ||
One should meditate upon it as "the foundation"; he shall become possessed of a foundation.
For the fruit corresponds to the meditation, just as it is here. (58)

He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "That is its support" (*tatpratiṣṭhā*)—namely, that for the meditator, the very result is a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), because Brahman, established as the self of space, is characterized by the quality of being a support—with the words "That is its support.
He demonstrates that the principle shown regarding meditation on Brahman as having the quality of support applies to all forms of meditation with the words "Meditation... (verse 58).
One should worship [the Self] with the thought "I am great" (tad-maha); from that, the fruit follows:
he becomes great through progeny and so forth, just as the Śruti declares. 59.
He explains the meaning of "That Great One" and so forth: "That is Brahman. || 59 ||
One should meditate upon it as "the mind"; one becomes possessed of a keen intellect among men.
The meaning of "namas" is the state of being bowed; this is said to be its fruit.
The objects of the senses, which produce enjoyment, bend to his will according to his desire. || 60 ||

He states the meaning of "tanmana" and so forth: "tanmana iti. The meaning is that since Brahman, whose nature is space, is characterized by the quality of mind (manas), the fruit for the worshiper is the possession of a refined mind. He states the meaning of "tannama" and so forth:
"prahvībhāva iti" (the state of being humble). || 60 ||
"But he who should meditate upon that as Brahman, exactly as it has been described," (61)
"I have previously declared that the fruit of that [act] shall be exactly that;
at that time, the Brahman was indeed the death (parimara) of the Brahmin. (62)
He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "That Brahman" as follows: "But he who... (verse 61).

The phrase "as has been stated" indicates that Brahman has the nature of space (*ākāśātmatva*). Relying on the Śruti passage, "As he [meditates] upon it," he explains the declaration of the fruit with the word "fruit. In the preceding section, greatness was described by means of progeny and so forth. Bra...

But here, the distinction is "by means of knowledge" (vidyayā). He demonstrates the meaning of the sentence beginning with "that [is] of Brahman" (tad brahmaṇaḥ) as follows: [Tenth Section, accompanied by the commentary of Ānandagiri, page 217]

Regarding the phrase "of Brahman": the meaning is that for the worshipper who possesses the specific qualities of the *parimara* [the ritual of circumambulation] belonging to Brahman—that is, to the Brāhmaṇa, which consists of the nature of space (*ākāśa*)—that which is to be described in this meditation will be accomplished. || 62 ||
Since the Śruti declares that lightning, the moon, the sun,
and fire merge into the wind, it is for this reason that the wind is celebrated as "parimara" (the place of dissolution).

Anticipating the objection as to how space can possess the quality of being "appropriated" (parimara), he demonstrates its appropriateness by first relying on the scriptural teaching regarding the "appropriator" (saṃvarga) of air—namely, the passage beginning with "lightning. || 63 ||
This space is non-different from the wind and the ether of the Brahmas;
his enemies, whether they hate him or do not hate him, all die.

Anticipating the objection—"Even if air alone is subject to dissolution (*parimarana*), what follows for space?"—the author says: "Non-different" (*ananya*). This space is non-different from air, because it has that as its cause and is therefore of the same nature as it. Furthermore, space does not differ from Brahman, because it is its effect and thus lacks any existence apart from it.

Therefore, "space is the *parimara* of Brahman" means that Brahman has the quality (*guṇa*) of being the *parimara*. Thus, he states the fruit for the meditator who possesses such qualities: "And those who hate him... (64).

By the preceding [passage], beginning with "Breath indeed is food" and ending with "space," the scripture has declared the relationship of eater and food between the composite [body] and its effects, for it is indeed composed of effects.
How indeed is its state of being both the eaten and the eater perceived? || 65 ||

Having explained the meaning of the two sentences beginning with "He seeks after this" (*paryeṇam*), he reveals the intention behind showing that the conventional usage of "food" (*anna*) and "eater of food" (*annāda*) resides in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, by means of the passage starting from "The vital breath indeed is food" (*prāṇo vā annam*) and ending with "Space is the eater of food" (*ākāśo 'nnādaḥ*). [Thus: "The vital breath indeed... (65).
Let there not be attachment to that which is beyond the range of mind and speech.

Therefore, worldly transaction characterized by the eater, the food, and so forth, should be understood as having ignorance as its object; it does not exist in that which is characterized by reality and the like.
He states "of this very [one]" for the purpose of restriction, saying: "lest it be so. || 66 ||

218 Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika— [Bhṛguvallī]:
Transmigration, which resides in the non-self because it is a manifestation of ignorance regarding the inner self (pratyag-avidyā), cannot possibly exist in the Self.
The meaning is that it appears as superimposed upon the self through ignorance. || 67 ||

Arising from ignorance, characterized by the appearance of duality and the relationship between the enjoyed and the enjoyer—this is what the scripture beginning with "Where indeed there is duality" has taught us. (68)
Regarding that which was stated—that transmigratory existence arises from ignorance—he states the proof for it: "It arises from ignorance" (verse 68).

But where [the text says] "but where [there is this 'as it is']"—in that state characterized by the total destruction of all ignorance—it negates here, within the Self, duality which is always superimposed by ignorance. (69)
To show that, in reality, there is no transmigratory existence within the Self apart from ignorance, he cites scripture here as well: "But where [there is... (69).
And because of oneness, there is no saṃsāra characterized by action and agent; if it is asked "How so?", it is said: "He is that which is this. (70)

Having stated the scriptural authority for the fact that transmigratory existence is imagined through ignorance within the Self, he presents the logical argument for that very point—namely, "and because of oneness. He raises an objection: since the Self is non-different from Brahman, the transmigratory existence appearing therein must indeed be imagined; however, there is no proof for the Self's non-difference from Brahman.
Why? To establish the identity of the self with Brahman as the means of valid knowledge, he introduces the scriptural passage with the word "therein" (tatra). || 70 ||
Now follows the determination of that which was mentioned regarding power (*bala*):
how indeed does the wise man enjoy all objects of desire simultaneously? To facilitate the understanding of this matter, the supreme Śruti proceeded. (71)

Having stated the purport of these three sentences alone, he states the purport of the entire subsequent section with the words "together" (*saha*). The meaning is that the entire subsequent text beginning with "He who is this [person here]" (*sa yaścāyam*) serves as the definitive explanation of what was said in the phrase "he enjoys all desires together" (*so'śnute sarvānkāmānsaha*). He clarifies this very point by means of a question:
How so? || 71 ||
This third case ending is not used here in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*), for the logic regarding that has already been stated previously;
therefore, this third case here should be understood as indicating a characteristic state (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā*).

It has already been stated that the subsequent passage beginning with "sa yaścāyam... is intended to elaborate upon the attainment of all desires for the wise man, which was described as being of the nature of Brahman; this is further clarified by the phrase "brahmaṇā vipaścitā," where the instrumental case (third case) is used [to denote the instrument], and not [in the sense of] the Self. (Note: *mānāpti* in manuscript *ga* and *gha* is a scribal error for *sarvāpti*).

Having set aside what was not intended to be said, he states what is intended by means of the words beginning with "no" (na). The logical principle is that no difference is possible between the knower and Brahman. || 72 ||
Or rather, this instrumental case ending in the word "brahmaṇā" may have the sense of a cause;
for the consumption of all desires is possible only through Brahman. (73)
He shows another meaning of the third [case-ending] with the words "hetvartha" (having the sense of a reason). He elucidates that very same meaning in the form of a reason.
The commentator says: "All desires. The meaning is that since everything is nothing but Brahman, it is logical for the knower of Brahman to consume all desires by means of Brahman. || 73 ||
Since Brahman is the Self of everything that is devoid of self, and because it consists of the nature of truth, knowledge, and so forth, this very point is now being stated. (74)

It establishes that everything is nothing but Brahman with the words "of that which is without self" (*nirātmakasya*). Since it is accepted that Brahman is the self—that is, the essential nature—of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it follows that for that [world], which is naturally devoid of its own form, being Brahman alone is logical;
this is the meaning. Because Brahman consists of reality, consciousness, infinity, and bliss, it possesses ultimate reality. Since...

Therefore, he establishes that Brahman is the Self of the entire phenomenal world by the words "satya" (the Real) and so forth. He introduces the scriptural passage concerning the statement that Brahman is the Self of the entire phenomenal world with the words "tadetad" (this very thing). || 74 ||

The statement "He who is that" and so forth is indeed for the purpose of swallowing—that is, subsuming—the entire treatise concerning the eater and the food and so on, which is devoted to the knowledge of Brahman.
He states another intended meaning of the subsequent portion of the text beginning with "He who is that" as follows: "He who is that," etc.
The "swallowing" of the entire phenomenal world, which was introduced as consisting of the eater and the eaten, means its sublation by the power of knowledge.
For that purpose, the subsequent portion of the text beginning with "He who is this... is here stated as being primarily concerned with the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā).
Therefore, the meaning is that duality is to be sublated by knowledge, while non-duality is the ultimate reality. || 75 ||
Having transcended through knowledge all that arises from ignorance and is non-self,
he, by means of the Self, has attained the Self characterized by reality, invisibility, and so forth.

Having thus demonstrated the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he explains the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) with the words "having transcended" (*saṃkramya*). The wise one—having pierced through the five sheaths (*kośa*) which are non-self by means of the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self arising from such passages as "He who is this [Self]" and so forth;
and having realized the Self as the non-dual Brahman, whose nature is Being, Consciousness, and the like, and which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*aprapañca*)—remains established in his purpose.
The meaning is "by way of its true nature. || 76 ||

Being devoid of even the most excellent [knowledge], one [transmigrates through] these worlds born of ritual action. *Suresvarācārya-kṛtaṃ Taittirīyopaniṣad-bhāṣya-vārtikaṃ* — [Bhṛguvallī] — page 223, verse 220.
Eating at will and assuming forms at will, he wanders among the limiting adjuncts.

He states the literal meaning of the passage beginning with "having led these worlds and desires" (imāl lokān kāmān nītvā), etc., as follows: "The eminent," and so forth. The connection is as follows: the wise man under discussion, having become Brahman, being devoid of excellence and deficiency, remains moving along with the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) which appear through the persistence of what has been sublated. || 77 ||
For there is no direct movement for Brahman, who is changeless; indeed, the scriptural teaching states: "It is as if it meditates. (78)

Anticipating the objection that there is a movement [of the self] from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), he says "No" (na hi) to show that this is not so, because it contradicts both scripture and reasoning. || 78 ||
Seeing all these worlds as his own self because he is the self of all, the wise one remains with his purpose fulfilled, singing this equal Sāman.

Anticipating the objection as to how one who is wise and inactive can move through the worlds, and accepting that "moving" (anusaṃcaraṇa) is merely an experience according to the maxim "the path of the Buddha has the sense of going," he explains the passage beginning with "this is his Sāman" with the words "because of being the self of all. || 79 ||
All this is divided into two: food and the eater of food.
Let it be observed that I alone am this, whose nature consists of the seer and so forth, arising from Truth. (80)

Regarding the two Sāman chants beginning with "I am food, I am the eater of food," he states their meaning as follows: "In two ways. The meaning is that the entire world, divided into food and the eater of food, which consists of the real and the visible and so forth, is to be seen as being of the very nature of the Self;
this is the statement of the wise man. || 80 ||
The relationship between these two is that of the enjoyed and the enjoyer, as expressed in the verse:
"I alone am the Self as described; indeed, there exists nothing other than Me. (81)

"I am the author of the verse"—thus he explains the other *sāman* with the words "of those two. The meaning is: "I alone am the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the connection between those two. (81)
Seeing the self within the self as liberated from action and its factors, one should utter "triraho"; this is known as *stobha*, and it is intended to convey a sense of wonder.

In response to the inquiry as to who experiences [the world] as being identical with the Self, as previously stated, he qualifies that person by saying "Kriyā," in order to declare that it is indeed the knower (vidvān).
"Hā 3 vu hā 3 vu hā 3 vu"—this is the triad of *stobhas*; he states their meaning as "Viri. || 82 ||

The triple repetition here is intended to express reverence; thus it is accepted that "I am food.
This is stated for the sake of providing a means of practice for those people who lack faith. || 83 ||
In the passage beginning with "I am food" (*aham annam*), there is a threefold repetition; he states its purport as "the triple utterance.
The mention of "food" (*anna*) is an elliptical indication for both the one who takes the food and the one who composes the verse. (83)

I am indeed not possessed of that which consists of this embodied and unembodied [reality], whose nature is that of the eater and the eaten; for the Śruti declares: "The one born before that does not eat it. (84)

He states the meaning of the passage beginning with "I am" (aham asmi) as follows: "The embodied," etc. *Ṛtam* means truth; it refers to the five elements (*bhūtapañcaka*), which constitute the well-known entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the manifest and unmanifest, and comprising food and the eater of food. Being "born first"—existing prior to—that [world], I am in reality distinct from it. Regarding this, he provides the authoritative proof: "Not..."

The word "that" (tat) refers to the fact that the wise one, having become Brahman, is distinct from both effect and cause; and since his true nature does not exist apart from that [Brahman], it is logical that he stands beyond the twofold phenomenal world (prapañca), untouched by it—this is the meaning. || 84 ||
Even before the gods, I am the navel of immortality;
because of being the cause, I am the navel, or rather, the culmination and the very nature of immortality.

He explains the meaning of the phrase "pūrvaṃ devebhyaḥ" (before the gods) as follows: "devebhyaḥ" (from the gods). Since the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are grasped by the word *ṛta*, and the individual souls (*jīva*), which are mere reflections of consciousness, are grasped by the word *deva*, the meaning is: "I stand before them, pure, being devoid of the division between 'I' and 'not-I'. Regarding the phrase "amṛtasya," etc.:

He states the meaning [of the verse] with the words "the navel" (*nābhi*). Taking the well-known sense of "immortality" (*amṛta*), he establishes that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the "navel" by virtue of being its substratum, on the grounds of its being the cause (*kāraṇatvāt*). Then, taking the word "immortality" to mean liberation (*kaivalya*), he states another interpretation: that the very nature of Brahman, which is liberation, is indeed the inner self—thus [he says] "in me" (*manni-*).
Thus [it is said]. || 86 ||
But that glutton who eats me without first giving food to the worthy recipients— I, in turn, do not eat the food of that man who eats without offering.
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "I am food, eating the eater of food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2.1) as follows: "Without having given... (verse 86).
Whoever gives me, along with the appropriate place and time, to worthy recipients—giving food in this manner, such a person indeed protects me at all times. (87)

Having stated that one incurs demerit by not giving food in accordance with the place, time, and recipient, he says "He who me... (verse 87) to show that one partakes in prosperity by giving food accordingly.

222 Sureśvarācārya’s Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika—[In the Bhṛguvallī]:
I am of the nature of truth, knowledge, and so forth; [I destroy] everything arising from ignorance without remainder.
For I alone overwhelm them, just as the sun overcomes the darkness of night. || 88 ||

Having raised the objection that Brahman appears to be accompanied by the phenomenal world (*saprapañca*) because its qualified form was described in the passage beginning with "He who gives me," the author states the meaning of the passage beginning with "I am the universe" in order to dispel that doubt—namely, the word "Satya. The inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is devoid of cause and effect, is called "I. And that [Self] is the witness of all ignorance and the effects of ignorance.

The meaning is that [the Self], being manifested by the mental modification (vṛtti) arising from the sentence, overcomes— that is, sublates— it. Anticipating the objection that even when the inner self (pratyagātman) is manifested by the mental modification arising from the sentence, it will remove ignorance and the effects of ignorance only by taking up action or the practice of knowledge as auxiliary means, and not independently, [the author] says "suvar" and so forth.
He states the purport of the sentence with the words "For I... This Upaniṣad proceeds in this manner.

The meaning is that the wise person who realizes this Upaniṣad in the manner described becomes established as being of the very nature of that Brahman—the fearless, supreme bliss—and thus attains perfect fulfillment (nirvṛṇoti). || 88 ||
Thus ends the tenth section. || 10 ||

Having attained the Unborn One— who has utterly destroyed all defects and innate delusion— by means of their inward-turned consciousness, yogis of pure intellect, whose minds are firmly fixed in one-pointed meditation, [realize Him].
May He, into whom they enter—the one, stainless God—protect us. 89.
Now, summarizing the meaning of the two verses and showing it under the guise of a protective summary, he concludes with the words "dhyāna" and so forth:

meditation (*dhyāna*) is a continuous flow of cognitions directed toward the Supreme Self as the inner self; its "one-pointedness" (*ekatāna*) is the expansion of that [flow] into a single [stream], which is the state of being established in homogeneous cognitions; and its "density" (*nibiḍatva*) is the absence of heterogeneous cognitions.

Those whose minds are "concentrated in a single stream of meditation" (dhyānaikatananibida-hitacetasah)— meaning their minds have been withdrawn from all objects and established in that one-pointedness by being rendered continuous through the removal of intervening thoughts— are ascetics who possess the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana).

The connection is: "May He, whom the foremost renunciants enter, protect [us]. He shows that the Supreme Self is immutably established (*kūṭastha*) because it is free from all modifications such as birth and so forth, and is to be approached by the liberated—this is indicated by the word "That" (*tat*).
He states its eternal purity, consisting in the fact that its own ignorance and its effects have been dispelled, by the word "forever-purified" (*pradhvasta-*) and so on.

"Om," he said: "The Supreme Self, in whom resides all transmigratory existence— including innate delusion (*moha*) and its resulting defects such as agency (*kartṛtva*), which exist within His own self and as objects of support, appearing as a single, staff-like [non-dual] entity through the power of the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) arising from the Great Sentence (the Mahāvākya), and which is characterized by a specific state of destruction such that it can never rise again."

This is the construction [of the sentence]. He states that very [Self] possesses self-arisen lordship (*svayamprabhutva*), established by scripture and reasoning, with the word "the Divine" (*devam*).

He states its non-duality—its being without a second—by virtue of its being devoid of differentiation in every respect, with the word "one" (*ekam*). Since its eternal purity has already been described by the words beginning with "destroyed" (*pradhvasta*), he declares its eternal liberation with the word "stainless" (*amalam*). By what?

In response to the inquiry as to how renunciants enter the Supreme Self as described by the path, [the author] states "The Inner Self" (pratyak), etc., asserting that they enter it by means of the path of knowledge— having first accepted the Supreme Self under discussion through the purification of categories,
having known It directly as their own inner self (*pratyagātman*) by means of the sentence, and thereby entering It via that path of knowledge. For those...

He distinguishes those ascetics (*yatis*) who, through the attainment of knowledge, enter the Supreme Self, as being fit for that aforementioned attainment of knowledge— by means of the phrase "pure" (*śubha*). Having become renunciants of all actions through the gateway of discernment and dispassion arising from a stainless internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in dependence upon the performance of auspicious deeds consistent with their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), they possess the full complement of means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*).
May He, whom those endowed with virtue and desiring liberation alone enter by means of the knowledge of reality as it has been described, protect us;
that is to say, may He protect those who are established in Brahman and seeking liberation by granting Himself. || 89 ||
This is the supreme nectar of the Vārttika on the essence of the Taittirīyaka,
which is an exposition of the commentary composed by Maskarīndra.

Having briefly concluded the meaning of the two verses under the guise of a benediction, he now concludes the present *Vārttika* with the words "taittirīyaka... and so forth. A *maskara* is a bamboo staff. The venerable author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*), who is the most eminent among the renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) endowed with that [staff], composed this work belonging to the Taittirīya branch...

The commentary on the *Rasopaniṣad* is this very analysis; it is the nectar of the *Vārttika*, free from all defects and the means for attaining the unsurpassed human goal. The connection [of the sentence] is that the ascetic named Sureśa composed it. || 90 ||
Sureśa, the knower of the great meaning, out of devotion to him, composed [this work] for the ascetic Bhavanābhṛta, who was a caravan leader of those seeking liberation.

Thus ends the *Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārtika*, the work of the venerable Sureśvarācārya, the disciple of the worshipful Śrīmacchaṅkarabhagavatpāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya*).

He indicates the worthiness of this *Vārttika* for the learned by virtue of its being based on a traditional lineage, stating: "of the caravan-leader of those seeking liberation. Those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) are renunciants (*saṃnyāsin*) characterized by the fourfold qualifications; their "caravan" (*sārtha*) is their assembly, and the Blessed One exists as the one who leads it—that is, he functions as its guide therein.

The author of the commentary was a disciple of that foremost of ascetics, the blessed Lord Mahādeva— who bears the name Śaṅkara and is renowned everywhere by that very name— and he became famous in the world by the title Sureśvara. And he, in turn, fulfilled the command of that very teacher.
The construction is as follows: [he] composed the Vārttika exactly as stated, placing devotion to the Teacher alone at the forefront.
To the question of how a Vārttika composed through mere devotion can be accepted by the learned, he says: "He who knows the great meaning" (*mahārthavit*).
He is so called because he knows the "great"—that is, manifold and uncontradicted—meaning. And thus:
The meaning is that this Vārtika composed by him, being drawn from the essence [of the system], must indeed be accepted with faith by the elders. || 91 ||
Having bowed to the supreme and subordinate gurus, the Taittirīyaka-vārtika has been explained in brief, in accordance with the traditional lineage.
And may this very prophecy, producing joy in the Blessed One alone, endure for a long time in Kṛṣṇa, having abandoned the thirst directed toward others. (2)
Thus ends the commentary on the Taittirīyaka-vārtika composed by the venerable Ānandajñāna, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Śuddhānanda-pūjyapāda.
